abstract: In the analog VLSI implementation of neural systems, it is sometimes convenient to build lateral inhibition networks by using a locally connected on-chip resistive grid. A serious problem of unwanted spontaneous oscillation often arises with these circuits and renders them unusable in practice. This paper reports a design approach that guarantees such a system will be stable, even though the values of designed elements and parasitic elements in the resistive grid may be unknown. The method is based on a rigorous, somewhat novel mathematical analysis using Tellegen's theorem and the idea of Popov multipliers from control theory. It is thoroughly practical because the criteria are local in the sense that no overall analysis of the interconnected system is required, empirical in the sense that they involve only measurable frequency response data on the individual cells, and robust in the sense that unmodelled parasitic resistances and capacitances in the inter(cid:173) connection network cannot affect the analysis. I.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a practical obstacle in analog neural hardware: lateral inhibition circuits built with local resistive grids can spontaneously oscillate. These unwanted oscillations can make a circuit unusable. Designing against them is difficult when the grid contains resistances and capacitances whose values are uncertain or not explicitly modeled.

The proposed design method guarantees stability using mathematical analysis based on Tellegen's theorem and Popov multipliers from control theory. Its central practical feature is that the stability criteria can be checked locally. Designers use measured frequency responses of individual cells without having to analyze the complete interconnected circuit as one large system.

The analysis remains applicable even when the resistive interconnection grid contains unmodeled parasitic resistances and capacitances. This makes the guarantee useful for physical implementations, where the circuit includes more than its deliberately designed elements. The contribution is therefore both theoretical and operational: it turns a whole-network stability problem into measurable cell-level criteria while accounting for uncertainty in the connecting grid.
summary.tldr: Local measurements of individual circuit cells can guarantee stable lateral inhibition despite unknown resistive-grid parasitics.

title: A Method for the Design of Stable Lateral Inhibition Networks that is Robust in the Presence of Circuit Parasitics

paragraphs: The paper presents a programmable chip for implementing binary synaptic connections in electronic neural networks. It contains a 32-by-32 array of long-channel NMOSFET connection elements made in a 3-micrometer bulk CMOS process. The neurons remain off the chip, making the device a dedicated component for the network's connections.

This separation lets the synaptic chip act as a cascadable building block. Multiple chips can form a synaptic network as large as 512 by 512. The design therefore addresses scaling through the composition of connection arrays, with neuron circuitry supplied separately. The paper discusses performance in a 32-neuron breadboard used for an associative-memory application.

The authors also explore an alternative way to make weak connections: thin-film resistors placed in series with FET switches on CMOS test chips. Depositing and patterning the resistors adds manufacturing steps, but promises substantial savings in silicon area. This presents a concrete engineering tradeoff between fabrication complexity and the space occupied by synaptic elements.
summary.tldr: A programmable 32-by-32 synaptic chip supports larger multichip networks, while an alternative resistor-based connection design promises silicon-area savings.

title: Programmable Synaptic Chip for Electronic Neural Networks

abstract: An efficient method of self-organizing associative databases is proposed together with applications to robot eyesight systems. The proposed databases can associate any input with some output. In the first half part of discussion, an algorithm of self-organization is proposed. From an aspect of hardware, it produces a new style of neural network. In the latter half part, an applicability to handwritten letter recognition and that to an autonomous mobile robot system are demonstrated.

The proposed databases can associate any input with some output. In the first half part of discussion, an algorithm of self-organization is proposed. paragraphs: The paper proposes an efficient method for creating self-organizing associative databases. These databases associate inputs with outputs, making the relationship between an observed input and its corresponding response the central function. The work connects this idea to robot eyesight systems, where visual information must support useful recognition or behavior.

The first part develops the self-organization algorithm. The abstract also describes the resulting arrangement as a new style of neural network when viewed from a hardware perspective. This gives the proposal both an algorithmic side, concerning how associations become organized, and an implementation side, concerning the network that embodies those associations.

The second part demonstrates applicability to handwritten-letter recognition and an autonomous mobile robot system. These examples place the associative database in both a recognition task and a robotic setting. The contribution is therefore a self-organization method accompanied by demonstrations of use. Its relevance lies in connecting a general input-output association mechanism to concrete visual applications, including the perceptual needs of an autonomous robot.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing associative database is proposed and demonstrated in handwritten-letter recognition and an autonomous mobile robot system.

title: Self-Organization of Associative Database and Its Applications

abstract: We compare the performance of the modular architecture, composed of competing expert networks, suggested by Jacobs, Jordan, Nowlan and Hinton (1991) to the performance of a single back-propagation network on a complex, but low-dimensional, vowel recognition task. Simulations reveal that this system is capable of uncovering interesting decompositions in a complex task. The type of decomposition is strongly influenced by the nature of the input to the gating network that decides which expert to use for each case. The modular architecture also exhibits consistently better generalization on many variations of the task.

Simulations reveal that this system is capable of uncovering interesting decompositions in a complex task. The type of decomposition is strongly influenced by the nature of the input to the gating network that decides which expert to use for each case. paragraphs: This paper evaluates a modular neural architecture on a vowel recognition task that is complex despite having few input dimensions. The architecture contains several competing expert networks and a gating network that decides which expert to use for each case. The comparison is with a single network trained by backpropagation.

The simulations show that the modular system can discover useful ways to divide the task among experts. A central finding is that this division depends strongly on the information supplied to the gating network. The gate therefore influences the kind of specialization that emerges, making its input representation an important part of the overall learning setup.

Across many variations of the task, the modular architecture also shows consistently better generalization than the single-network comparison. The result connects two aspects of the design: dividing a complex recognition problem into expert responsibilities and choosing how to route individual cases. The reported findings make the gate's inputs consequential for both understanding the learned decomposition and interpreting the modular architecture.
summary.tldr: Competing expert networks generalize better on vowel recognition variants, while gating inputs strongly shape their specialization.

title: Evaluation of Adaptive Mixtures of Competing Experts

abstract: Neurons encoding simple visual features in area VI such as orientation, direction of motion and color are organized in retinotopic maps. How(cid:173) ever, recent physiological experiments have shown that the responses of many neurons in VI and other cortical areas are modulated by the di(cid:173) rection of gaze. We have developed a neural network model of the visual cortex to explore the hypothesis that visual features are encoded in head(cid:173) centered coordinates at early stages of visual processing. New experiments are suggested for testing this hypothesis using electrical stimulations and psychophysical observations.

We have developed a neural network model of the visual cortex to explore the hypothesis that visual features are encoded in head(cid:173) centered coordinates at early stages of visual processing. paragraphs: Early visual neurons encode features such as orientation, motion direction, and color in maps organized around retinal position. The paper starts from physiological observations that many neurons in early visual cortex and other cortical areas also change their responses with gaze direction. This means their activity reflects more than where a feature falls on the retina.

The authors develop a neural-network model to explore whether visual features could already be represented in coordinates relative to the head at an early processing stage. Retinal and head-centered coordinates answer different location questions. When gaze changes, a feature's retinal position can change even though its position relative to the head remains the same.

The model provides a way to investigate how gaze-dependent activity could support that coordinate transformation. The authors also suggest experiments involving electrical stimulation and psychophysical observations to test the hypothesis. The contribution is a computational account linked to proposed empirical tests; early head-centered encoding is the hypothesis being investigated.
summary.tldr: A visual-cortex model explores whether gaze-dependent responses support head-centered feature encoding early in visual processing.

title: Hierarchical Transformation of Space in the Visual System

paragraphs: Neighboring image regions often share a coherent underlying property, such as surface depth. Earlier unsupervised learning exploited that coherence to discover depth and interpolate it from nearby values. This paper addresses the important exception: a depth discontinuity separates surfaces that should not be averaged together.

The authors propose two approaches. One detects discontinuity cases and rejects them from the ordinary interpolation procedure. The other learns a mixture of specialized interpolators, recognizing boundary locations and selecting asymmetric experts that use information from the appropriate side rather than crossing the boundary.

The contribution extends coherence-based learning to scenes whose structure is only piecewise smooth. A boundary changes which nearby observations are informative, so local prediction must depend on more than spatial proximity alone. The expert-based construction offers a way to retain useful interpolation within surfaces while avoiding the false continuity created by blending across separate objects.
summary.tldr: Discontinuity-aware models detect surface boundaries and select asymmetric interpolators that preserve depth coherence without crossing edges.

title: Learning to Make Coherent Predictions in Domains with Discontinuities

abstract: The perfonnance of dedicated VLSI neural processing hardware depends critically on the design of the implemented algorithms. We have pre(cid:173) viously proposed an algorithm for acoustic transient classification [1]. Having implemented and demonstrated this algorithm in a mixed-mode architecture, we now investigate variants on the algorithm, using time and frequency channel differencing, input and output nonnalization, and schemes to binarize and train the template values, with the goal of achiev(cid:173) ing optimal classification perfonnance for the chosen hardware.
originalAbstract: The perfonnance of dedicated VLSI neural processing hardware depends critically on the design of the implemented algorithms. We have pre(cid:173) viously proposed an algorithm for acoustic transient classification [1]. Having implemented and demonstrated this algorithm in a mixed-mode architecture, we now investigate variants on the algorithm, using time and frequency channel differencing, input and output nonnalization, and schemes to binarize and train the template values, with the goal of achiev(cid:173) ing optimal classification perfonnance for the chosen hardware.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to adapt an acoustic transient classifier to the dedicated hardware that runs it. The starting point is a previously proposed correlation algorithm that has already been implemented and demonstrated in a mixed-mode architecture. The new work investigates algorithm variants intended to improve classification on that chosen hardware.

The variants change several parts of the computation. Time-channel and frequency-channel differencing alter how changes in the input are represented. Input and output normalization adjust the values entering and leaving the classifier. Other variants concern how template values are trained and converted to binary form, making the template representation itself part of the optimization.

These choices matter because the performance of a dedicated VLSI system depends on the algorithm implemented within it. The paper therefore treats representation, normalization, and template design as connected hardware-facing decisions. Its stated contribution is an investigation of those alternatives for acoustic transient classification, with the objective of finding the best classification behavior for an already selected processing architecture.
summary.tldr: The paper explores differencing, normalization, and template design to optimize an acoustic transient classifier for dedicated VLSI hardware.

title: Optimizing Correlation Algorithms for Hardware-Based Transient Classification

abstract: Human and animal studies show that mammalian brain undergoes massive synaptic pruning during childhood , removing about half of the synapses until puberty. We have previously shown that main(cid:173) taining network memory performance while synapses are deleted, requires that synapses are properly modified and pruned, remov(cid:173) ing the weaker synapses. We now show that neuronal regulation , a mechanism recently observed to maintain the average neuronal in(cid:173) put field , results in weight-dependent synaptic modification . Under the correct range of the degradation dimension and synaptic up(cid:173) per bound, neuronal regulation removes the weaker synapses and judiciously modifies the remaining synapses . It implements near optimal synaptic modification, and maintains the memory perfor(cid:173) mance of a network undergoing massive synaptic pruning. Thus , this paper shows that in addition to the known effects of Hebbian changes, neuronal regulation may play an important role in the self-organization of brain networks during development.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how a neural network can preserve memory performance while losing many synapses. Mammalian development motivates the question, since substantial synaptic pruning occurs during childhood. Earlier work by the authors indicated that preserving performance requires appropriate changes to the remaining connections and preferential removal of weaker synapses.

Here they examine neuronal regulation, a mechanism observed to maintain the average input field of a neuron. They show that it produces synaptic changes that depend on connection strength. Within the correct range of the degradation dimension and the upper bound on synaptic strength, the mechanism removes weaker connections and modifies those that remain.

Under those stated conditions, neuronal regulation implements nearly optimal synaptic modification and maintains memory performance through extensive pruning. This provides a possible mechanism linking regulation of neuronal input to useful restructuring of network connections. The broader developmental conclusion is qualified: alongside Hebbian changes, neuronal regulation may play an important role in how brain networks organize themselves as they mature.
summary.tldr: Under suitable parameter conditions, neuronal regulation preferentially prunes weak synapses while modifying surviving connections to preserve network memory.

title: Neuronal Regulation Implements Efficient Synaptic Pruning

abstract: We formulate the problem of retrieving images from visual databases as a problem of Bayesian inference. This leads to natural and effective solutions for two of the most challenging issues in the design of a retrieval system: providing support for region-based queries without requiring prior image segmentation, and accounting for user-feedback during a retrieval session. We present a new learning algorithm that relies on belief propagation to account for both positive and negative examples of the user's interests.
originalAbstract: We formulate the problem of retrieving images from visual databases as a problem of Bayesian inference. This leads to natural and effective solutions for two of the most challenging issues in the design of a retrieval system: providing support for region-based queries without requiring prior image segmentation, and accounting for user-feedback during a retrieval session. We present a new learning algorithm that relies on belief propagation to account for both positive and negative examples of the user's interests.

paragraphs: The paper treats image retrieval as Bayesian inference: a system uses available evidence to reason about which images match a user's interests. This formulation brings two difficult design problems into one framework. A user may care about a region within an image, and their judgments during a search session can clarify what they want.

For region-based queries, the approach does not require images to have been segmented beforehand. This matters because supporting a query about part of an image need not depend on a prior division of the entire image into regions. The Bayesian formulation is presented as providing a natural and effective solution to this retrieval requirement.

The authors also introduce a learning algorithm based on belief propagation to incorporate feedback. It accounts for both examples the user likes and examples the user rejects, allowing both kinds of evidence to inform the session. The contribution is a probabilistic treatment that connects region-level search with learning from user responses, rather than treating feedback as separate from the retrieval problem.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian image-retrieval framework supports region queries without prior segmentation and learns from positive and negative user feedback.

title: Learning from User Feedback in Image Retrieval Systems

abstract: In this paper, we derive a second order mean field theory for directed graphical probability models. By using an information theoretic argu(cid:173) ment it is shown how this can be done in the absense of a partition function. This method is a direct generalisation of the well-known TAP approximation for Boltzmann Machines. In a numerical example, it is shown that the method greatly improves the first order mean field ap(cid:173) proximation. For a restricted class of graphical models, so-called single overlap graphs, the second order method has comparable complexity to the first order method. For sigmoid belief networks, the method is shown to be particularly fast and effective.

By using an information theoretic argu(cid:173) ment it is shown how this can be done in the absense of a partition function. In a numerical example, it is shown that the method greatly improves the first order mean field ap(cid:173) proximation. paragraphs: This paper develops a second-order mean-field approximation for directed graphical probability models. Mean-field methods simplify probabilistic calculations, and the second-order construction aims to improve on the first-order version. The authors derive it using an information-theoretic argument that works without a partition function, addressing a feature of the directed-model setting.

The resulting theory directly generalizes the TAP approximation used for Boltzmann machines. This connects a known approximation method to a different family of graphical models. In a numerical example, the second-order method substantially improves on first-order mean field, demonstrating that the extra approximation terms can make a meaningful difference to the calculation.

The computational cost depends on graph structure. For a restricted class called single-overlap graphs, the second-order method has complexity comparable to the first-order method. The authors also show that it is particularly fast and effective for sigmoid belief networks. These findings identify settings where a more accurate approximation can be practical, while keeping the comparable-cost claim tied to the stated restricted graph class.
summary.tldr: A second-order mean-field theory improves directed-model approximation and retains first-order-like complexity for a restricted graph class.

title: Second Order Approximations for Probability Models

abstract: In many discrimination problems a large amount of data is available but only a few of them are labeled. This provides a strong motivation to improve or develop methods for semi-supervised learning. In this paper, boosting is generalized to this task within the optimization framework of MarginBoost . We extend the margin definition to unlabeled data and develop the gradient descent algorithm that corresponds to the resulting margin cost function. This meta-learning scheme can be applied to any base classifier able to benefit from unlabeled data. We propose here to apply it to mixture models trained with an Expectation-Maximization algorithm. Promising results are presented on benchmarks with different rates of labeled data.

This provides a strong motivation to improve or develop methods for semi-supervised learning. In this paper, boosting is generalized to this task within the optimization framework of MarginBoost . We extend the margin definition to unlabeled data and develop the gradient descent algorithm that corresponds to the resulting margin cost function. This meta-learning scheme can be applied to any base classifier able to benefit from unlabeled data. We propose here to apply it to mixture models trained with an Expectation-Maximization algorithm. Promising results are presented on benchmarks with different rates of labeled data.

paragraphs: Many classification problems provide abundant observations but labels for only a small fraction of them. The paper extends boosting to this semi-supervised setting through the optimization framework of MarginBoost. The aim is to let the learning procedure make use of unlabeled examples alongside labeled ones.

The central step is extending the definition of a margin to unlabeled data. From the resulting margin-based cost, the authors derive a gradient descent algorithm. This ties the semi-supervised extension to an explicit optimization objective, rather than simply adding unlabeled observations to a procedure designed only for labeled examples.

The resulting meta-learning scheme can work with any base classifier capable of benefiting from unlabeled data. The paper instantiates it using mixture models trained by expectation-maximization. Benchmark experiments vary the proportion of labeled observations and produce results the authors describe as promising. The contribution is therefore both a general boosting framework and a concrete demonstration, with its applicability depending on the base learner’s ability to use the unlabeled portion of the data.
summary.tldr: Semi-supervised MarginBoost extends margins to unlabeled examples and derives a boosting procedure for base learners that can use them.

title: Semi-supervised MarginBoost

abstract: We describe a neural network which enhances and completes salient closed contours. Our work is different from all previous work in three important ways. First, like the input provided to V1 by LGN, the in- put to our computation is isotropic. That is, the input is composed of spots not edges. Second, our network computes a well deﬁned function of the input based on a distribution of closed contours characterized by a random process. Third, even though our computation is implemented in a discrete network, its output is invariant to continuous rotations and translations of the input pattern.
originalAbstract: We describe a neural network which enhances and completes salient closed contours. Our work is different from all previous work in three important ways. First, like the input provided to V1 by LGN, the in- put to our computation is isotropic. That is, the input is composed of spots not edges. Second, our network computes a well deﬁned function of the input based on a distribution of closed contours characterized by a random process. Third, even though our computation is implemented in a discrete network, its output is invariant to continuous rotations and translations of the input pattern.

paragraphs: The paper describes a neural network for strengthening and completing visually prominent closed contours. Its starting point is unusual: the input consists of spots without a preferred orientation, rather than already identified edges. The authors relate this choice to the kind of input that reaches the visual area V1 from the LGN.

The network’s computation is defined through a probability distribution over closed contours generated by a random process. This gives contour enhancement a precise mathematical target. The network is computing a specified function of the input, making its behavior interpretable in terms of the underlying contour distribution.

A central result concerns geometric invariance. Although the network itself is discrete, its output is invariant to continuous rotations and translations of the input pattern. This connects a practical representational choice with a strong geometric property: contour saliency does not depend on a particular position or orientation. Together, the spot-based input, probabilistic definition, and invariance distinguish the proposed approach.
summary.tldr: A discrete neural network enhances and completes closed contours from spot-based input while preserving invariance to continuous rotations and translations.

title: A Rotation and Translation Invariant Discrete Saliency Network

abstract: We construct a nonlinear mapping from a high-dimensional sample space to a low-dimensional vector space, effectively recovering a Cartesian coordinate system for the manifold from which the data is sampled. The mapping preserves local geometric relations in the manifold and is pseudo-invertible. We show how to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold from samples, decompose the sample data into locally linear low-dimensional patches, merge these patches into a single lowdimensional coordinate system, and compute forward and reverse mappings between the sample and coordinate spaces. The objective functions are convex and their solutions are given in closed form.
originalAbstract: We construct a nonlinear mapping from a high-dimensional sample space to a low-dimensional vector space, effectively recovering a Cartesian coordinate system for the manifold from which the data is sampled. The mapping preserves local geometric relations in the manifold and is pseudo-invertible. We show how to estimate the intrinsic dimensionality of the manifold from samples, decompose the sample data into locally linear low-dimensional patches, merge these patches into a single lowdimensional coordinate system, and compute forward and reverse mappings between the sample and coordinate spaces. The objective functions are convex and their solutions are given in closed form.

paragraphs: Data described by many measurements can lie on an underlying surface with far fewer dimensions. This paper constructs a nonlinear mapping from the original sample space into a smaller vector space. The aim is to recover a Cartesian coordinate system for the manifold from which the observations were sampled.

The method first estimates the manifold's intrinsic dimensionality from samples. It then divides the data into low-dimensional patches that are locally linear and merges those patches into one coordinate system. This local-to-global construction preserves nearby geometric relationships while providing a shared representation across the sampled manifold.

The authors also compute mappings in both directions between the sample space and the coordinate space. They describe the mapping as pseudo-invertible, supporting a reverse map without asserting an unrestricted exact inverse. The objective functions are convex and have closed-form solutions. Together, these properties make the contribution a method for constructing and navigating a compact coordinate representation, with explicitly solvable optimization problems underlying the construction.
summary.tldr: Locally linear patches are combined into a compact manifold coordinate system with forward and reverse mappings and closed-form optimization solutions.

title: Charting a Manifold

abstract: We generalise the Gaussian process (GP) framework for regression by learning a nonlinear transformation of the GP outputs. This allows for non-Gaussian processes and non-Gaussian noise. The learning algo- rithm chooses a nonlinear transformation such that transformed data is well-modelled by a GP. This can be seen as including a preprocessing transformation as an integral part of the probabilistic modelling problem, rather than as an ad-hoc step. We demonstrate on several real regression problems that learning the transformation can lead to signiﬁcantly better performance than using a regular GP, or a GP with a ﬁxed transformation.
originalAbstract: We generalise the Gaussian process (GP) framework for regression by learning a nonlinear transformation of the GP outputs. This allows for non-Gaussian processes and non-Gaussian noise. The learning algo- rithm chooses a nonlinear transformation such that transformed data is well-modelled by a GP. This can be seen as including a preprocessing transformation as an integral part of the probabilistic modelling problem, rather than as an ad-hoc step. We demonstrate on several real regression problems that learning the transformation can lead to signiﬁcantly better performance than using a regular GP, or a GP with a ﬁxed transformation.

paragraphs: The paper extends Gaussian process regression by learning a nonlinear transformation of the outputs. The goal is to find a transformed scale on which the data are well described by a Gaussian process. This expands the framework to accommodate non-Gaussian processes and non-Gaussian noise through the learned transformation.

The key change is to make that transformation part of the probabilistic modeling problem. Instead of choosing an output transformation beforehand as a separate preprocessing decision, the learning algorithm selects it along with the model. This allows the representation of the outputs to adapt to the regression problem rather than being fixed independently of learning.

On several real regression problems, the authors show that learning the transformation can significantly improve performance over both a regular Gaussian process and one using a fixed transformation. The evidence supports adaptability in the output scale as a useful modeling choice. The claim is that this can improve performance, rather than that every dataset requires a transformation or benefits from learning one.
summary.tldr: Learning an output transformation within Gaussian process regression can improve performance and accommodate non-Gaussian behavior.

title: Warped Gaussian Processes

abstract: Density estimation with Gaussian Mixture Models is a popular gener- ative technique used also for clustering. We develop a framework to incorporate side information in the form of equivalence constraints into the model estimation procedure. Equivalence constraints are deﬁned on pairs of data points, indicating whether the points arise from the same source (positive constraints) or from different sources (negative con- straints). Such constraints can be gathered automatically in some learn- ing problems, and are a natural form of supervision in others. For the estimation of model parameters we present a closed form EM procedure which handles positive constraints, and a Generalized EM procedure us- ing a Markov net which handles negative constraints. Using publicly available data sets we demonstrate that such side information can lead to considerable improvement in clustering tasks, and that our algorithm is preferable to two other suggested methods using the same type of side information.

Such constraints can be gathered automatically in some learn- ing problems, and are a natural form of supervision in others. For the estimation of model parameters we present a closed form EM procedure which handles positive constraints, and a Generalized EM procedure us- ing a Markov net which handles negative constraints. Using publicly available data sets we demonstrate that such side information can lead to considerable improvement in clustering tasks, and that our algorithm is preferable to two other suggested methods using the same type of side information.

paragraphs: Gaussian mixture models estimate a data distribution and can also be used for clustering. This paper adds supervision through statements about pairs of observations. A positive constraint says that two points come from the same source; a negative constraint says that they come from different sources. Such information can sometimes be collected automatically.

The authors incorporate these relationships into model estimation rather than leaving them outside the clustering procedure. They provide a closed-form EM procedure for positive constraints. For negative constraints, they develop a generalized EM procedure using a Markov network. The different treatments allow the estimation framework to address both forms of pairwise information.

Experiments on publicly available datasets show that these constraints can substantially improve clustering. The authors also report that their algorithm is preferable to two other methods using the same kind of supervision. The findings indicate that information about which observations belong together, or apart, can meaningfully guide mixture estimation even when supervision is expressed as relationships between points.
summary.tldr: The paper incorporates same-source and different-source pair constraints into Gaussian mixture estimation and reports improved clustering.

title: Computing Gaussian Mixture Models with EM Using Equivalence Constraints

abstract: Despite all the attention paid to variational methods based on sum-product message passing (loopy belief propagation, tree-reweighted sum-product), these methods are still bound to inference on a small set of probabilistic models. Mean field approximations have been applied to a broader set of problems, but the solutions are often poor. We propose a new class of conditionally-specified variational approximations based on mean field theory. While not usable on their own, combined with sequential Monte Carlo they produce guaranteed improvements over conventional mean field. Moreover, experiments on a well-studied problem-- inferring the stable configurations of the Ising spin glass--show that the solutions can be significantly better than those obtained using sum-product-based methods.

paragraphs: Probabilistic inference often requires approximating a distribution that is difficult to handle directly. The paper identifies a tradeoff between two existing approaches: methods based on sum-product message passing cover a relatively restricted collection of models, while mean field approximations apply more broadly but can produce poor solutions. The goal is to improve the latter approach.

The authors introduce a family of variational approximations specified through conditional distributions and based on mean field theory. These approximations are not usable by themselves. Their proposed role is within a combination with sequential Monte Carlo, and it is this combined construction that provides guaranteed improvements over conventional mean field.

Experiments examine inference of stable configurations in an Ising spin glass. On this problem, the resulting solutions can be substantially better than those from sum-product methods. The paper therefore offers both a guarantee relative to conventional mean field and empirical evidence against another class of inference methods, with the latter comparison demonstrated on the stated problem.
summary.tldr: Conditional mean field approximations combined with sequential Monte Carlo guarantee improvements over conventional mean field.

title: Conditional mean field

abstract: Loopy belief propagation has been employed in a wide variety of applications with great empirical success, but it comes with few theoretical guarantees. In this paper we investigate the use of the max-product form of belief propagation for weighted matching problems on general graphs. We show that max-product converges to the correct answer if the linear programming (LP) relaxation of the weighted matching problem is tight and does not converge if the LP relaxation is loose. This provides an exact characterization of max-product performance and reveals connections to the widely used optimization technique of LP relaxation. In addition, we demonstrate that max-product is effective in solving practical weighted matching problems in a distributed fashion by applying it to the problem of self-organization in sensor networks.

paragraphs: Loopy belief propagation has worked well empirically in many applications, but its behavior often lacks theoretical guarantees. This paper examines the max-product version for weighted matching on general graphs. The question is when the message-passing procedure converges to the correct solution and when it fails to converge.

The authors connect that behavior to a linear-programming relaxation of the matching problem. When the relaxation is tight, max-product converges to the correct answer. When the relaxation is loose, it does not converge. This gives an exact characterization for the studied setting by tying the algorithm's behavior to a property of a related optimization problem.

The connection matters because it turns a question about iterative messages into a question about the relaxation's relationship to the original matching task. The paper also applies max-product to self-organization in sensor networks, demonstrating its effectiveness for practical distributed matching. The theoretical result concerns weighted matching on general graphs; the application shows how the message-passing approach can support computation distributed across a network.
summary.tldr: For the studied weighted-matching setting, max-product converges correctly when the LP relaxation is tight and fails to converge when it is loose.

title: Linear programming analysis of loopy belief propagation for weighted matching

abstract: We provide sharp bounds for Rademacher and Gaussian complexities of (constrained) linear classes. These bounds make short work of providing a number of corollaries including: risk bounds for linear prediction (including settings where the weight vectors are constrained by either $L_2$ or $L_1$ constraints), margin bounds (including both $L_2$ and $L_1$ margins, along with more general notions based on relative entropy), a proof of the PAC-Bayes theorem, and $L_2$ covering numbers (with $L_p$ norm constraints and relative entropy constraints). In addition to providing a unified analysis, the results herein provide some of the sharpest risk and margin bounds (improving upon a number of previous results). Interestingly, our results show that the uniform convergence rates of empirical risk minimization algorithms tightly match the regret bounds of online learning algorithms for linear prediction (up to a constant factor of 2).

paragraphs: The paper develops sharp bounds on Rademacher and Gaussian complexities for constrained classes of linear predictors. These complexity measures support mathematical analysis of how reliably learning from a sample can carry over to prediction. The aim is to derive several learning guarantees from a shared analysis of the underlying predictor classes.

Consequences include risk bounds under L1 and L2 weight constraints, margin bounds, a proof of the PAC-Bayes theorem, and covering-number bounds. The treatment also includes constraints and margin notions involving relative entropy. Bringing these results together shows how multiple forms of regularization and generalization analysis can be handled through common mathematical tools.

The authors report improvements over several previous risk and margin bounds. They also show that uniform convergence rates for empirical risk minimization closely match online-learning regret bounds for linear prediction, within a factor of two. This connects guarantees about learning from a fixed sample with guarantees about accumulating errors during sequential prediction, while preserving the quantitative distinction between the two settings.
summary.tldr: Sharp complexity bounds unify several linear-prediction guarantees and connect statistical convergence rates with online regret bounds.

title: On the Complexity of Linear Prediction: Risk Bounds, Margin Bounds, and Regularization

abstract: Although it is widely believed that reinforcement learning is a suitable tool for describing behavioral learning, the mechanisms by which it can be implemented in networks of spiking neurons are not fully understood. Here, we show that different learning rules emerge from a policy gradient approach depending on which features of the spike trains are assumed to influence the reward signals, i.e., depending on which neural code is in effect. We use the framework of Williams (1992) to derive learning rules for arbitrary neural codes. For illustration, we present policy-gradient rules for three different example codes - a spike count code, a spike timing code and the most general ``full spike train code - and test them on simple model problems. In addition to classical synaptic learning, we derive learning rules for intrinsic parameters that control the excitability of the neuron. The spike count learning rule has structural similarities with established Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro rules. If the distribution of the relevant spike train features belongs to the natural exponential family, the learning rules have a characteristic shape that raises interesting prediction problems.

paragraphs: This paper asks how reward-based learning could operate in neurons that communicate through spikes. Its central point is that the learning rule depends on the neural code: which aspects of a spike sequence are assumed to influence reward. Counting spikes and considering their precise timing can therefore lead to different rules for changing a neuron.

The authors use a policy-gradient framework to derive rules for arbitrary neural codes. They illustrate the framework with spike counts, spike timing, and the complete spike sequence, then test those examples on simple model problems. They also derive updates for intrinsic parameters controlling neuronal excitability, extending the treatment beyond changes to synaptic connections.

The spike-count rule has structural similarities to established Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro learning rules. Another result is conditional: when the relevant spike features follow a distribution in the natural exponential family, the learning rules take a characteristic form that raises prediction questions. The contribution is a framework connecting assumptions about what spikes encode to the learning mechanisms those assumptions imply.
summary.tldr: Different assumptions about how spikes influence reward lead to different policy-gradient learning rules for neurons.

title: Code-specific policy gradient rules for spiking neurons

abstract: Locality information is crucial in datasets where each variable corresponds to a measurement in a manifold (silhouettes, motion trajectories, 2D and 3D images). Although these datasets are typically under-sampled and high-dimensional, they often need to be represented with low-complexity statistical models, which are comprised of only the important probabilistic dependencies in the datasets. Most methods attempt to reduce model complexity by enforcing structure sparseness. However, sparseness cannot describe inherent regularities in the structure. Hence, in this paper we first propose a new class of Gaussian graphical models which, together with sparseness, imposes local constancy through ${\ell}_1$-norm penalization. Second, we propose an efficient algorithm which decomposes the strictly convex maximum likelihood estimation into a sequence of problems with closed form solutions. Through synthetic experiments, we evaluate the closeness of the recovered models to the ground truth. We also test the generalization performance of our method in a wide range of complex real-world datasets and demonstrate that it can capture useful structures such as the rotation and shrinking of a beating heart, motion correlations between body parts during walking and functional interactions of brain regions. Our method outperforms the state-of-the-art structure learning techniques for Gaussian graphical models both for small and large datasets.

paragraphs: When variables measure locations on shapes, trajectories, or images, their arrangement carries useful information. Sparse graphical models keep only selected probabilistic dependencies, but sparsity alone does not express local regularities in those dependencies. This paper introduces Gaussian graphical models that encourage both sparse structure and local constancy.

The model uses an l1-norm penalty to impose these structural preferences. The authors also develop an efficient algorithm that breaks a strictly convex maximum-likelihood estimation problem into a sequence of subproblems with closed-form solutions. The approach therefore addresses both what structure should be learned and how to estimate it.

Synthetic experiments assess recovery against known ground truth, while real-data experiments examine generalization. Reported examples capture heart rotation and shrinking, correlations between body parts during walking, and interactions among brain regions. The method outperforms leading Gaussian graphical structure-learning techniques on both small and large datasets in the reported evaluations. These findings support using locality alongside sparsity when modeling structured measurements.
summary.tldr: Gaussian graphical models that encourage both sparsity and local constancy recover useful structure and improve reported generalization.

title: Sparse and Locally Constant Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: We provide a clustering algorithm that approximately optimizes the k-means objective, in the one-pass streaming setting. We make no assumptions about the data, and our algorithm is very light-weight in terms of memory, and computation. This setting is applicable to unsupervised learning on massive data sets, or resource-constrained devices. The two main ingredients of our theoretical work are: a derivation of an extremely simple pseudo-approximation batch algorithm for k-means, in which the algorithm is allowed to output more than k centers (based on the recent k-means++"), and a streaming clustering algorithm in which batch clustering algorithms are performed on small inputs (fitting in memory) and combined in a hierarchical manner. Empirical evaluations on real and simulated data reveal the practical utility of our method."

Empirical evaluations on real and simulated data reveal the practical utility of our method."

paragraphs: Clustering a massive dataset can be difficult when observations can be processed only once or memory is limited. This paper presents a one-pass streaming algorithm that approximately optimizes the k-means objective. The authors make no assumptions about the data and emphasize low memory and computation requirements, making the setting relevant to large datasets and resource-constrained devices.

The method combines two ideas. First, a simple batch procedure based on k-means++ obtains a pseudo-approximation by allowing more than k centers. Second, a streaming procedure runs batch clustering on small inputs that fit in memory and combines their results hierarchically. This gives manageable local computations a role in processing the larger stream.

The permission to use extra centers is an explicit feature of the batch ingredient's approximation formulation. The hierarchical construction then supplies the streaming organization. Evaluations on real and simulated data demonstrate practical utility, supporting the approach as a way to perform approximate clustering when retaining and repeatedly revisiting the full dataset is impractical.
summary.tldr: A lightweight one-pass k-means approximation combines small batch clusterings hierarchically and demonstrates practical utility on real and simulated data.

title: Streaming k-means approximation

abstract: Conditional random fields (CRF) are quite successful on sequence labeling tasks such as natural language processing and biological sequence analysis. CRF models use linear potential functions to represent the relationship between input features and outputs. However, in many real-world applications such as protein structure prediction and handwriting recognition, the relationship between input features and outputs is highly complex and nonlinear, which cannot be accurately modeled by a linear function. To model the nonlinear relationship between input features and outputs we propose Conditional Neural Fields (CNF), a new conditional probabilistic graphical model for sequence labeling. Our CNF model extends CRF by adding one (or possibly several) middle layer between input features and outputs. The middle layer consists of a number of hidden parameterized gates, each acting as a local neural network node or feature extractor to capture the nonlinear relationship between input features and outputs. Therefore, conceptually this CNF model is much more expressive than the linear CRF model. To better control the complexity of the CNF model, we also present a hyperparameter optimization procedure within the evidence framework. Experiments on two widely-used benchmarks indicate that this CNF model performs significantly better than a number of popular methods. In particular, our CNF model is the best among about ten machine learning methods for protein secondary tructure prediction and also among a few of the best methods for handwriting recognition.

paragraphs: Conditional Neural Fields address sequence-labeling problems in which the relationship between input features and output labels is nonlinear. The paper starts from conditional random fields with linear potential functions and argues that those functions cannot accurately represent some complex relationships found in applications such as protein structure prediction and handwriting recognition.

The proposed model inserts one or more intermediate layers between inputs and outputs. These layers contain parameterized hidden gates that act as neural-network nodes or local feature extractors. Their purpose is to capture nonlinear relationships while retaining a conditional probabilistic graphical model for sequence labeling. The authors also introduce evidence-based hyperparameter optimization to better control model complexity.

Experiments on two established benchmarks indicate significant improvements over several popular methods. The model ranks best among roughly ten methods examined for protein secondary structure prediction and among a few of the best for handwriting recognition. These results support the practical value of learning nonlinear features within the sequence model on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: Conditional Neural Fields add hidden nonlinear feature extractors to sequence models and achieve strong results on protein and handwriting benchmarks.

title: Conditional Neural Fields

abstract: Feature selection is an important component of many machine learning applications. Especially in many bioinformatics tasks, efficient and robust feature selection methods are desired to extract meaningful features and eliminate noisy ones. In this paper, we propose a new robust feature selection method with emphasizing joint ℓ2,1-norm minimization on both loss function and regularization. The ℓ2,1-norm based loss function is robust to outliers in data points and the ℓ2,1-norm regularization selects features across all data points with joint sparsity. An efficient algorithm is introduced with proved convergence. Our regression based objective makes the feature selection process more efficient. Our method has been applied into both genomic and proteomic biomarkers discovery. Extensive empirical studies were performed on six data sets to demonstrate the effectiveness of our feature selection method.

paragraphs: Feature selection aims to retain meaningful measurements while removing noisy or unhelpful ones. This is especially relevant to biological data, where the selected measurements may serve as candidate biomarkers. The paper proposes a regression-based feature-selection objective that addresses two requirements together: resistance to unusual data points and consistent selection of features across the data.

The method uses the same mathematical norm, the ℓ2,1 norm, in two different parts of the objective. In the loss function, it provides robustness to outliers. In the regularization term, it encourages joint sparsity, so that feature selection is shared across data points. These two uses connect the treatment of unreliable observations with the search for a compact set of useful features.

The authors introduce an efficient optimization algorithm and prove that it converges. They apply the method to genomic and proteomic biomarker discovery, evaluating it on six datasets. Those empirical studies support the method's effectiveness, while the convergence result supplies a separate theoretical guarantee about the proposed algorithm.
summary.tldr: Using ℓ2,1 norms for both loss and regularization combines outlier robustness with joint feature selection in an efficient, convergent algorithm.

title: Efficient and Robust Feature Selection via Joint ℓ2,1-Norms Minimization

abstract: We consider the problem of reinforcement learning in high-dimensional spaces when the number of features is bigger than the number of samples. In particular, we study the least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) learning algorithm when a space of low dimension is generated with a random projection from a high-dimensional space. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis of the LSTD with random projections and derive performance bounds for the resulting algorithm. We also show how the error of LSTD with random projections is propagated through the iterations of a policy iteration algorithm and provide a performance bound for the resulting least-squares policy iteration (LSPI) algorithm.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of reinforcement learning in high-dimensional spaces when the number of features is bigger than the number of samples. In particular, we study the least-squares temporal difference (LSTD) learning algorithm when a space of low dimension is generated with a random projection from a high-dimensional space. We provide a thorough theoretical analysis of the LSTD with random projections and derive performance bounds for the resulting algorithm. We also show how the error of LSTD with random projections is propagated through the iterations of a policy iteration algorithm and provide a performance bound for the resulting least-squares policy iteration (LSPI) algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning when the feature representation has more dimensions than there are samples. It focuses on least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, after a random projection maps the original features into a lower-dimensional space. The question is how this reduction affects the resulting learning procedure.

The authors provide a theoretical analysis and derive performance bounds for LSTD with random projections. These bounds give a formal way to assess the quality of the projected method. The contribution is therefore more than introducing a smaller representation: it analyzes the consequences of using that representation within temporal difference learning.

The analysis then follows the error through repeated policy-iteration steps and provides a performance bound for the resulting least-squares policy iteration algorithm. This extension matters because error in one learning step can influence later steps that build on its output. By treating both the projected LSTD procedure and its role inside policy iteration, the paper connects dimensionality reduction to the performance of the broader reinforcement-learning process.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds the performance of randomly projected LSTD and analyzes how its error propagates through policy iteration.

title: LSTD with Random Projections

abstract: This paper introduces two new frameworks for learning action models for planning. In the mistake-bounded planning framework, the learner has access to a planner for the given model representation, a simulator, and a planning problem generator, and aims to learn a model with at most a polynomial number of faulty plans. In the planned exploration framework, the learner does not have access to a problem generator and must instead design its own problems, plan for them, and converge with at most a polynomial number of planning attempts. The paper reduces learning in these frameworks to concept learning with one-sided error and provides algorithms for successful learning in both frameworks. A specific family of hypothesis spaces is shown to be efficiently learnable in both the frameworks.

In the mistake-bounded planning framework, the learner has access to a planner for the given model representation, a simulator, and a planning problem generator, and aims to learn a model with at most a polynomial number of faulty plans. In the planned exploration framework, the learner does not have access to a problem generator and must instead design its own problems, plan for them, and converge with at most a polynomial number of planning attempts. The paper reduces learning in these frameworks to concept learning with one-sided error and provides algorithms for successful learning in both frameworks. A specific family of hypothesis spaces is shown to be efficiently learnable in both the frameworks.

paragraphs: A planning system needs an action model to predict what its actions will do. This paper introduces two frameworks for learning such models while using them to construct plans. Both frameworks measure learning progress through planning behavior, making failures and attempts part of the formal account of how learning proceeds.

In mistake-bounded planning, the learner receives a planner for its model representation, a simulator, and a generator of planning problems. Its goal is to learn with at most a polynomial number of faulty plans. In planned exploration, the learner has no problem generator. It must choose its own problems, plan for them, and converge within a polynomial number of planning attempts.

The authors reduce learning in these settings to concept learning with one-sided error and provide successful algorithms for both frameworks. They also identify a particular family of hypothesis spaces that is efficiently learnable in each. This gives a formal basis for autonomous model acquisition while keeping the efficiency claim tied to the demonstrated family of model spaces.
summary.tldr: Two frameworks formalize learning action models through planning, with polynomial bounds and efficient learning for a specific family of hypothesis spaces.

title: Autonomous Learning of Action Models for Planning

abstract: We consider the problem of adaptive stratified sampling for Monte Carlo integration of a differentiable function given a finite number of evaluations to the function. We construct a sampling scheme that samples more often in regions where the function oscillates more, while allocating the samples such that they are well spread on the domain (this notion shares similitude with low discrepancy). We prove that the estimate returned by the algorithm is almost as accurate as the estimate that an optimal oracle strategy (that would know the variations of the function everywhere) would return, and we provide a finite-sample analysis.
originalAbstract: We consider the problem of adaptive stratified sampling for Monte Carlo integration of a differentiable function given a finite number of evaluations to the function. We construct a sampling scheme that samples more often in regions where the function oscillates more, while allocating the samples such that they are well spread on the domain (this notion shares similitude with low discrepancy). We prove that the estimate returned by the algorithm is almost as accurate as the estimate that an optimal oracle strategy (that would know the variations of the function everywhere) would return, and we provide a finite-sample analysis.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate the integral of a differentiable function when only a limited number of function evaluations are available. The central decision is where to spend those evaluations. Regions where the function changes more deserve additional attention, but concentrating samples there must be balanced against covering the whole domain.

The proposed adaptive stratified sampling scheme addresses both needs. It allocates more samples to regions with greater variation while keeping the sample locations well distributed. The abstract connects this spatial coverage to the idea of low discrepancy: the arrangement of samples matters alongside the number assigned to each region.

The authors prove that their estimate is almost as accurate as one produced by an optimal oracle that already knows the function's variation everywhere. This comparison matters because the proposed method must adapt without that advance knowledge. A finite-sample analysis supports the result for a limited evaluation budget, rather than describing accuracy only as the sample count grows indefinitely.
summary.tldr: An adaptive integration method balances extra sampling in variable regions with broad coverage and achieves accuracy close to an informed oracle.

title: Adaptive Stratified Sampling for Monte-Carlo integration of Differentiable functions

abstract: Motivated by various applications in machine learning, the problem of minimizing a convex smooth loss function with trace norm regularization has received much attention lately. Currently, a popular method for solving such problem is the proximal gradient method (PGM), which is known to have a sublinear rate of convergence. In this paper, we show that for a large class of loss functions, the convergence rate of the PGM is in fact linear. Our result is established without any strong convexity assumption on the loss function. A key ingredient in our proof is a new Lipschitzian error bound for the aforementioned trace norm-regularized problem, which may be of independent interest.

Currently, a popular method for solving such problem is the proximal gradient method (PGM), which is known to have a sublinear rate of convergence. Our result is established without any strong convexity assumption on the loss function. paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems that combine a smooth convex loss with trace norm regularization. A widely used solver for this combination is the proximal gradient method. Although its established general convergence guarantee is sublinear, the authors ask whether the structure of these particular problems supports a faster theoretical rate.

They prove linear convergence for a large class of loss functions without assuming that the loss is strongly convex. Linear convergence means that the error decreases geometrically, providing a stronger rate than the general sublinear guarantee. The conclusion applies to the class covered by their analysis rather than every possible smooth convex loss.

The central proof ingredient is a new Lipschitzian error bound for the trace norm-regularized problem. This supplies the quantitative control needed to establish the faster convergence result. The contribution is primarily an improved understanding of an existing optimization method: it identifies substantial settings where the proximal gradient method has stronger guarantees than its usual general analysis suggests, without requiring strong convexity.
summary.tldr: A new error bound establishes linear proximal-gradient convergence for a broad class of trace norm-regularized losses without strong convexity.

title: On the Linear Convergence of the Proximal Gradient Method for Trace Norm Regularization

abstract: We present SDA-Bayes, a framework for (S)treaming, (D)istributed, (A)synchronous computation of a Bayesian posterior. The framework makes streaming updates to the estimated posterior according to a user-specified approximation primitive function. We demonstrate the usefulness of our framework, with variational Bayes (VB) as the primitive, by fitting the latent Dirichlet allocation model to two large-scale document collections. We demonstrate the advantages of our algorithm over stochastic variational inference (SVI), both in the single-pass setting SVI was designed for and in the streaming setting, to which SVI does not apply.

We demonstrate the usefulness of our framework, with variational Bayes (VB) as the primitive, by fitting the latent Dirichlet allocation model to two large-scale document collections. We demonstrate the advantages of our algorithm over stochastic variational inference (SVI), both in the single-pass setting SVI was designed for and in the streaming setting, to which SVI does not apply.

paragraphs: The paper introduces SDA-Bayes, a framework for estimating a Bayesian posterior as data arrive. Its design supports streaming data, distributed computation, and asynchronous operation. The posterior estimate is updated through an approximation function supplied by the user, making the framework broader than one particular approximation technique.

To demonstrate the idea, the authors choose variational Bayes as that approximation function and fit latent Dirichlet allocation to two large document collections. This gives a concrete test of the framework in a model for document collections while retaining the distinction between the general updating framework and the particular inference method used inside it.

The experiments show advantages over stochastic variational inference in a single-pass setting and also demonstrate the streaming setting, to which the compared SVI approach does not apply. The distinction matters because processing a collection once and supporting ongoing posterior updates are different operational requirements. The contribution is a framework that accommodates those ongoing updates and distributed asynchronous computation, supported by the reported large-scale document-modeling results.
summary.tldr: SDA-Bayes supports streaming, distributed, asynchronous posterior approximation and demonstrates advantages with variational Bayes on large document collections.

title: Streaming Variational Bayes

abstract: We propose a method that learns a discriminative yet semantic space for object categorization, where we also embed auxiliary semantic entities such as supercategories and attributes. Contrary to prior work which only utilized them as side information, we explicitly embed the semantic entities into the same space where we embed categories, which enables us to represent a category as their linear combination. By exploiting such a unified model for semantics, we enforce each category to be generated as a sparse combination of a supercategory + attributes, with an additional exclusive regularization to learn discriminative composition. The proposed reconstructive regularization guides the discriminative learning process to learn a better generalizing model, as well as generates compact semantic description of each category, which enables humans to analyze what has been learned.

paragraphs: Object categorization needs representations that distinguish categories, but a useful representation can also express what categories mean. This paper learns a shared space containing object categories, broader supercategories, and attributes. Placing these semantic entities directly in the category space allows the model to describe a category through a linear combination of meaningful components.

The method encourages each category to use a sparse combination of a supercategory and attributes. Sparsity keeps the description compact by limiting the components involved. An additional exclusive regularization term encourages compositions that discriminate between categories. The semantic reconstruction requirement therefore participates in learning the representation, rather than serving only as extra information supplied alongside it.

The authors state that this reconstructive regularization guides discriminative learning toward better generalization. It also produces compact semantic descriptions that people can inspect to understand what the model has learned. The contribution connects predictive usefulness with interpretability: category distinctions and their semantic explanations are developed within the same representation.
summary.tldr: A shared embedding represents object categories as sparse combinations of supercategories and attributes, supporting discrimination and interpretable descriptions.

title: A Unified Semantic Embedding: Relating Taxonomies and Attributes

abstract: While topic models can discover patterns of word usage in large corpora, it is difficult to meld this unsupervised structure with noisy, human-provided labels, especially when the label space is large. In this paper, we present a model-Label to Hierarchy (L2H)-that can induce a hierarchy of user-generated labels and the topics associated with those labels from a set of multi-labeled documents. The model is robust enough to account for missing labels from untrained, disparate annotators and provide an interpretable summary of an otherwise unwieldy label set. We show empirically the effectiveness of L2H in predicting held-out words and labels for unseen documents.

paragraphs: Document collections can contain both recurring word patterns and human-assigned labels, but the two sources of organization do not necessarily align neatly. Labels may be numerous, noisy, or missing. This paper introduces Label to Hierarchy, or L2H, to learn a hierarchy of user-generated labels together with topics associated with those labels.

The input consists of documents that can each have multiple labels. The model combines their textual structure with those annotations, accounting for missing labels supplied by different, untrained annotators. Organizing labels hierarchically provides an interpretable summary of a label collection that would otherwise be difficult to understand as a large flat set.

The authors evaluate the model by predicting held-out words and labels for previously unseen documents and report empirical effectiveness on both tasks. These evaluations connect the learned organization to predictive usefulness as well as interpretability. The result is a model that relates document content and imperfect annotations through a jointly learned conceptual hierarchy.
summary.tldr: L2H learns an interpretable hierarchy of document labels and associated topics while accounting for missing human annotations.

title: Learning a Concept Hierarchy from Multi-labeled Documents

abstract: We present new ensemble learning algorithms for multi-class classification. Our algorithms can use as a base classifier set a family of deep decision trees or other rich or complex families and yet benefit from strong generalization guarantees. We give new data-dependent learning bounds for convex ensembles in the multi-class classification setting expressed in terms of the Rademacher complexities of the sub-families composing the base classifier set, and the mixture weight assigned to each sub-family. These bounds are finer than existing ones both thanks to an improved dependency on the number of classes and, more crucially, by virtue of a more favorable complexity term expressed as an average of the Rademacher complexities based on the ensemble’s mixture weights. We introduce and discuss several new multi-class ensemble algorithms benefiting from these guarantees, prove positive results for the H-consistency of several of them, and report the results of experiments showing that their performance compares favorably with that of multi-class versions of AdaBoost and Logistic Regression and their L1-regularized counterparts.

paragraphs: The paper develops ensemble algorithms for classification with multiple classes. The ensembles can include deep decision trees or other complex base classifiers while retaining strong generalization guarantees. The main question is how to account for the complexity of the classifiers used when assessing the combined model's ability to generalize.

The authors derive data-dependent bounds for convex ensembles using the Rademacher complexities of sub-families of base classifiers. Each sub-family's contribution depends on its assigned mixture weight, producing a weighted average complexity term. The bounds also improve the dependence on the number of classes. This makes the analysis sensitive to how the ensemble distributes weight among its available classifier families.

Several new algorithms follow from these guarantees, and the authors prove positive H-consistency results for several of them. Experiments show favorable performance against multi-class versions of AdaBoost and logistic regression, including their L1-regularized counterparts. Together, the theory and experiments support building multi-class ensembles from rich classifier families while controlling complexity through the ensemble's actual mixture.
summary.tldr: New multi-class boosting algorithms use complex base classifiers with generalization bounds that reflect their ensemble mixture weights.

title: Multi-Class Deep Boosting

abstract: We consider the task of building compact deep learning pipelines suitable for deploymenton storage and power constrained mobile devices. We propose a uni-fied framework to learn a broad family of structured parameter matrices that arecharacterized by the notion of low displacement rank. Our structured transformsadmit fast function and gradient evaluation, and span a rich range of parametersharing configurations whose statistical modeling capacity can be explicitly tunedalong a continuum from structured to unstructured. Experimental results showthat these transforms can significantly accelerate inference and forward/backwardpasses during training, and offer superior accuracy-compactness-speed tradeoffsin comparison to a number of existing techniques. In keyword spotting applicationsin mobile speech recognition, our methods are much more effective thanstandard linear low-rank bottleneck layers and nearly retain the performance ofstate of the art models, while providing more than 3.5-fold compression.

paragraphs: Deploying deep-learning systems on mobile devices requires managing limited storage and power. This paper proposes learning structured parameter matrices to make those systems more compact and computationally efficient. The matrices belong to a broad family characterized by low displacement rank, which provides a unified way to describe different parameter-sharing arrangements.

The framework allows modeling capacity to be tuned along a continuum from strongly structured matrices toward unstructured ones. Its transforms also support fast function and gradient evaluation, so the intended computational benefit applies both when making predictions and during training. This connects compact parameterization with the cost of forward and backward computation.

Experiments report improved tradeoffs among accuracy, compactness, and speed compared with several existing techniques. In mobile speech keyword spotting, the proposed methods are much more effective than standard linear low-rank bottleneck layers. They achieve more than 3.5-fold compression while nearly retaining state-of-the-art model performance. The results support structured transforms as a practical way to reduce model size without sacrificing comparable amounts of predictive quality.
summary.tldr: Learnable structured matrices improve accuracy–size–speed tradeoffs and achieve over 3.5-fold compression with nearly retained performance in mobile keyword spotting.

title: Structured Transforms for Small-Footprint Deep Learning

abstract: We introduce the Gaussian Process Convolution Model (GPCM), a two-stage nonparametric generative procedure to model stationary signals as the convolution between a continuous-time white-noise process and a continuous-time linear filter drawn from Gaussian process. The GPCM is a continuous-time nonparametric-window moving average process and, conditionally, is itself a Gaussian process with a nonparametric kernel defined in a probabilistic fashion. The generative model can be equivalently considered in the frequency domain, where the power spectral density of the signal is specified using a Gaussian process. One of the main contributions of the paper is to develop a novel variational free-energy approach based on inter-domain inducing variables that efficiently learns the continuous-time linear filter and infers the driving white-noise process. In turn, this scheme provides closed-form probabilistic estimates of the covariance kernel and the noise-free signal both in denoising and prediction scenarios. Additionally, the variational inference procedure provides closed-form expressions for the approximate posterior of the spectral density given the observed data, leading to new Bayesian nonparametric approaches to spectrum estimation. The proposed GPCM is validated using synthetic and real-world signals.
