paragraphs: The Gaussian Process Convolution Model builds a stationary signal by passing continuous-time white noise through a linear filter that is itself drawn from a Gaussian process. This makes the filter something to learn probabilistically. Conditional on the filter, the resulting signal is also a Gaussian process, with a flexibly specified covariance kernel.

The same construction has a frequency-domain interpretation in which a Gaussian process specifies the signal's power spectral density. The authors develop a variational free-energy method using inducing variables across domains to learn the filter efficiently and infer the driving noise. This connects learning temporal dependence with estimating how signal power is distributed across frequencies.

The inference procedure yields closed-form probabilistic estimates of the covariance kernel and noise-free signal for denoising and prediction. It also provides closed-form expressions for an approximate posterior over spectral density. Validation uses synthetic and real-world signals. The overall contribution is a shared probabilistic model for signal reconstruction, prediction, and spectrum estimation, with uncertainty represented in the learned quantities.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian-process model of random filters learns flexible stationary signal structure for denoising, prediction, and probabilistic spectrum estimation.

title: Learning Stationary Time Series using Gaussian Processes with Nonparametric Kernels

abstract: We propose to prune a random forest (RF) for resource-constrained prediction. We first construct a RF and then prune it to optimize expected feature cost & accuracy. We pose pruning RFs as a novel 0-1 integer program with linear constraints that encourages feature re-use. We establish total unimodularity of the constraint set to prove that the corresponding LP relaxation solves the original integer program. We then exploit connections to combinatorial optimization and develop an efficient primal-dual algorithm, scalable to large datasets. In contrast to our bottom-up approach, which benefits from good RF initialization, conventional methods are top-down acquiring features based on their utility value and is generally intractable, requiring heuristics. Empirically, our pruning algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art resource-constrained algorithms.

We then exploit connections to combinatorial optimization and develop an efficient primal-dual algorithm, scalable to large datasets. In contrast to our bottom-up approach, which benefits from good RF initialization, conventional methods are top-down acquiring features based on their utility value and is generally intractable, requiring heuristics. paragraphs: Prediction can be expensive when obtaining the features needed by a model consumes limited resources. This paper first constructs a random forest and then prunes it to balance expected feature cost with accuracy. Starting from a trained forest provides the structure that the pruning procedure refines for budget-constrained prediction.

The authors formulate pruning as a binary integer program with linear constraints that encourage feature reuse. They prove that the constraints are totally unimodular, a structural property allowing the corresponding linear-programming relaxation to solve the original integer problem. This supplies an exact optimization route for the stated formulation despite its discrete decisions.

Connections to combinatorial optimization then lead to an efficient primal-dual algorithm that scales to large datasets. The approach benefits from the initial forest and differs from conventional methods that acquire features through top-down utility decisions requiring heuristics. Empirically, the pruning algorithm outperforms existing resource-constrained methods. The contribution combines an explicit cost-and-accuracy objective, a tractable formulation, and an implementation strategy for applying it at scale.
summary.tldr: The paper prunes trained random forests through a tractable optimization that balances prediction accuracy and feature acquisition cost.

title: Pruning Random Forests for Prediction on a Budget

abstract: Adaptive stochastic gradient methods such as AdaGrad have gained popularity in particular for training deep neural networks. The most commonly used and studied variant maintains a diagonal matrix approximation to second order information by accumulating past gradients which are used to tune the step size adaptively. In certain situations the full-matrix variant of AdaGrad is expected to attain better performance, however in high dimensions it is computationally impractical. We present Ada-LR and RadaGrad two computationally efficient approximations to full-matrix AdaGrad based on randomized dimensionality reduction. They are able to capture dependencies between features and achieve similar performance to full-matrix AdaGrad but at a much smaller computational cost. We show that the regret of Ada-LR is close to the regret of full-matrix AdaGrad which can have an up-to exponentially smaller dependence on the dimension than the diagonal variant. Empirically, we show that Ada-LR and RadaGrad perform similarly to full-matrix AdaGrad. On the task of training convolutional neural networks as well as recurrent neural networks, RadaGrad achieves faster convergence than diagonal AdaGrad.

They are able to capture dependencies between features and achieve similar performance to full-matrix AdaGrad but at a much smaller computational cost. paragraphs: Adaptive gradient methods use past gradients to adjust optimization steps. The common diagonal form of AdaGrad tracks information separately for each coordinate. Full-matrix AdaGrad can also capture dependencies between features and may perform better in some situations, but its computational requirements become impractical in high-dimensional problems.

The paper introduces Ada-LR and RadaGrad, two approximations based on randomized dimensionality reduction. They aim to retain useful cross-feature information while reducing the cost of full-matrix adaptation. The theoretical analysis shows that Ada-LR's regret is close to that of full-matrix AdaGrad, whose dependence on dimension can be up to exponentially smaller than the diagonal variant's.

Experiments find that both approximations perform similarly to full-matrix AdaGrad at substantially lower computational cost. In convolutional and recurrent neural-network training, RadaGrad converges faster than diagonal AdaGrad in the reported evaluations. These findings support random projection as a practical way to preserve benefits of richer adaptive updates. The strongest dimensional advantage remains a possibility in favorable situations, rather than a guarantee that full-matrix information always produces that improvement.
summary.tldr: Randomized low-dimensional approximations retain full-matrix AdaGrad's feature dependencies at lower cost, with theoretical and empirical support.

title: Scalable Adaptive Stochastic Optimization Using Random Projections

abstract: Most deep reinforcement learning algorithms are data inefficient in complex and rich environments, limiting their applicability to many scenarios. One direction for improving data efficiency is multitask learning with shared neural network parameters, where efficiency may be improved through transfer across related tasks. In practice, however, this is not usually observed, because gradients from different tasks can interfere negatively, making learning unstable and sometimes even less data efficient. Another issue is the different reward schemes between tasks, which can easily lead to one task dominating the learning of a shared model. We propose a new approach for joint training of multiple tasks, which we refer to as Distral (DIStill & TRAnsfer Learning). Instead of sharing parameters between the different workers, we propose to share a distilled policy that captures common behaviour across tasks. Each worker is trained to solve its own task while constrained to stay close to the shared policy, while the shared policy is trained by distillation to be the centroid of all task policies. Both aspects of the learning process are derived by optimizing a joint objective function. We show that our approach supports efficient transfer on complex 3D environments, outperforming several related methods. Moreover, the proposed learning process is more robust and more stable---attributes that are critical in deep reinforcement learning.

Instead of sharing parameters between the different workers, we propose to share a distilled policy that captures common behaviour across tasks. Each worker is trained to solve its own task while constrained to stay close to the shared policy, while the shared policy is trained by distillation to be the centroid of all task policies. Both aspects of the learning process are derived by optimizing a joint objective function. We show that our approach supports efficient transfer on complex 3D environments, outperforming several related methods. Moreover, the proposed learning process is more robust and more stable---attributes that are critical in deep reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Learning several reinforcement-learning tasks together could reduce the experience needed for each one. Directly sharing neural-network parameters can undermine that benefit, however: updates from different tasks may conflict, and differences in rewards can let one task dominate. Distral introduces a shared behavioral reference to organize transfer across tasks.

Each task has its own policy, trained to solve that task while remaining close to a shared distilled policy. The shared policy is updated through distillation to represent a centroid of the individual policies. A joint objective governs both directions of learning, so task-specific behavior contributes to the common policy and the common policy guides each task.

This arrangement gives the tasks a common source of behavior while preserving their separate learning objectives. In complex three-dimensional environments, the authors report efficient transfer and better performance than several related methods. They also find the training process more stable and robust. These empirical findings address the interference and instability that motivated the approach to joint training.
summary.tldr: Distral transfers behavior through a shared distilled policy, improving multitask reinforcement learning in the evaluated three-dimensional environments.

title: Distral: Robust multitask reinforcement learning

abstract: We study causal discovery in a multi-environment setting, in which the functional relations for producing the variables from their direct causes remain the same across environments, while the distribution of exogenous noises may vary. We introduce the idea of using the invariance of the functional relations of the variables to their causes across a set of environments for structure learning. We define a notion of completeness for a causal inference algorithm in this setting and prove the existence of such algorithm by proposing the baseline algorithm. Additionally, we present an alternate algorithm that has significantly improved computational and sample complexity compared to the baseline algorithm. Experiment results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the other existing algorithms.

We introduce the idea of using the invariance of the functional relations of the variables to their causes across a set of environments for structure learning. We define a notion of completeness for a causal inference algorithm in this setting and prove the existence of such algorithm by proposing the baseline algorithm. Additionally, we present an alternate algorithm that has significantly improved computational and sample complexity compared to the baseline algorithm. Experiment results show that the proposed algorithm outperforms the other existing algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover causal relationships from observations gathered in multiple environments. Its setting assumes that the functional relationship between each variable and its direct causes stays fixed across environments. The distributions of external noise may change. That distinction supplies the stable structure the authors use to reason about causality.

The proposed approach uses invariance of those causal relationships as evidence for learning the causal structure. The authors define a notion of completeness for an inference algorithm in this setting, then construct a baseline algorithm that establishes the existence of an algorithm meeting that definition. This gives the approach a formal foundation under the specified environment assumptions.

A second algorithm significantly improves computational and sample complexity relative to the baseline. Experiments also show that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing algorithms considered in the evaluation. The work combines an existence result with a more efficient procedure, illustrating how changes in noise across environments can help structure learning when the underlying causal functions remain invariant.
summary.tldr: The paper learns causal structures across environments by exploiting stable causal functions despite changing external-noise distributions.

title: Learning Causal Structures Using Regression Invariance

abstract: The option framework integrates temporal abstraction into the reinforcement learning model through the introduction of macro-actions (i.e., options). Recent works leveraged on the mapping of Markov decision processes (MDPs) with options to semi-MDPs (SMDPs) and introduced SMDP-versions of exploration-exploitation algorithms (e.g., RMAX-SMDP and UCRL-SMDP) to analyze the impact of options on the learning performance. Nonetheless, the PAC-SMDP sample complexity of RMAX-SMDP can hardly be translated into equivalent PAC-MDP theoretical guarantees, while UCRL-SMDP requires prior knowledge of the parameters characterizing the distributions of the cumulative reward and duration of each option, which are hardly available in practice. In this paper, we remove this limitation by combining the SMDP view together with the inner Markov structure of options into a novel algorithm whose regret performance matches UCRL-SMDP's up to an additive regret term. We show scenarios where this term is negligible and the advantage of temporal abstraction is preserved. We also report preliminary empirical result supporting the theoretical findings.

Recent works leveraged on the mapping of Markov decision processes (MDPs) with options to semi-MDPs (SMDPs) and introduced SMDP-versions of exploration-exploitation algorithms (e.g., RMAX-SMDP and UCRL-SMDP) to analyze the impact of options on the learning performance. Nonetheless, the PAC-SMDP sample complexity of RMAX-SMDP can hardly be translated into equivalent PAC-MDP theoretical guarantees, while UCRL-SMDP requires prior knowledge of the parameters characterizing the distributions of the cumulative reward and duration of each option, which are hardly available in practice. In this paper, we remove this limitation by combining the SMDP view together with the inner Markov structure of options into a novel algorithm whose regret performance matches UCRL-SMDP's up to an additive regret term. We show scenarios where this term is negligible and the advantage of temporal abstraction is preserved. We also report preliminary empirical result supporting the theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Options are macro-actions that let a reinforcement-learning agent act over extended periods. They support temporal abstraction, but analyzing learning with them creates difficulties. Existing approaches based on semi-Markov decision processes either have guarantees that are difficult to translate back to the underlying process or require prior information about option rewards and durations.

This paper removes the prior-knowledge requirement of UCRL-SMDP by combining the semi-Markov perspective with the internal Markov structure of options. The resulting algorithm uses both levels of the problem: options as extended actions and the structure of what happens within them. This permits a regret analysis without the same advance knowledge of distributional parameters.

Its regret matches UCRL-SMDP up to an additional term. The authors identify scenarios where that term is negligible, preserving the learning advantage of temporal abstraction. Preliminary empirical results support the theory. The guarantee therefore makes the cost of removing prior knowledge explicit and shows circumstances in which that cost does not erase the benefit of using options.
summary.tldr: An option-based learning algorithm removes prior reward-and-duration knowledge requirements while preserving regret advantages in identified scenarios.

title: Regret Minimization in MDPs with Options without Prior Knowledge

abstract: We propose novel first-order stochastic approximation algorithms for canonical correlation analysis (CCA). Algorithms presented are instances of inexact matrix stochastic gradient (MSG) and inexact matrix exponentiated gradient (MEG), and achieve $\epsilon$-suboptimality in the population objective in $\operatorname{poly}(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ iterations. We also consider practical variants of the proposed algorithms and compare them with other methods for CCA both theoretically and empirically.
originalAbstract: We propose novel first-order stochastic approximation algorithms for canonical correlation analysis (CCA). Algorithms presented are instances of inexact matrix stochastic gradient (MSG) and inexact matrix exponentiated gradient (MEG), and achieve $\epsilon$-suboptimality in the population objective in $\operatorname{poly}(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ iterations. We also consider practical variants of the proposed algorithms and compare them with other methods for CCA both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: This paper develops first-order stochastic approximation algorithms for canonical correlation analysis, or CCA. Its focus is on obtaining useful optimization guarantees for stochastic procedures. The authors evaluate progress against the population objective, so the target of the guarantee is the underlying statistical objective rather than only an objective computed from a particular finite dataset.

The proposed algorithms are inexact versions of matrix stochastic gradient and matrix exponentiated gradient methods. The analysis shows that they achieve ε-suboptimality in a number of iterations polynomial in 1/ε. In plain language, the objective can be brought within a chosen tolerance of optimality with an iteration requirement that grows polynomially as that tolerance becomes stricter.

The paper also considers practical variants and compares its methods with other CCA approaches both theoretically and empirically. This combines convergence analysis with an examination of implementations intended for use. The stated contribution is a family of stochastic algorithms with population-level accuracy guarantees and comparative evaluation; the abstract does not claim that one method dominates all alternatives.
summary.tldr: Inexact stochastic matrix-gradient methods for CCA achieve population-objective accuracy in polynomially many iterations.

title: Stochastic Approximation for Canonical Correlation Analysis

abstract: We study adversarial attacks that manipulate the reward signals to control the actions chosen by a stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithm. We propose the first attack against two popular bandit algorithms: $\epsilon$-greedy and UCB, \emph{without} knowledge of the mean rewards. The attacker is able to spend only logarithmic effort, multiplied by a problem-specific parameter that becomes smaller as the bandit problem gets easier to attack. The result means the attacker can easily hijack the behavior of the bandit algorithm to promote or obstruct certain actions, say, a particular medical treatment. As bandits are seeing increasingly wide use in practice, our study exposes a significant security threat.
originalAbstract: We study adversarial attacks that manipulate the reward signals to control the actions chosen by a stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithm. We propose the first attack against two popular bandit algorithms: $\epsilon$-greedy and UCB, \emph{without} knowledge of the mean rewards. The attacker is able to spend only logarithmic effort, multiplied by a problem-specific parameter that becomes smaller as the bandit problem gets easier to attack. The result means the attacker can easily hijack the behavior of the bandit algorithm to promote or obstruct certain actions, say, a particular medical treatment. As bandits are seeing increasingly wide use in practice, our study exposes a significant security threat.

paragraphs: A stochastic multi-armed bandit algorithm learns which actions to choose from the rewards it observes. This paper examines what happens when an attacker can manipulate those reward signals. The attack targets the feedback driving learning, allowing the attacker to influence later action choices through the evidence the algorithm receives.

The authors develop attacks against two widely used algorithms, epsilon-greedy and UCB, without requiring knowledge of the actions' mean rewards. That distinction matters because the attacker does not need the underlying reward averages in advance to steer behavior. The paper characterizes the required attack effort as logarithmic, multiplied by a problem-specific factor that decreases when the setting is easier to attack.

The result shows that these learning algorithms can be redirected to favor or suppress particular actions with limited manipulation effort under the studied setup. A medical treatment is given as an example of an action whose selection could be affected, rather than as a reported deployment. The contribution exposes a security weakness in relying on reward feedback that an adversary can alter.
summary.tldr: Reward manipulation can steer epsilon-greedy and UCB bandits with logarithmic attack effort without knowing their mean rewards.

title: Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits

abstract: We introduce a game-theoretic approach to the study of recommendation systems with strategic content providers. Such systems should be fair and stable. Showing that traditional approaches fail to satisfy these requirements, we propose the Shapley mediator. We show that the Shapley mediator satisfies the fairness and stability requirements, runs in linear time, and is the only economically efficient mechanism satisfying these properties.

paragraphs: The paper studies recommendation systems in which content providers act strategically. This makes recommendation a problem involving incentives as well as selecting content: the system must account for providers who make choices within it. The authors use game theory to examine two requirements for such systems, fairness and stability, and show that traditional approaches do not satisfy these requirements.

Their proposed solution is the Shapley mediator, a mechanism for handling recommendations in this strategic setting. The central result is that it satisfies both the fairness and stability requirements established in the paper. These properties are considered together, so the contribution addresses their compatibility within one recommendation mechanism.

The authors also show that the mediator runs in linear time and is the unique economically efficient mechanism satisfying these properties. This uniqueness claim concerns the paper's particular requirements and setting. The findings connect a computationally efficient recommendation rule with formal guarantees about how a system treats strategic providers and remains stable.
summary.tldr: The Shapley mediator provides a linear-time recommendation mechanism with fairness, stability, and a uniqueness guarantee among economically efficient mechanisms.

title: A Game-Theoretic Approach to Recommendation Systems with Strategic Content Providers

abstract: Recently, considerable research effort has been devoted to developing deep architectures for topic models to learn topic structures. Although several deep models have been proposed to learn better topic proportions of documents, how to leverage the benefits of deep structures for learning word distributions of topics has not yet been rigorously studied. Here we propose a new multi-layer generative process on word distributions of topics, where each layer consists of a set of topics and each topic is drawn from a mixture of the topics of the layer above. As the topics in all layers can be directly interpreted by words, the proposed model is able to discover interpretable topic hierarchies. As a self-contained module, our model can be flexibly adapted to different kinds of topic models to improve their modelling accuracy and interpretability. Extensive experiments on text corpora demonstrate the advantages of the proposed model.

paragraphs: A topic model describes both how documents combine topics and how each topic distributes probability over words. Earlier deep topic models had largely focused on improving the document-side proportions. This paper develops a multilayer generative model for the word distributions themselves, making the internal structure of topics the object of hierarchical learning.

Every layer contains topics, and each topic is drawn from a mixture of topics in the layer above. That connection lets topics at different levels contribute to one another through a shared generative structure. Because every layer still represents topics through words, the hierarchy remains directly interpretable rather than becoming a sequence of features with no explicit vocabulary-level meaning.

The proposed construction is a self-contained module that can be incorporated into different topic models. Its intended benefit is to improve modeling accuracy while also revealing understandable relationships among topics. Experiments on text corpora demonstrate advantages of the approach. The contribution is therefore a reusable way to learn topic hierarchies through word distributions, alongside evidence that this structure is useful in practice.
summary.tldr: Dirichlet belief networks build interpretable topic hierarchies by generating each topic from mixtures of topics in the layer above.

title: Dirichlet belief networks for topic structure learning

abstract: Non-local methods exploiting the self-similarity of natural signals have been well studied, for example in image analysis and restoration. Existing approaches, however, rely on k-nearest neighbors (KNN) matching in a fixed feature space. The main hurdle in optimizing this feature space w.r.t. application performance is the non-differentiability of the KNN selection rule. To overcome this, we propose a continuous deterministic relaxation of KNN selection that maintains differentiability w.r.t. pairwise distances, but retains the original KNN as the limit of a temperature parameter approaching zero. To exploit our relaxation, we propose the neural nearest neighbors block (N3 block), a novel non-local processing layer that leverages the principle of self-similarity and can be used as building block in modern neural network architectures. We show its effectiveness for the set reasoning task of correspondence classification as well as for image restoration, including image denoising and single image super-resolution, where we outperform strong convolutional neural network (CNN) baselines and recent non-local models that rely on KNN selection in hand-chosen features spaces.

paragraphs: Non-local image methods use similarities between different parts of a signal to help process it. Many select the nearest neighbors in a fixed feature space, but the discrete selection rule makes it difficult to learn that space directly for the application. The paper addresses this obstacle by replacing hard neighbor selection with a differentiable relaxation.

The relaxation is continuous and deterministic, and remains differentiable with respect to pairwise distances. A temperature parameter controls its behavior, with ordinary nearest-neighbor selection recovered as the temperature approaches zero. The authors incorporate this mechanism into the neural nearest neighbors block, or N3 block, which can serve as a non-local layer inside a neural network.

The block lets networks exploit self-similarity while making the matching representation amenable to optimization. The authors demonstrate effectiveness on correspondence classification, image denoising, and single-image super-resolution. For image restoration, they report outperforming strong convolutional baselines and recent non-local models using nearest-neighbor selection in hand-chosen feature spaces. These findings support learning the matching process together with the application.
summary.tldr: A differentiable relaxation of nearest-neighbor selection lets neural networks learn non-local matching for restoration and correspondence tasks.

title: Neural Nearest Neighbors Networks

abstract: We propose a new parametric framework, called k-ReLU, for computing precise and scalable convex relaxations used to certify neural networks. The key idea is to approximate the output of multiple ReLUs in a layer jointly instead of separately. This joint relaxation captures dependencies between the inputs to different ReLUs in a layer and thus overcomes the convex barrier imposed by the single neuron triangle relaxation and its approximations. The framework is parametric in the number of k ReLUs it considers jointly and can be combined with existing verifiers in order to improve their precision. Our experimental results show that k-ReLU en- ables significantly more precise certification than existing state-of-the-art verifiers while maintaining scalability.

paragraphs: Neural network certification uses mathematical approximations to establish properties of a network. The precision of those approximations matters: a loose representation can leave a verifier unable to establish a property. This paper focuses on convex relaxations of ReLU activations and the precision barrier created by treating each neuron separately.

The proposed framework, k-ReLU, approximates groups of ReLUs within a layer jointly. This lets the approximation retain relationships between the inputs of different neurons. Those dependencies are lost in the single-neuron triangle relaxation and its approximations. The parameter k specifies how many ReLUs are considered together, making the size of the joint treatment an explicit part of the framework.

The method can be incorporated into existing verifiers to improve their precision. Experiments report substantially more precise certification than the compared state-of-the-art systems while retaining scalability. The contribution is therefore both a richer mathematical approximation and a way to strengthen verification tools by accounting for interactions that independent neuron approximations discard.
summary.tldr: k-ReLU improves neural network certification by jointly approximating groups of neurons and preserving dependencies between them.

title: Beyond the Single Neuron Convex Barrier for Neural Network Certification

abstract: Word2Vec (W2V) and Glove are popular word embedding algorithms that perform well on a variety of natural language processing tasks. The algorithms are fast, efficient and their embeddings widely used. Moreover, the W2V algorithm has recently been adopted in the field of graph embedding, where it underpins several leading algorithms. However, despite their ubiquity and the relative simplicity of their common architecture, what the embedding parameters of W2V and Glove learn, and why that it useful in downstream tasks largely remains a mystery. We show that different interactions of PMI vectors encode semantic properties that can be captured in low dimensional word embeddings by suitable projection, theoretically explaining why the embeddings of W2V and Glove work, and, in turn, revealing an interesting mathematical interconnection between the semantic relationships of relatedness, similarity, paraphrase and analogy.

paragraphs: Word2Vec and GloVe produce useful word representations, yet their effectiveness leaves a theoretical question: what semantic information do their parameters capture? This paper addresses that question through pointwise mutual information, or PMI, vectors. It seeks a probabilistic explanation connecting the statistics represented by embeddings with the semantic relationships they support.

The authors show that different interactions among PMI vectors encode different semantic properties. Suitable projections can preserve these properties in low-dimensional word embeddings. This supplies a theoretical account of why Word2Vec and GloVe work: their compact representations can capture meaningful relationships that are already present in the underlying PMI-vector structure.

The analysis also reveals mathematical connections among relatedness, similarity, paraphrase, and analogy. These relationships are treated as connected consequences of the same probabilistic representation, helping explain how several kinds of semantic behavior can coexist in an embedding. The contribution is an account of what the embeddings learn and why it can be useful, tying their observed utility to explicit mathematical relationships.
summary.tldr: Interactions among PMI vectors explain how Word2Vec and GloVe embeddings capture connected semantic relationships such as similarity, paraphrase, and analogy.

title: What the Vec? Towards Probabilistically Grounded Embeddings

abstract: Flow-based generative models parameterize probability distributions through an invertible transformation and can be trained by maximum likelihood. Invertible residual networks provide a flexible family of transformations where only Lipschitz conditions rather than strict architectural constraints are needed for enforcing invertibility. However, prior work trained invertible residual networks for density estimation by relying on biased log-density estimates whose bias increased with the network's expressiveness. We give a tractable unbiased estimate of the log density, and reduce the memory required during training by a factor of ten. Furthermore, we improve invertible residual blocks by proposing the use of activation functions that avoid gradient saturation and generalizing the Lipschitz condition to induced mixed norms. The resulting approach, called Residual Flows, achieves state-of-the-art performance on density estimation amongst flow-based models, and outperforms networks that use coupling blocks at joint generative and discriminative modeling.

However, previous density-estimation methods for these networks used biased log-density estimates, and that bias grew as the networks became more expressive. This paper addresses that obstacle.

The resulting model achieves reported state-of-the-art density-estimation performance among flow-based approaches. It also outperforms coupling-block networks on joint generative and discriminative modeling. The work connects a correction to the training estimator with memory savings and architectural improvements, showing that flexible residual transformations can support strong density modeling without the earlier estimator's expressiveness-dependent bias.
summary.tldr: Residual Flows combines unbiased log-density estimation, lower training memory, and improved invertible residual blocks for strong generative modeling.

title: Residual Flows for Invertible Generative Modeling

abstract: Future neural interfaces will read and write population neural activity with high spatial and temporal resolution, for diverse applications. For example, an artificial retina may restore vision to the blind by electrically stimulating retinal ganglion cells. Such devices must tune their function, based on stimulating and recording, to match the function of the circuit. However, existing methods for characterizing the neural interface scale poorly with the number of electrodes, limiting their practical applicability. This work tests the idea that using prior information from previous experiments and closed-loop measurements may greatly increase the efficiency of the neural interface. Large-scale, high-density electrical recording and stimulation in primate retina were used as a lab prototype for an artificial retina. Three key calibration steps were optimized: spike sorting in the presence of stimulation artifacts, response modeling, and adaptive stimulation. For spike sorting, exploiting the similarity of electrical artifact across electrodes and experiments substantially reduced the number of required measurements. For response modeling, a joint model that captures the inverse relationship between recorded spike amplitude and electrical stimulation threshold from previously recorded retinas resulted in greater consistency and efficiency. For adaptive stimulation, choosing which electrodes to stimulate based on probability estimates from previous measurements improved efficiency. Similar improvements resulted from using either non-adaptive stimulation with a joint model across cells, or adaptive stimulation with an independent model for each cell. Finally, image reconstruction revealed that these improvements may translate to improved performance of an artificial retina.

paragraphs: Neural interfaces that stimulate cells need calibration to determine how electrical inputs produce neural responses. As electrode counts increase, collecting enough measurements becomes difficult. This paper studies whether information from earlier experiments and measurements chosen during calibration can reduce that burden, using electrical recording and stimulation in primate retina as a laboratory prototype for an artificial retina.

The authors improve three calibration components. For spike sorting, similarities in electrical stimulation artifacts across electrodes and experiments reduce the measurements needed. For response modeling, a joint model uses a relationship observed in previous retinas: larger recorded spike amplitudes correspond to lower stimulation thresholds. For adaptive stimulation, probability estimates from existing measurements guide which electrodes to stimulate next.

Both sharing information across cells and choosing measurements adaptively improve efficiency. Similar gains arise from non-adaptive stimulation with a joint model and adaptive stimulation with separate models for individual cells. Image reconstruction results suggest that more efficient calibration may improve artificial-retina performance, while keeping that potential application distinct from the demonstrated laboratory calibration improvements.
summary.tldr: Prior experimental information and adaptive stimulation make retinal-interface calibration more efficient, with reconstruction results suggesting potential artificial-retina benefits.

title: Efficient characterization of electrically evoked responses for neural interfaces

abstract: We present a novel class of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for set functions, i.e., data indexed with the powerset of a finite set. The convolutions are derived as linear, shift-equivariant functions for various notions of shifts on set functions. The framework is fundamentally different from graph convolutions based on the Laplacian, as it provides not one but several basic shifts, one for each element in the ground set. Prototypical experiments with several set function classification tasks on synthetic datasets and on datasets derived from real-world hypergraphs demonstrate the potential of our new powerset CNNs.

paragraphs: A set function assigns values to subsets of a finite collection. Its inputs are therefore indexed by the collection's powerset: the set of all possible subsets. This paper introduces convolutional neural networks designed for that structure, providing a way to define convolution when the underlying data organization consists of subsets.

The authors derive convolutions as linear functions that respect specified shifts on set functions. Shift equivariance means that shifting the input corresponds to shifting the output in the appropriate way. Their framework permits several notions of shift and includes a basic shift for each element of the underlying set, making its construction fundamentally different from graph convolutions based on a Laplacian.

The paper evaluates prototype powerset networks on several set-function classification tasks. These use synthetic data and data derived from real-world hypergraphs. The experiments demonstrate the potential of the proposed architecture. The central contribution is a structured definition of convolution for set functions, accompanied by initial classification evidence that the resulting networks can be useful.
summary.tldr: Powerset CNNs define shift-equivariant convolutions for data indexed by subsets and show promise on set-function classification tasks.

title: Powerset Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Dynamic mechanisms offer powerful techniques to improve on both revenue and efficiency by linking sequential auctions using state information, but these techniques rely on exact distributional information of the buyers’ valuations (present and future), which limits their use in learning settings. In this paper, we consider the problem of contextual auctions where the seller gradually learns a model of the buyer's valuation as a function of the context (e.g., item features) and seeks a pricing policy that optimizes revenue. Building on the concept of a bank account mechanism---a special class of dynamic mechanisms that is known to be revenue-optimal---we develop a non-clairvoyant dynamic mechanism that is robust to both estimation errors in the buyer's value distribution and strategic behavior on the part of the buyer. We then tailor its structure to achieve a policy with provably low regret against a constant approximation of the optimal dynamic mechanism in contextual auctions. Our result substantially improves on previous results that only provide revenue guarantees against static benchmarks.

paragraphs: Sequential auctions let a seller connect decisions across time instead of treating each sale independently. That flexibility can improve revenue, but existing dynamic mechanisms depend on knowing buyers’ present and future valuation distributions exactly. The paper addresses a seller who must learn how item features or other context influence a buyer’s value.

The proposed mechanism builds on a bank account mechanism, a class of mechanisms that carries state between auctions and is known to support revenue optimality. The authors develop a version that does not need advance knowledge of future valuations. Its design accounts for both errors in estimated valuation distributions and a buyer’s strategic behavior.

The resulting pricing policy has a provably low regret guarantee against a constant approximation of the optimal dynamic mechanism. This qualification matters: the comparison is to an approximation of that dynamic benchmark. The advance over earlier guarantees is the benchmark itself, which captures revenue opportunities from linking auctions rather than evaluating the seller only against static policies.
summary.tldr: A dynamic auction mechanism learns contextual valuations while handling estimation errors and strategic buyers, with low regret against an approximate dynamic benchmark.

title: A Robust Non-Clairvoyant Dynamic Mechanism for Contextual Auctions

abstract: Unsupervised learning of generative models has seen tremendous progress over recent years, in particular due to generative adversarial networks (GANs), variational autoencoders, and flow-based models. GANs have dramatically improved sample quality, but suffer from two drawbacks: (i) they mode-drop, \ie, do not cover the full support of the train data, and (ii) they do not allow for likelihood evaluations on held-out data. In contrast likelihood-based training encourages models to cover the full support of the train data, but yields poorer samples. These mutual shortcomings can in principle be addressed by training generative latent variable models in a hybrid adversarial-likelihood manner. However, we show that commonly made parametric assumptions create a conflict between them, making successful hybrid models non trivial. As a solution, we propose the use of deep invertible transformations in the latent variable decoder. This approach allows for likelihood computations in image space, is more efficient than fully invertible models, and can take full advantage of adversarial training. We show that our model significantly improves over existing hybrid models: offering GAN-like samples, IS and FID scores that are competitive with fully adversarial models and improved likelihood scores.

paragraphs: The paper addresses a tension between producing convincing generated images and assigning probabilities to real images. Adversarial models can produce strong samples while missing parts of the training distribution. Likelihood-based training encourages broader coverage, but the abstract describes its samples as poorer. Combining the two objectives is therefore attractive, yet technically difficult.

The authors show that commonly used parametric assumptions can make adversarial and likelihood objectives conflict. Their proposed solution places deep invertible transformations inside a latent-variable model's decoder. This design permits likelihood calculations directly in image space while retaining the benefits of adversarial training. It is also described as more efficient than making the entire model invertible.

The reported model improves over existing hybrid approaches, producing samples described as GAN-like alongside better likelihood scores. Its IS and FID scores are competitive with fully adversarial models. These findings support the proposed decoder as a way to reconcile the objectives more successfully; they do not establish that combining objectives automatically eliminates missing modes.
summary.tldr: Invertible transformations inside a latent-variable decoder improve the combination of adversarial sample quality and likelihood-based modeling.

title: Adaptive Density Estimation for Generative Models

abstract: We propose a novel method for computing exact pointwise robustness of deep neural networks for all convex lp norms. Our algorithm, GeoCert, finds the largest lp ball centered at an input point x0, within which the output class of a given neural network with ReLU nonlinearities remains unchanged. We relate the problem of computing pointwise robustness of these networks to that of computing the maximum norm ball with a fixed center that can be contained in a non-convex polytope. This is a challenging problem in general, however we show that there exists an efficient algorithm to compute this for polyhedral complices. Further we show that piecewise linear neural networks partition the input space into a polyhedral complex. Our algorithm has the ability to almost immediately output a nontrivial lower bound to the pointwise robustness which is iteratively improved until it ultimately becomes tight. We empirically show that our approach generates a distance lower bounds that are tighter compared to prior work, under moderate time constraints.

paragraphs: GeoCert measures robustness around a specific input to a ReLU neural network. It seeks the largest ball centered on that input within which the predicted class stays unchanged. The method covers all convex lp norms, allowing the size of an input perturbation to be measured in different norm geometries.

The authors reformulate this task as fitting a fixed-center norm ball inside a nonconvex polyhedral region. Although that geometric problem is difficult in general, they identify an efficient algorithm for polyhedral complexes and show that piecewise-linear neural networks partition input space into such a complex. This structure connects network behavior to a geometric computation.

GeoCert can produce a nontrivial robustness lower bound almost immediately and improve it iteratively until it becomes exact. An intermediate bound therefore certifies a region of unchanged classification even before the full computation finishes. Under moderate time limits, the reported experiments produce tighter distance lower bounds than prior work, supporting the usefulness of these progressively refined certificates.
summary.tldr: GeoCert uses neural-network geometry to progressively certify and ultimately compute exact pointwise robustness for convex lp norms.

title: Provable Certificates for Adversarial Examples: Fitting a Ball in the Union of Polytopes

abstract: Capsule networks have recently gained a great deal of interest as a new architecture of neural networks that can be more robust to input perturbations than similar-sized CNNs. Capsule networks have two major distinctions from the conventional CNNs: (i) each layer consists of a set of capsules that specialize in disjoint regions of the feature space and (ii) the routing-by-agreement coordinates connections between adjacent capsule layers. Although the routing-by-agreement is capable of filtering out noisy predictions of capsules by dynamically adjusting their influences, its unsupervised clustering nature causes two weaknesses: (i) high computational complexity and (ii) cluster assumption that may not hold in presence of heavy input noise. In this work, we propose a novel and surprisingly simple routing strategy called self-routing where each capsule is routed independently by its subordinate routing network. Therefore, the agreement between capsules is not required anymore but both poses and activations of upper-level capsules are obtained in a way similar to Mixture-of-Experts. Our experiments on CIFAR-10, SVHN and SmallNORB show that the self-routing performs more robustly against white-box adversarial attacks and affine transformations, requiring less computation.

paragraphs: Capsule networks organize each layer into capsules that specialize in different regions of feature space. Traditional routing by agreement coordinates connections between neighboring layers and can filter noisy capsule predictions. This paper identifies two drawbacks of that process: substantial computation and a clustering assumption that may break down under heavy input noise.

The authors replace agreement-based coordination with self-routing. Each capsule uses its own subordinate routing network to determine its routing independently. Upper-layer capsule poses and activations are then obtained through a mechanism similar to a mixture of experts. This removes the requirement for capsules to agree with one another before establishing their influence on the next layer.

Experiments on CIFAR-10, SVHN, and SmallNORB show greater robustness to white-box adversarial attacks and affine transformations while requiring less computation. The findings indicate that the simpler routing mechanism can improve both efficiency and empirical robustness in the tested settings. They also support reconsidering whether agreement-based clustering is necessary to obtain useful capsule behavior.
summary.tldr: Self-routing lets capsules route independently, reducing computation and improving robustness to tested adversarial attacks and affine transformations.

title: Self-Routing Capsule Networks

abstract: For joint inference over multiple variables, a variety of structured prediction techniques have been developed to model correlations among variables and thereby improve predictions. However, many classical approaches suffer from one of two primary drawbacks: they either lack the ability to model high-order correlations among variables while maintaining computationally tractable inference, or they do not allow to explicitly model known correlations. To address this shortcoming, we introduce ‘Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks,’ for which we develop inference techniques that allow to both model explicit local and implicit higher-order correlations while maintaining tractability of inference. We apply the proposed method to tasks from the natural language processing and computer vision domain and demonstrate its general utility.
originalAbstract: For joint inference over multiple variables, a variety of structured prediction techniques have been developed to model correlations among variables and thereby improve predictions. However, many classical approaches suffer from one of two primary drawbacks: they either lack the ability to model high-order correlations among variables while maintaining computationally tractable inference, or they do not allow to explicitly model known correlations. To address this shortcoming, we introduce ‘Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks,’ for which we develop inference techniques that allow to both model explicit local and implicit higher-order correlations while maintaining tractability of inference. We apply the proposed method to tasks from the natural language processing and computer vision domain and demonstrate its general utility.

paragraphs: Structured prediction makes decisions about multiple related variables together. Accounting for their relationships can improve the resulting predictions, but modeling those relationships creates a computational challenge. The paper identifies two recurring shortcomings: some methods struggle to represent higher-order correlations while keeping inference tractable, and others cannot explicitly incorporate correlations that are already known.

Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks are designed to address both needs within one model. They combine explicitly represented local correlations with implicitly represented higher-order correlations. The authors also develop inference techniques that retain computational tractability. This pairing matters because greater expressive power is useful only if the model can still produce joint predictions through a manageable inference procedure.

The method is applied to tasks in natural language processing and computer vision, where the authors report evidence of its general utility. The contribution is the combination of explicit relational structure, richer implicit dependencies, and tractable inference. The supplied findings support usefulness across those application areas without establishing a particular numerical improvement or claiming that every structured prediction task benefits equally.
summary.tldr: Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks combine explicit local and implicit higher-order correlations while keeping joint inference tractable.

title: Graph Structured Prediction Energy Networks

abstract: Finding an effective medical treatment often requires a search by trial and error. Making this search more efficient by minimizing the number of unnecessary trials could lower both costs and patient suffering. We formalize this problem as learning a policy for finding a near-optimal treatment in a minimum number of trials using a causal inference framework. We give a model-based dynamic programming algorithm which learns from observational data while being robust to unmeasured confounding. To reduce time complexity, we suggest a greedy algorithm which bounds the near-optimality constraint. The methods are evaluated on synthetic and real-world healthcare data and compared to model-free reinforcement learning. We find that our methods compare favorably to the model-free baseline while offering a more transparent trade-off between search time and treatment efficacy.

paragraphs: Finding an effective treatment can require trying several options, making the sequence of trials part of the problem. This paper formalizes the goal as learning a policy that finds a near-optimal treatment using as few trials as possible. The objective explicitly connects treatment quality with the effort required to discover a suitable option.

The authors develop a model-based dynamic-programming algorithm within a causal inference framework. It learns from observational data and is described as robust to unmeasured confounding. They also propose a greedy alternative to reduce computational complexity. That alternative bounds the near-optimality constraint, linking the simplified search procedure to the requirement that the selected treatment be sufficiently effective.

Evaluations use synthetic data and real-world healthcare data, with model-free reinforcement learning as a comparison. The proposed methods compare favorably in those evaluations while making the trade-off between search length and treatment efficacy more transparent. The contribution is a way to study treatment selection as a sequential causal search problem, where avoiding unnecessary trials and finding an effective treatment are jointly represented in the objective.
summary.tldr: Causal treatment-search algorithms learn from observational data to balance fewer trials against finding a near-optimal treatment.

title: Learning to search efficiently for causally near-optimal treatments

abstract: Non-local self-similarity in natural images has been well studied as an effective prior in image restoration. However, for single image super-resolution (SISR), most existing deep non-local methods (e.g., non-local neural networks) only exploit similar patches within the same scale of the low-resolution (LR) input image. Consequently, the restoration is limited to using the same-scale information while neglecting potential high-resolution (HR) cues from other scales. In this paper, we explore the cross-scale patch recurrence property of a natural image, i.e., similar patches tend to recur many times across different scales. This is achieved using a novel cross-scale internal graph neural network (IGNN). Specifically, we dynamically construct a cross-scale graph by searching k-nearest neighboring patches in the downsampled LR image for each query patch in the LR image. We then obtain the corresponding k HR neighboring patches in the LR image and aggregate them adaptively in accordance to the edge label of the constructed graph. In this way, the HR information can be passed from k HR neighboring patches to the LR query patch to help it recover more detailed textures. Besides, these internal image-specific LR/HR exemplars are also significant complements to the external information learned from the training dataset. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of IGNN against the state-of-the-art SISR methods including existing non-local networks on standard benchmarks.

The authors argue that this leaves useful detail cues unused: a pattern appearing at another scale can provide information relevant to reconstructing a low-resolution patch.

This transfers detail from image-specific examples to the patch being reconstructed. Those internal low- and high-resolution relationships complement information learned from the external training dataset. Experiments on standard benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach against state-of-the-art super-resolution methods, including existing non-local networks, supporting the value of searching across scales.
summary.tldr: A graph network uses recurring patches across image scales to supply image-specific detail cues for super-resolution.

title: Cross-Scale Internal Graph Neural Network for Image Super-Resolution

abstract: We propose a general physics-based deep learning architecture for wave-based imaging problems. A key difficulty in imaging problems with a varying background wave speed is that the medium ``bends'' the waves differently depending on their position and direction. This space-bending geometry makes the equivariance to translations of convolutional networks an undesired inductive bias. We build an interpretable neural architecture inspired by Fourier integral operators (FIOs) which approximate the wave physics. FIOs model a wide range of imaging modalities, from seismology and radar to Doppler and ultrasound. We focus on learning the geometry of wave propagation captured by FIOs, which is implicit in the data, via a loss based on optimal transport. The proposed FIONet performs significantly better than the usual baselines on a number of imaging inverse problems, especially in out-of-distribution tests.

paragraphs: Wave-based imaging becomes difficult when wave speed varies across the background medium. Waves bend differently depending on where they travel and their direction. The paper argues that this geometry makes the translation equivariance built into convolutional networks an unsuitable bias for these problems: moving a pattern can change its relationship to wave propagation.

The proposed FIONet architecture takes inspiration from Fourier integral operators, which approximate wave physics across imaging modalities including seismology, radar, Doppler imaging, and ultrasound. Its interpretable structure focuses learning on the geometry of propagation that is implicit in the data. A loss based on optimal transport is used to learn that geometry.

On a number of imaging inverse problems, FIONet performs significantly better than the usual baselines considered, with particularly strong results on out-of-distribution tests. These findings support the value of matching a network's structure to the way waves actually move through a varying medium. The paper's central contribution is a physics-based architectural approach that learns the relevant propagation geometry from data.
summary.tldr: FIONet learns wave-propagation geometry through a physics-inspired architecture and outperforms usual baselines, especially in out-of-distribution imaging tests.

title: Learning the Geometry of Wave-Based Imaging

abstract: We present a new method for linear and nonlinear, lagged and contemporaneous constraint-based causal discovery from observational time series in the presence of latent confounders. We show that existing causal discovery methods such as FCI and variants suffer from low recall in the autocorrelated time series case and identify low effect size of conditional independence tests as the main reason. Information-theoretical arguments show that effect size can often be increased if causal parents are included in the conditioning sets. To identify parents early on, we suggest an iterative procedure that utilizes novel orientation rules to determine ancestral relationships already during the edge removal phase. We prove that the method is order-independent, and sound and complete in the oracle case. Extensive simulation studies for different numbers of variables, time lags, sample sizes, and further cases demonstrate that our method indeed achieves much higher recall than existing methods for the case of autocorrelated continuous variables while keeping false positives at the desired level. This performance gain grows with stronger autocorrelation. At github.com/jakobrunge/tigramite we provide Python code for all methods involved in the simulation studies.

paragraphs: Causal discovery from observational time series becomes difficult when variables are autocorrelated and hidden confounders may be present. This paper addresses both lagged and contemporaneous relationships, including linear and nonlinear cases. It identifies weak effect sizes in conditional independence tests as a main reason existing methods can miss causal relationships in autocorrelated data.

Information-theoretic arguments suggest that conditioning on causal parents can often strengthen those test effects. The proposed algorithm therefore tries to identify parents earlier in discovery. It iteratively uses new orientation rules to establish ancestral relationships while edges are still being removed, allowing emerging causal information to guide subsequent testing.

The authors prove order independence and establish soundness and completeness in the oracle case, where the required independence information is available without testing error. Simulations across different variable counts, lags, and sample sizes show substantially higher recall for autocorrelated continuous variables while maintaining false positives at the desired level. The gains increase with stronger autocorrelation, supporting the method's focus on improving the effectiveness of independence tests.
summary.tldr: Early identification of causal parents improves simulated causal-discovery recall in autocorrelated time series with hidden confounders while controlling false positives.

title: High-recall causal discovery for autocorrelated time series with latent confounders

abstract: Despite tremendous success in many application scenarios, deep learning faces serious intellectual property (IP) infringement threats. Considering the cost of designing and training a good model, infringements will significantly infringe the interests of the original model owner. Recently, many impressive works have emerged for deep model IP protection. However, they either are vulnerable to ambiguity attacks, or require changes in the target network structure by replacing its original normalization layers and hence cause significant performance drops. To this end, we propose a new passport-aware normalization formulation, which is generally applicable to most existing normalization layers and only needs to add another passport-aware branch for IP protection. This new branch is jointly trained with the target model but discarded in the inference stage. Therefore it causes no structure change in the target model. Only when the model IP is suspected to be stolen by someone, the private passport-aware branch is added back for ownership verification. Through extensive experiments, we verify its effectiveness in both image and 3D point recognition models. It is demonstrated to be robust not only to common attack techniques like fine-tuning and model compression, but also to ambiguity attacks. By further combining it with trigger-set based methods, both black-box and white-box verification can be achieved for enhanced security of deep learning models deployed in real systems.

paragraphs: Protecting a trained model's ownership can be difficult when verification methods are vulnerable to attacks or alter the network in ways that reduce performance. This paper introduces passport-aware normalization, a formulation applicable to most existing normalization layers. It adds a private branch for ownership protection while preserving the target model's structure during ordinary inference.

The passport-aware branch is trained jointly with the model, then discarded for inference. If ownership is disputed, the private branch is attached again for verification. This arrangement separates the additional ownership-verification machinery from the deployed inference structure. The authors also combine the approach with trigger-set methods to support both black-box and white-box verification.

Experiments on image-recognition and three-dimensional point-recognition models demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The reported robustness covers fine-tuning, model compression, and ambiguity attacks, which are among the threats motivating the work. These findings support a practical protection mechanism that can be added during training and restored when verification is needed. The security claims reflect the attacks evaluated, rather than establishing resistance to every possible method of compromising ownership verification.
summary.tldr: A privately retained normalization branch enables model-ownership verification without changing the model's inference structure and withstands several tested attacks.

title: Passport-aware Normalization for Deep Model Protection

abstract: Measuring and promoting policy diversity is critical for solving games with strong non-transitive dynamics where strategic cycles exist, and there is no consistent winner (e.g., Rock-Paper-Scissors). With that in mind, maintaining a pool of diverse policies via open-ended learning is an attractive solution, which can generate auto-curricula to avoid being exploited. However, in conventional open-ended learning algorithms, there are no widely accepted definitions for diversity, making it hard to construct and evaluate the diverse policies. In this work, we summarize previous concepts of diversity and work towards offering a unified measure of diversity in multi-agent open-ended learning to include all elements in Markov games, based on both Behavioral Diversity (BD) and Response Diversity (RD). At the trajectory distribution level, we re-define BD in the state-action space as the discrepancies of occupancy measures. For the reward dynamics, we propose RD to characterize diversity through the responses of policies when encountering different opponents. We also show that many current diversity measures fall in one of the categories of BD or RD but not both. With this unified diversity measure, we design the corresponding diversity-promoting objective and population effectivity when seeking the best responses in open-ended learning. We validate our methods in both relatively simple games like matrix game, non-transitive mixture model, and the complex \textit{Google Research Football} environment. The population found by our methods reveals the lowest exploitability, highest population effectivity in matrix game and non-transitive mixture model, as well as the largest goal difference when interacting with opponents of various levels in \textit{Google Research Football}.

These findings support considering both behavioral variation and opponent-dependent outcomes when constructing policy populations.
summary.tldr: Combining behavioral and opponent-response diversity improves policy populations in evaluated games with cyclic strategic relationships.

title: Towards Unifying Behavioral and Response Diversity for Open-ended Learning in Zero-sum Games

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning aims to improve the sample efficiency of policy learning by modeling the dynamics of the environment. Recently, the latent dynamics model is further developed to enable fast planning in a compact space. It summarizes the high-dimensional experiences of an agent, which mimics the memory function of humans. Learning policies via imagination with the latent model shows great potential for solving complex tasks. However, only considering memories from the true experiences in the process of imagination could limit its advantages. Inspired by the memory prosthesis proposed by neuroscientists, we present a novel model-based reinforcement learning framework called Imagining with Derived Memory (IDM). It enables the agent to learn policy from enriched diverse imagination with prediction-reliability weight, thus improving sample efficiency and policy robustness. Experiments on various high-dimensional visual control tasks in the DMControl benchmark demonstrate that IDM outperforms previous state-of-the-art methods in terms of policy robustness and further improves the sample efficiency of the model-based method.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning uses a learned account of environment dynamics to improve policy learning from experience. Latent dynamics models make this possible in a compact representation of high-dimensional observations. This paper argues that imagination can be restricted when it considers only memories derived from actual experiences, and proposes Imagining with Derived Memory, or IDM.

Inspired by the idea of a memory prosthesis, IDM enriches the diversity of imagined experience available for policy learning. It also weights that imagination by prediction reliability. The combination aims to provide more varied learning material while accounting for how dependable the model's predictions are, linking the amount of imagined experience to its usefulness.

Experiments examine high-dimensional visual control tasks in the DMControl benchmark. The authors report stronger policy robustness than previous state-of-the-art methods and improved sample efficiency for model-based learning. These findings support enriching the imagination process as a way to make better use of learned dynamics in the evaluated control tasks.
summary.tldr: IDM enriches imagined experience and weights it by prediction reliability to improve visual-control policy robustness and sample efficiency.

title: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning via Imagination with Derived Memory

abstract: Biological synaptic plasticity exhibits nonlinearities that are not accounted for by classic Hebbian learning rules. Here, we introduce a simple family of generalized nonlinear Hebbian learning rules. We study the computations implemented by their dynamics in the simple setting of a neuron receiving feedforward inputs. These nonlinear Hebbian rules allow a neuron to learn tensor decompositions of its higher- order input correlations. The particular input correlation decomposed and the form of the decomposition depend on the location of nonlinearities in the plasticity rule. For simple, biologically motivated parameters, the neuron learns eigenvectors of higher-order input correlation tensors. We prove that tensor eigenvectors are attractors and determine their basins of attraction. We calculate the volume of those basins, showing that the dominant eigenvector has the largest basin of attraction. We then study arbitrary learning rules and find that any learning rule that admits a finite Taylor expansion into the neural input and output also has stable equilibria at generalized eigenvectors of higher-order input correlation tensors. Nonlinearities in synaptic plasticity thus allow a neuron to encode higher-order input correlations in a simple fashion.

This paper introduces generalized nonlinear Hebbian rules and studies a single neuron receiving feedforward inputs. The goal is to identify the computations that emerge from those learning dynamics, particularly their ability to represent higher-order relationships among inputs.

title: Tensor decompositions of higher-order correlations by nonlinear Hebbian plasticity

abstract: We study the generalization performance of $\text{\emph{full-batch}}$ optimization algorithms for stochastic convex optimization: these are first-order methods that only access the exact gradient of the empirical risk (rather than gradients with respect to individual data points), that include a wide range of algorithms such as gradient descent, mirror descent, and their regularized and/or accelerated variants. We provide a new separation result showing that, while algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent can generalize and optimize the population risk to within $\epsilon$ after $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, full-batch methods either need at least $\Omega(1/\epsilon^4)$ iterations or exhibit a dimension-dependent sample complexity.

We provide a new separation result showing that, while algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent can generalize and optimize the population risk to within $\epsilon$ after $O(1/\epsilon^2)$ iterations, full-batch methods either need at least $\Omega(1/\epsilon^4)$ iterations or exhibit a dimension-dependent sample complexity.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether using the exact gradient of an entire training set is enough for efficient generalization in stochastic convex optimization. Its full-batch algorithms access only that aggregate empirical-risk gradient, rather than gradients from individual examples. The category includes gradient descent, mirror descent, and regularized or accelerated variants, so the question concerns a broad class of first-order methods.

The authors prove a separation between these methods and algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent. Stochastic gradient descent can optimize population risk to accuracy epsilon in O(1/epsilon^2) iterations. Full-batch methods face a different requirement: they either need at least Omega(1/epsilon^4) iterations or have a sample complexity that depends on dimension.

The distinction concerns performance on the underlying population, beyond fitting the observed training data. It shows that access to an exact empirical gradient does not eliminate the statistical and computational difficulties captured by this setting. The result is a lower-bound separation for the specified information-access model, with an explicit alternative between more iterations and dimension-dependent data requirements.
summary.tldr: Full-batch gradient methods face a provable population-risk tradeoff: more iterations than stochastic gradient descent or dimension-dependent sample complexity.

title: Never Go Full Batch (in Stochastic Convex Optimization)

abstract: A new line of research for feature selection based on neural networks has recently emerged. Despite its superiority to classical methods, it requires many training iterations to converge and detect the informative features. For datasets with a large number of samples or a very high dimensional feature space, the computational time becomes prohibitively long. In this paper, we present a new efficient unsupervised method for feature selection based on sparse autoencoders. In particular, we propose a new sparse training algorithm that optimizes a model's sparse topology during training to quickly pay attention to informative features. The attention-based adaptation of the sparse topology enables fast detection of informative features after a few training iterations. We performed extensive experiments on 10 datasets of different types, including image, speech, text, artificial, and biological. They cover a wide range of characteristics, such as low and high-dimensional feature spaces, as well as few and large training samples. Our proposed approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of the selection of informative features while reducing training iterations and computational costs substantially. Moreover, the experiments show the robustness of our method in extremely noisy environments.
