paragraphs: Optimizing a safety-critical system becomes harder when both performance and safety conditions change over time. The decision-maker must improve an unknown reward while respecting unknown constraints that may also move. This paper addresses that setting, motivated by sequential decision problems such as robotics and process control.

TVSAFEOPT uses Bayesian optimization with a spatio-temporal kernel, incorporating both the decision variables and time into its model. It can safely track a changing safe region without a separate mechanism for explicitly detecting changes. The authors also provide optimality guarantees when the optimization problem becomes stationary, giving the method a stated guarantee for the case where the environment stops changing.

On synthetic data, TVSAFEOPT compares favorably with SAFEOPT in both safety and optimality. A realistic gas-compressor case study further demonstrates safe optimization with unknown, time-varying reward and constraint functions. These findings support explicitly modeling temporal change when choosing safe actions, while the optimality result has the specific condition that the problem eventually becomes stationary.
summary.tldr: TVSAFEOPT tracks changing safe regions through spatio-temporal Bayesian optimization and provides optimality guarantees when the problem becomes stationary.

title: Safe Time-Varying Optimization based on Gaussian Processes with Spatio-Temporal Kernel

abstract: This work proposes a self-supervised training strategy designed for combinatorial problems. An obstacle in applying supervised paradigms to such problems is the need for costly target solutions often produced with exact solvers. Inspired by semi- and self-supervised learning, we show that generative models can be trained by sampling multiple solutions and using the best one according to the problem objective as a pseudo-label. In this way, we iteratively improve the model generation capability by relying only on its self-supervision, eliminating the need for optimality information. We validate this Self-Labeling Improvement Method (SLIM) on the Job Shop Scheduling (JSP), a complex combinatorial problem that is receiving much attention from the neural combinatorial community. We propose a generative model based on the well-known Pointer Network and train it with SLIM. Experiments on popular benchmarks demonstrate the potential of this approach as the resulting models outperform constructive heuristics and state-of-the-art learning proposals for the JSP. Lastly, we prove the robustness of SLIM to various parameters and its generality by applying it to the Traveling Salesman Problem.

paragraphs: Training a model to solve a combinatorial problem often requires expensive example solutions from an exact solver. This paper proposes a way to train without those targets. Its Self-Labeling Improvement Method, or SLIM, lets a generative model create its own supervision by comparing the solutions it already knows how to produce.

At each iteration, the model samples several candidate solutions. The candidate with the best value under the problem's objective becomes a pseudo-label for training. Repeating this process improves the model's generation capability without requiring knowledge of whether a candidate is globally optimal. The key resource is the ability to evaluate proposed solutions, allowing the training signal to come from the model's own alternatives.

The authors apply SLIM to job-shop scheduling using a generative model based on a Pointer Network. On popular benchmarks, the resulting models outperform constructive heuristics and state-of-the-art learning approaches for that problem. They also report robustness across several parameters and demonstrate application to the Traveling Salesman Problem, providing evidence that the strategy extends beyond scheduling.
summary.tldr: SLIM trains combinatorial solvers by repeatedly using the best of their own sampled solutions as supervision, without optimal-solution labels.

title: Self-Labeling the Job Shop Scheduling Problem

abstract: The Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) is a well-known metric for evaluating instance-level long-tail learning problems. In the past two decades, many AUC optimization methods have been proposed to improve model performance under long-tail distributions. In this paper, we explore AUC optimization methods in the context of pixel-level long-tail semantic segmentation, a much more complicated scenario. This task introduces two major challenges for AUC optimization techniques. On one hand, AUC optimization in a pixel-level task involves complex coupling across loss terms, with structured inner-image and pairwise inter-image dependencies, complicating theoretical analysis. On the other hand, we find that mini-batch estimation of AUC loss in this case requires a larger batch size, resulting in an unaffordable space complexity. To address these issues, we develop a pixel-level AUC loss function and conduct a dependency-graph-based theoretical analysis of the algorithm's generalization ability. Additionally, we design a Tail-Classes Memory Bank (T-Memory Bank) to manage the significant memory demand. Finally, comprehensive experiments across various benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our proposed AUCSeg method. The code is available at https://github.com/boyuh/AUCSeg.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each pixel, and a long-tail distribution means some categories appear far less often than others. AUCSeg investigates whether optimizing the area under the ROC curve, or AUC, can help in this setting. Although AUC optimization has been studied for individual examples, applying it to pixels introduces additional dependencies and memory demands.

The difficulty is that pixel-level loss terms are linked both within an image and across pairs of images. Those links complicate analysis of how well a trained model will generalize. The authors develop a pixel-level AUC loss and analyze its generalization using a dependency graph, explicitly accounting for the relationships that make this setting different.

A second obstacle is that estimating the AUC loss from mini-batches requires larger batches, making memory use impractical. AUCSeg introduces a Tail-Classes Memory Bank to manage that demand. Experiments across several benchmarks support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution combines an objective tailored to pixel imbalance, a corresponding theoretical analysis, and a mechanism addressing the memory cost of using that objective.
summary.tldr: AUCSeg adapts AUC optimization to imbalanced pixel classification with dependency-aware theory and a memory bank for rare classes.

title: AUCSeg: AUC-oriented Pixel-level Long-tail Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Graph Auto-Encoders (GAEs) are powerful tools for graph representation learning. In this paper, we develop a novel Hierarchical Cluster-based GAE (HC-GAE), that can learn effective structural characteristics for graph data analysis. To this end, during the encoding process, we commence by utilizing the hard node assignment to decompose a sample graph into a family of separated subgraphs. We compress each subgraph into a coarsened node, transforming the original graph into a coarsened graph. On the other hand, during the decoding process, we adopt the soft node assignment to reconstruct the original graph structure by expanding the coarsened nodes. By hierarchically performing the above compressing procedure during the decoding process as well as the expanding procedure during the decoding process, the proposed HC-GAE can effectively extract bidirectionally hierarchical structural features of the original sample graph. Furthermore, we re-design the loss function that can integrate the information from either the encoder or the decoder. Since the associated graph convolution operation of the proposed HC-GAE is restricted in each individual separated subgraph and cannot propagate the node information between different subgraphs, the proposed HC-GAE can significantly reduce the over-smoothing problem arising in the classical convolution-based GAEs. The proposed HC-GAE can generate effective representations for either node classification or graph classification, and the experiments demonstrate the effectiveness on real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Graph autoencoders learn representations by compressing graph information and reconstructing it. HC-GAE builds this process around hierarchical clusters so that the representation captures structural patterns at multiple levels. During encoding, hard node assignments divide the graph into separate subgraphs, each of which is compressed into a node in a smaller, coarsened graph.

During decoding, soft assignments expand the coarsened nodes to reconstruct the original structure. The hierarchical compression and expansion provide structural features in both directions. A redesigned loss incorporates information from either the encoder or decoder, allowing the learning objective to use information generated across the reconstruction process.

Graph convolution is restricted to individual separated subgraphs, preventing that operation from propagating node information between them. The authors argue that this significantly reduces oversmoothing, where repeated convolution makes representations overly similar. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate effective representations for both node and graph classification. The approach therefore combines multilevel structural learning with a restriction on information mixing intended to preserve distinctions within the learned representations.
summary.tldr: HC-GAE learns hierarchical graph representations through cluster compression and reconstruction while restricting convolution to reduce oversmoothing.

title: HC-GAE: The Hierarchical Cluster-based Graph Auto-Encoder for Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Recent advancements in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have greatly improved their abilities in image understanding. However, these models often struggle with grasping pixel-level semantic details, e.g., the keypoints of an object. To bridge this gap, we introduce the novel challenge of Semantic Keypoint Comprehension, which aims to comprehend keypoints across different task scenarios, including keypoint semantic understanding, visual prompt-based keypoint detection, and textual prompt-based keypoint detection. Moreover, we introduce KptLLM, a unified multimodal model that utilizes an identify-then-detect strategy to effectively address these challenges. KptLLM underscores the initial discernment of semantics in keypoints, followed by the precise determination of their positions through a chain-of-thought process. With several carefully designed modules, KptLLM adeptly handles various modality inputs, facilitating the interpretation of both semantic contents and keypoint locations. Our extensive experiments demonstrate KptLLM's superiority in various keypoint detection benchmarks and its unique semantic capabilities in interpreting keypoints.

paragraphs: Multimodal language models can understand images broadly while struggling with the meaning of precise points on an object. This paper introduces Semantic Keypoint Comprehension to study that gap. The challenge covers understanding a keypoint’s meaning, locating keypoints from visual prompts, and locating them from textual prompts.

KptLLM addresses these tasks with a unified model built around an identify-then-detect strategy. It first determines the semantic identity of the requested keypoint and then uses a chain-of-thought process to determine its position. Purpose-designed modules accommodate different input modalities and support both semantic interpretation and localization. This organization makes identifying what a point represents an explicit part of finding where it is.

The authors report superior performance across multiple keypoint-detection benchmarks, alongside semantic capabilities for interpreting keypoints. These findings support evaluating fine-grained image understanding through both location and meaning. The contribution is therefore twofold: a broader task definition for keypoint comprehension and a model that connects language-based interpretation with precise visual detection.
summary.tldr: KptLLM first identifies a keypoint’s meaning and then locates it, unifying semantic understanding with text- and image-prompted detection.

title: KptLLM: Unveiling the Power of Large Language Model for Keypoint Comprehension

abstract: Adverse weather conditions can significantly degrade the video frames, causing existing video semantic segmentation methods to produce erroneous predictions. In this work, we target adverse weather conditions and introduce an end-to-end domain adaptation strategy that leverages a fusion block, temporal-spatial teacher-student learning, and a temporal weather degradation augmentation approach. The fusion block integrates temporal information from adjacent frames at the feature level, trained end-to-end, eliminating the need for pretrained optical flow, distinguishing our method from existing approaches. Our teacher-student approach involves two teachers: one focuses on exploring temporal information from adjacent frames, and the other harnesses spatial information from the current frame. Finally, we apply temporal weather degradation augmentation to consecutive frames to more accurately represent adverse weather degradations. Our method achieves a performance of 25.4 and 33.0 mIoU on the adaptation from VIPER and Synthia to MVSS, respectively, representing an improvement of 4.3 and 5.8 mIoU over the existing state-of-the-art method.

paragraphs: Video semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel, but adverse weather can degrade frames and cause incorrect predictions. This paper develops an end-to-end domain-adaptation approach that combines information across time with information within the current frame. The aim is to improve segmentation when the target videos contain weather degradation.

A trainable fusion block combines features from adjacent frames without requiring pretrained optical flow. The learning setup uses two teachers: one emphasizes temporal information from neighboring frames, while the other emphasizes spatial information in the current frame. The method also applies weather-degradation augmentation to consecutive frames, so the training inputs better represent how adverse weather affects a video sequence.

On adaptation from VIPER to MVSS, the method achieves 25.4 mean intersection-over-union, improving on the existing leading method by 4.3 points. For Synthia to MVSS, it reaches 33.0, an improvement of 5.8 points. These results support the combined use of temporal feature fusion, complementary teachers, and sequence-level weather augmentation in the two reported adaptation settings.
summary.tldr: Temporal feature fusion, two complementary teachers, and weather augmentation improve video segmentation in two adverse-weather adaptation benchmarks.

title: End-to-End Video Semantic Segmentation in Adverse Weather using Fusion Blocks and Temporal-Spatial Teacher-Student Learning

abstract: Advances in 3D generative AI have enabled the creation of physical objects from text prompts, but challenges remain in creating objects involving multiple component types. We present a pipeline that integrates 3D generative AI with vision-language models (VLMs) to enable the robotic assembly of multi-component objects from natural language. Our method leverages VLMs for zero-shot, multi-modal reasoning about geometry and functionality to decompose AI-generated meshes into multi-component 3D models using predefined structural and panel components. We demonstrate that a VLM is capable of determining which mesh regions need panel components in addition to structural components based on object functionality. Evaluation across test objects shows that users preferred the VLM-generated assignments 90.6\% of the time, compared to 59.4\% for rule-based and 2.5\% for random assignment. Lastly, the system allows users to refine component assignments through conversational feedback, enabling greater human control and agency in making physical objects with generative AI and robotics.

paragraphs: This paper connects text-based 3D generation with robotic assembly of objects containing different component types. The central problem is deciding how a generated shape should be realized using predefined structural and panel pieces. Geometry alone does not capture every decision, because the object’s intended function also affects where panels belong.

The pipeline uses a vision-language model for zero-shot reasoning about both shape and functionality. It decomposes generated meshes into component-based models and determines which regions need panels in addition to structural elements. Users can then refine these assignments through conversational feedback, keeping a direct role in shaping the physical design.

Across test objects, the authors report user preference rates of 90.6% for the model-generated assignments, 59.4% for rule-based assignments, and 2.5% for random assignments. These results support the usefulness of functional reasoning for the component-selection task studied. The broader contribution links generated geometry, component decisions, robotic making, and conversational refinement within one workflow.
summary.tldr: Vision-language reasoning turns generated 3D meshes into structural-and-panel assembly plans that users can refine conversationally.

title: Text to Robotic Assembly of Multi Component Objects using 3D Generative AI and Vision Language Models

abstract: With the emergence of new storage and communication methods, the insertion, deletion, and substitution (IDS) channel has attracted considerable attention. However, many topics on the IDS channel and the associated Levenshtein distance remain open, making the invention of a novel IDS-correcting code a hard task. Furthermore, current studies on single-IDS-correcting code misalign with the requirements of applications which necessitates the correcting of multiple errors. Compromise solutions have involved shortening codewords to reduce the chance of multiple errors. However, the code rates of existing codes are poor at short lengths, diminishing the overall storage density. In this study, a novel method is introduced for designing high-code-rate single-IDS-correcting codewords through deep Levenshtein distance embedding. A deep learning model is utilized to project the sequences into embedding vectors that preserve the Levenshtein distances between the original sequences. This embedding space serves as a proxy for the complex Levenshtein domain, within which algorithms for codeword search and segment correcting is developed. While the concept underpinning this approach is straightforward, it bypasses the mathematical challenges typically encountered in code design. The proposed method results in a code rate that outperforms existing combinatorial solutions, particularly for designing short-length codewords.

paragraphs: Insertions, deletions, and substitutions can corrupt stored or transmitted sequences. Designing codes that correct these errors is difficult because the relevant edit-distance relationships are mathematically challenging. Shortening codewords reduces the chance of encountering multiple errors within one word, but existing short codes can devote too much space to redundancy, reducing storage density.

DoDo-Code uses a deep learning model to embed sequences into vectors that preserve their Levenshtein distances, the edit distances between the original sequences. The authors then develop codeword-search and segment-correction algorithms in this vector space. The embedding acts as a more manageable proxy for the original distance domain, allowing code construction to proceed without directly resolving its usual mathematical obstacles.

The resulting method designs high-rate codewords for correcting a single insertion, deletion, or substitution in a four-symbol channel. The abstract reports better code rates than existing combinatorial approaches, especially at short lengths. Its contribution addresses the efficiency of single-error-correcting building blocks within the broader practical challenge posed by multiple errors.
summary.tldr: DoDo-Code uses learned edit-distance embeddings to construct efficient single-error-correcting codes, with particular gains for short codewords.

title: DoDo-Code: an Efficient Levenshtein Distance Embedding-based Code for 4-ary IDS Channel

abstract: Prompt tuning has emerged as a powerful parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique, allowing large pretrained Transformers to adapt to downstream tasks by optimizing a small set of prompt embeddings. Despite its empirical success, the extent to which prompt tuning can memorize data remains poorly understood. In this paper, we provide both theoretical and empirical analyses of data memorization ability of prompt-tuned Transformers. Building on recent theoretical frameworks, we derive an upper bound on the required prompt length for exact memorization of finite datasets and establish a trade-off between prompt length and the number of autoregressive generation steps. Specifically, we show that a constant-size Transformer can memorize $n$ input-output pairs with prompts of length $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{nN})$, where $N$ denotes the sequence length. Empirical results further demonstrate that prompt-tuned, randomly initialized Transformers are able to effectively memorize finite datasets. These models also capture the intrinsic low-rank structure of the data, leading to a reduction in the required prompt length. Finally, we analyze how the initialization of the Transformer backbone affects the performance of prompt tuning. Our findings provide new insights into the expressivity, efficiency, and underlying mechanisms of prompt tuning, bridging theoretical memorization limits with observed empirical behaviors.

paragraphs: Prompt tuning adapts a transformer by optimizing a small collection of prompt embeddings. This paper asks how much data those learned prompts can encode, studying exact memorization of finite input-output datasets. The question concerns the expressive capacity of prompt tuning: how prompt length and generation length affect what a fixed-size transformer can represent.

The theoretical analysis gives an upper bound on a sufficient prompt length and establishes a trade-off with the number of autoregressive generation steps. Specifically, a constant-size transformer can memorize n input-output pairs using prompts whose length scales as the square root of n times sequence length, up to logarithmic factors. This is a sufficiency result, rather than a claim that every dataset requires that many prompt positions.

Experiments show that prompt-tuned transformers with randomly initialized backbones can effectively memorize finite datasets. They also capture intrinsic low-rank data structure, reducing the needed prompt length. The authors further study the effect of backbone initialization. Together, the results relate theoretical memorization capacity to empirical behavior and explain how dataset structure can affect prompt efficiency.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds sufficient prompt length for dataset memorization and shows how generation steps, data structure, and backbone initialization affect prompt tuning.

title: Prompt Tuning Transformers for Data Memorization

abstract: Diffusion models have shown remarkable abilities in generating realistic and high-quality images from text prompts. However, a trained model remains largely black-box; little do we know about the roles of its components in exhibiting a concept such as objects or styles. Recent works employ causal tracing to localize knowledge-storing layers in generative models without showing how other layers contribute to the target concept. In this work, we approach diffusion models' interpretability problem from a more general perspective and pose a question: \textit{``How do model components work jointly to demonstrate knowledge?''}. To answer this question, we decompose diffusion models using component attribution, systematically unveiling the importance of each component (specifically the model parameter) in generating a concept. The proposed framework, called \textbf{C}omponent \textbf{A}ttribution for \textbf{D}iffusion Model (CAD), discovers the localization of concept-inducing (positive) components, while interestingly uncovers another type of components that contribute negatively to generating a concept, which is missing in the previous knowledge localization work. Based on this holistic understanding of diffusion models, we present and empirically evaluate one utility of component attribution in controlling the generation process. Specifically, we introduce two fast, inference-time model editing algorithms, CAD-Erase and CAD-Amplify; in particular, CAD-Erase enables erasure and CAD-Amplify allows amplification of a generated concept by ablating the positive and negative components, respectively, while retaining knowledge of other concepts. Extensive experimental results validate the significance of both positive and negative components pinpointed by our framework, demonstrating the potential of providing a complete view of interpreting generative models.

paragraphs: Understanding a diffusion model requires more than locating layers associated with an object or style. This paper asks how components jointly contribute to generating a concept. Its Component Attribution for Diffusion Model framework, CAD, examines contributions at the level of model parameters, providing a more detailed account of where concept-related effects arise.

CAD identifies both positive components that support a concept and negative components that work against its generation. The negative contributions broaden the picture beyond locating knowledge-supporting components alone. This distinction also suggests two editing operations: remove positive components to suppress a concept, or remove negative components to make the concept more prominent.

The authors implement these operations as CAD-Erase and CAD-Amplify, fast model-editing algorithms applied at inference time. Experiments support the significance of both component types and demonstrate concept erasure or amplification while retaining knowledge of other concepts. The contribution combines interpretation with generation control: attribution describes opposing contributions inside the model and supplies concrete targets for changing the concepts it produces.
summary.tldr: CAD identifies parameters that promote or suppress concepts in diffusion models and uses them for targeted inference-time erasure or amplification.

title: Unveiling Concept Attribution in Diffusion Models

abstract: Symbolic regression aims to discover concise, interpretable mathematical expressions that satisfy desired objectives, such as fitting data, posing a highly combinatorial optimization problem. While genetic programming has been the dominant approach, recent efforts have explored reinforcement learning methods for improving search efficiency. Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), with its ability to balance exploration and exploitation through guided search, has emerged as a promising technique for symbolic expression discovery. However, its traditional bandit strategies and sequential symbol construction often limit performance. In this work, we propose an improved MCTS framework for symbolic regression that addresses these limitations through two key innovations: (1) an extreme bandit allocation strategy tailored for identifying globally optimal expressions, with finite-time performance guarantees under polynomial reward decay assumptions; and (2) evolution-inspired state-jumping actions such as mutation and crossover, which enable non-local transitions to promising regions of the search space. These state-jumping actions also reshape the reward landscape during the search process, improving both robustness and efficiency. We conduct a thorough numerical study to the impact of these improvements and benchmark our approach against existing symbolic regression methods on a variety of datasets, including both ground-truth and black-box datasets. Our approach achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art libraries in terms of recovery rate, attains favorable positions on the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus model complexity.

Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), with its ability to balance exploration and exploitation through guided search, has emerged as a promising technique for symbolic expression discovery. However, its traditional bandit strategies and sequential symbol construction often limit performance. In this work, we propose an improved MCTS framework for symbolic regression that addresses these limitations through two key innovations: (1) an extreme bandit allocation strategy tailored for identifying globally optimal expressions, with finite-time performance guarantees under polynomial reward decay assumptions; and (2) evolution-inspired state-jumping actions such as mutation and crossover, which enable non-local transitions to promising regions of the search space. These state-jumping actions also reshape the reward landscape during the search process, improving both robustness and efficiency. We conduct a thorough numerical study to the impact of these improvements and benchmark our approach against existing symbolic regression methods on a variety of datasets, including both ground-truth and black-box datasets. Our approach achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art libraries in terms of recovery rate, attains favorable positions on the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus model complexity.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression searches for mathematical expressions that explain data or satisfy another objective while remaining concise and interpretable. The number of possible expressions makes this a difficult combinatorial search. This paper improves Monte Carlo Tree Search by changing both how search effort is allocated and how the algorithm moves between candidate expressions.

The first change is an extreme bandit allocation strategy aimed at discovering globally optimal expressions. Its finite-time guarantees depend on assumptions about polynomial reward decay. The second introduces mutation and crossover as state-jumping actions, allowing movement to promising regions without constructing every expression through a strictly sequential series of symbol choices.

These jumps also change the reward landscape encountered during search, which the authors associate with improved robustness and efficiency. Numerical studies examine the contributions of the changes and compare the method on datasets with known underlying expressions and black-box datasets. Recovery rates are competitive with leading libraries, and the method achieves favorable tradeoffs between fitting accuracy and expression complexity.
summary.tldr: The method improves symbolic-regression tree search with specialized search allocation and mutation- and crossover-based jumps between expressions.

title: Improving Monte Carlo Tree Search for Symbolic Regression

abstract: Task planning under uncertainty is essential for home-service robots operating in the real world. Tasks involve ambiguous human instructions, hidden or unknown object locations, and open-vocabulary object types, leading to significant open-ended uncertainty and a boundlessly large planning space. To address these challenges, we propose Tru-POMDP, a planner that combines structured belief generation using Large Language Models (LLMs) with principled POMDP planning. Tru-POMDP introduces a hierarchical Tree of Hypotheses (TOH), which systematically queries an LLM to construct high-quality particle beliefs over possible world states and human goals. We further formulate an open-ended POMDP model that enables rigorous Bayesian belief tracking and efficient belief-space planning over these LLM-generated hypotheses. Experiments on complex object rearrangement tasks across diverse kitchen environments show that Tru-POMDP significantly outperforms state-of-the-art LLM-based and LLM-tree-search hybrid planners, achieving higher success rates with significantly better plans, stronger robustness to ambiguity and occlusion, and greater planning efficiency.

paragraphs: A home-service robot may receive ambiguous instructions while objects are hidden or their locations unknown. Open-ended object types make the range of possibilities even larger. Tru-POMDP addresses this planning problem by combining language-model-generated hypotheses with a probabilistic planner that explicitly tracks uncertainty.

Its Tree of Hypotheses queries a language model hierarchically to construct particle beliefs: collections of possible world states and human goals. An open-ended partially observable Markov decision process then supports Bayesian updates to these beliefs and planning over them. The language model supplies structured possibilities, while the planning framework manages uncertainty among those possibilities as the task proceeds.

Experiments use complex object-rearrangement tasks across diverse kitchen environments. The authors report higher success rates, better plans, greater robustness to ambiguity and occlusion, and more efficient planning than leading language-model and hybrid tree-search planners. These findings support combining structured hypothesis generation with explicit belief tracking when a robot must act without fully knowing either the environment or the intended goal.
summary.tldr: Tru-POMDP combines hierarchical language-model hypotheses with Bayesian belief-space planning to improve robot task planning under uncertainty.

title: Tru-POMDP: Task Planning Under Uncertainty via Tree of Hypotheses and Open-Ended POMDPs

abstract: Adapting billion-parameter language models to a downstream task is still costly, even with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT). We re-cast task adaptation as output-distribution alignment: the objective is to steer the output distribution toward the task distribution directly during decoding rather than indirectly through weight updates. Building on this view, we introduce Steering Vector Decoding (SVDecode), a lightweight, PEFT-compatible, and theoretically grounded method. We start with a short warm-start fine-tune and extract a task-aware steering vector from the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence gradient between the output distribution of the warm-started and pre-trained models. This steering vector is then used to guide the decoding process to steer the model's output distribution towards the task distribution. We theoretically prove that SVDecode is first-order equivalent to the gradient step of full fine-tuning and derive a globally optimal solution for the strength of the steering vector. Across three tasks and nine benchmarks, SVDecode paired with four standard PEFT methods improves multiple-choice accuracy by up to 5 percentage points and open-ended truthfulness by 2 percentage points, with similar gains (1-2 percentage points) on commonsense datasets without adding trainable parameters beyond the PEFT adapter. SVDecode thus offers a lightweight, theoretically grounded path to stronger task adaptation for large language models.

This paper frames adaptation as aligning the model’s output distribution with a task’s distribution. Steering Vector Decoding, or SVDecode, uses that perspective to guide generation directly, complementing parameter-efficient fine-tuning with a change to decoding.

It then derives a task-aware steering vector from the gradient of KL divergence between the warm-started and pretrained models’ output distributions. That vector guides subsequent decoding. The authors prove first-order equivalence to a full fine-tuning gradient step and derive a globally optimal steering strength within their formulation.

Across three tasks and nine benchmarks, combining SVDecode with four standard parameter-efficient methods improves multiple-choice accuracy by up to five percentage points and open-ended truthfulness by two points. Commonsense gains are one to two points. These improvements require no additional trainable parameters beyond the adapter, supporting decoding-time steering as a lightweight addition to task adaptation.
summary.tldr: SVDecode derives a task-aware vector from a short fine-tune and uses it during decoding to improve adaptation without extra trainable parameters.

title: Distribution-Aligned Decoding for Efficient LLM Task Adaptation

abstract: Benchmarks are pivotal in driving AI progress, and invalid benchmark questions frequently undermine their reliability. Manually identifying and correcting errors among thousands of benchmark questions is not only infeasible but also a critical bottleneck for reliable evaluation. In this work, we introduce a framework for systematic benchmark revision that leverages statistical analysis of response patterns to flag potentially invalid questions for further expert review. Our approach builds on a core assumption commonly used in AI evaluations that the mean score sufficiently summarizes model performance. This implies a unidimensional latent construct underlying the measurement experiment, yielding expected ranges for various statistics for each item. When empirically estimated values for these statistics fall outside the expected range for an item, the item is more likely to be problematic. Across nine widely used benchmarks, our method guides expert review to identify problematic questions with up to 84\% precision. In addition, we introduce an LLM‑judge first pass to review questions, further reducing human effort. Together, these components provide an efficient and scalable framework for systematic benchmark revision.

paragraphs: Faulty benchmark questions can undermine model evaluations, but reviewing thousands of items manually creates a major bottleneck. This paper proposes a statistical screening framework that identifies questions worth closer expert attention. It examines patterns in model responses, using unusual item-level behavior as evidence that a question may be problematic.

The method rests on an explicit assumption: a model's mean benchmark score adequately summarizes its performance. That assumption implies a single underlying dimension of ability in the measurement setup. From this structure, the authors derive expected ranges for item statistics. Questions whose observed statistics fall outside those ranges are flagged as more likely to contain problems, rather than automatically declared invalid.

Across nine widely used benchmarks, the screening process guides expert review with precision reaching 84%. The authors also introduce an initial review by an LLM judge to reduce human effort further. The framework's value lies in directing scarce review capacity toward suspicious items, while retaining expert inspection as part of systematic benchmark revision.
summary.tldr: Statistical response patterns help prioritize potentially faulty benchmark questions for expert review, reaching up to 84% precision.

title: Fantastic Bugs and Where to Find Them in AI Benchmarks

abstract: Video generation has achieved significant advances through rectified flow techniques, but issues like unsmooth motion and misalignment between videos and prompts persist. In this work, we develop a systematic pipeline that harnesses human feedback to mitigate these problems and refine the video generation model. Specifically, we begin by constructing a large-scale human preference dataset focused on modern video generation models, incorporating pairwise annotations across multi-dimensions. We then introduce VideoReward, a multi-dimensional video reward model, and examine how annotations and various design choices impact its rewarding efficacy. From a unified reinforcement learning perspective aimed at maximizing reward with KL regularization, we introduce three alignment algorithms for flow-based models. These include two training-time strategies: direct preference optimization for flow (Flow-DPO) and reward weighted regression for flow (Flow-RWR), and an inference-time technique, Flow-NRG, which applies reward guidance directly to noisy videos. Experimental results indicate that VideoReward significantly outperforms existing reward models, and Flow-DPO demonstrates superior performance compared to both Flow-RWR and supervised fine-tuning methods. Additionally, Flow-NRG lets users assign custom weights to multiple objectives during inference, meeting personalized video quality needs.

paragraphs: Flow-based video generators can produce impressive videos while still showing uneven motion or failing to match a prompt. This paper builds a human-feedback pipeline to address these problems. It begins with a large preference dataset containing pairwise judgments across multiple dimensions, then uses those annotations to develop a multidimensional reward model called VideoReward.

The authors investigate how annotation and model-design choices affect reward assessment. They also develop three alignment methods within a shared framework that balances reward maximization with KL regularization. Flow-DPO and Flow-RWR modify training through preference optimization and reward-weighted regression, respectively. Flow-NRG instead guides noisy videos during generation, making it an inference-time method.

In the reported experiments, VideoReward substantially outperforms existing reward models. Flow-DPO performs better than Flow-RWR and supervised fine-tuning. Flow-NRG adds a different capability: users can change the weights assigned to multiple objectives at inference time. The pipeline therefore addresses both learning from human judgments and adjusting generated videos to different quality preferences.
summary.tldr: A human-feedback pipeline combines multidimensional video rewards with training-time alignment and customizable guidance during generation.

title: Improving Video Generation with Human Feedback

abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is a powerful paradigm to align language models with human preferences using pairwise comparisons. However, its binary win-or-loss supervision often proves insufficient for training small models with limited capacity. Prior works attempt to distill information from large teacher models using behavior cloning or KL divergence. These methods often focus on mimicking current behavior and overlook distilling reward modeling. To address this issue, we propose \textit{Teacher Value-based Knowledge Distillation} (TVKD), which introduces an auxiliary reward from the value function of the teacher model to provide a soft guide. This auxiliary reward is formulated to satisfy potential-based reward shaping, ensuring that the global reward structure and optimal policy of DPO are preserved. TVKD can be integrated into the standard DPO training framework and does not require additional rollouts. Our experimental results show that TVKD consistently improves performance across various benchmarks and model sizes.

paragraphs: Direct Preference Optimization trains language models from pairs of preferred and disfavored responses. For small models, a binary win-or-loss signal can provide insufficient guidance. This paper explores transferring richer information from a larger teacher, focusing on its value function rather than only imitating its output behavior.

Teacher Value-based Knowledge Distillation adds an auxiliary reward derived from the teacher's value function. This supplies a softer learning signal within standard DPO training. The reward is constructed to satisfy potential-based reward shaping, preserving DPO's global reward structure and optimal policy. That property matters because the teacher's guidance can change the learning signal while retaining the original optimization target.

The method fits into the existing DPO framework and requires no additional rollouts. Experiments report consistent performance improvements across the evaluated benchmarks and model sizes. The contribution is therefore a way to make teacher information more useful to preference learning: it transfers guidance about value, beyond demonstrations of current behavior, while preserving the stated policy objective and avoiding an extra rollout requirement.
summary.tldr: TVKD improves preference training with teacher-value rewards designed to preserve DPO's optimal policy without requiring additional rollouts.

title: Preference Distillation via Value based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: This paper introduces PaZO, a preconditioned accelerated zeroth-order optimization algorithm for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). First, we theoretically demonstrate the necessity of preconditioning in zeroth-order optimization, proving that zeroth-order stochastic gradient descent (ZO-SGD) alone fails to achieve the ideal convergence rate. Building on this, we propose a Preconditioned Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation (PSPSA) and theoretical version of PaZO, and demonstrate that setting the order of preconditioner as $-1/2$ in PSPSA yields the improved convergence rate for PaZO. Moreover, we design a practical version of PaZO that stabilizes training via diagonal Hessian estimate and moving average technique. Extensive experiments on diverse downstream tasks with models like RoBERTa-large and OPT show PaZO’s effectiveness. Compared to other zeroth-order baselines, PaZO achieves better performance across models and tasks.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization adapts a model using information from objective evaluations rather than directly computing ordinary gradients. This paper develops PaZO, a preconditioned and accelerated method for fine-tuning language models in that setting. Its central concern is how to improve convergence by changing the way estimated optimization directions are scaled.

The authors first show theoretically that zeroth-order stochastic gradient descent alone does not achieve the ideal convergence rate considered in their analysis. They introduce Preconditioned Simultaneous Perturbation Stochastic Approximation and a theoretical version of PaZO. Setting the preconditioner's order to −1/2 in the proposed formulation yields an improved convergence rate, connecting the choice of scaling to the algorithm's theoretical behavior.

A practical version uses a diagonal estimate of the Hessian together with a moving average to stabilize training. Experiments cover diverse downstream tasks and models including RoBERTa-large and OPT. PaZO performs better than the other zeroth-order baselines in the reported comparisons. The contribution links a theoretical case for preconditioning to a usable optimization method for language-model adaptation.
summary.tldr: PaZO uses theoretically motivated preconditioning and practical stabilization to improve zeroth-order language-model fine-tuning over evaluated baselines.

title: PaZO: Preconditioned Accelerated Zeroth-Order Optimization for Fine-Tuning LLMs

abstract: Recent advancements underscore the significant role of Reinforcement Learning (RL) in enhancing the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). Two prominent RL algorithms, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), are central to these developments, showcasing different pros and cons. Autoregressive image generation, also interpretable as a sequential CoT reasoning process, presents unique challenges distinct from LLM-based CoT reasoning. These encompass ensuring text-image consistency, improving image aesthetic quality, and designing sophisticated reward models, rather than relying on simpler rule-based rewards. While recent efforts have extended RL to this domain, these explorations typically lack an in-depth analysis of the domain-specific challenges and the characteristics of different RL strategies. To bridge this gap, we provide the first comprehensive investigation of the GRPO and DPO algorithms in autoregressive image generation, evaluating their ***in-domain*** performance and ***out-of-domain*** generalization, while scrutinizing the impact of ***different reward models*** on their respective capabilities. Our findings reveal that GRPO and DPO exhibit distinct advantages, and crucially, that reward models possessing stronger intrinsic generalization capabilities potentially enhance the generalization potential of the applied RL algorithms. Furthermore, we systematically explore ***three prevalent scaling strategies*** to enhance both their in-domain and out-of-domain proficiency, deriving unique insights into efficiently scaling performance for each paradigm. We hope our study paves a new path for inspiring future work on developing more effective RL algorithms to achieve robust CoT reasoning in the realm of autoregressive image generation.

paragraphs: This study compares Direct Preference Optimization and Group Relative Policy Optimization for autoregressive image generation. It treats sequential image generation as a process that can be examined through the lens of chain-of-thought reasoning. The motivation is that success in images requires text-image agreement and visual quality, making reward design different from reasoning tasks with straightforward verifiable answers.

The authors investigate both performance within the training domain and generalization beyond it. They also vary the reward models used to guide learning, separating questions about the optimization algorithm from questions about the quality of its feedback. This comparison examines how the training procedure and the reward model jointly shape the resulting image generator.

The findings show distinct advantages for DPO and GRPO. They also suggest that reward models with stronger intrinsic generalization can potentially improve the generalization of the learning algorithms they guide. The study examines three prevalent scaling strategies and derives different insights for efficiently scaling each approach, contributing guidance for algorithm and reward design in this image-generation setting.
summary.tldr: A comparison of DPO and GRPO for image generation finds distinct strengths and suggests that reward-model generalization can help learning generalize.

title: Delving into RL for Image Generation with CoT: A Study on DPO vs. GRPO

abstract: Recent neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) methods have shown promising problem-solving ability without requiring domain-specific expertise. Most existing NCO methods use training and testing data with a fixed constraint value and lack research on the effect of constraint tightness on the performance of NCO methods. This paper takes the capacity-constrained vehicle routing problem (CVRP) as an example to empirically analyze the NCO performance under different tightness degrees of the capacity constraint. Our analysis reveals that existing NCO methods overfit the capacity constraint, and they can only perform satisfactorily on a small range of the constraint values but poorly on other values. To tackle this drawback of existing NCO methods, we develop an efficient training scheme that explicitly considers varying degrees of constraint tightness and propose a multi-expert module to learn a generally adaptable solving strategy. Experimental results show that the proposed method can effectively overcome the overfitting issue, demonstrating superior performance on the CVRP and CVRP with time windows (CVRPTW) with various constraint tightness degrees. The code is available at [https://github.com/CIAM-Group/Rethinking\_Constraint\_Tightness](https://github.com/CIAM-Group/Rethinking\_Constraint\_Tightness).

paragraphs: A learned vehicle-routing solver may work well at the capacity limit used during training yet struggle when that limit changes. This paper investigates that problem through the capacity-constrained vehicle routing problem. Its empirical analysis finds that existing neural optimization methods overfit constraint values, performing satisfactorily within only a narrow range of capacity settings.

The proposed response has two components. A training scheme explicitly includes different degrees of constraint tightness, and a multi-expert module learns a more broadly adaptable solving strategy. Together, these changes make variation in the constraints part of what the model learns, rather than treating one fixed constraint value as representative of the whole problem.

Experiments cover both capacity-constrained routing and its version with time windows. Across varying levels of constraint tightness, the method reports superior performance and effective mitigation of the observed overfitting. The findings highlight constraint variation as an important dimension of generalization: success on routing instances at one setting does not establish adaptability across differently constrained versions of the task.
summary.tldr: Training across constraint tightness levels with a multi-expert module improves neural routing solvers' adaptability to changing capacity and time-window constraints.

title: Rethinking Neural Combinatorial Optimization for Vehicle Routing Problems with Different Constraint Tightness Degrees

abstract: Recent advancements in generative models have enabled high-fidelity text-to-image generation. However, open-source image-editing models still lag behind their proprietary counterparts, primarily due to limited high-quality data and insufficient benchmarks.To overcome these limitations, we introduce **ImgEdit**, a large-scale, high-quality image-editing dataset comprising one million carefully curated edit pairs, which contain both novel and complex single-turn edits, as well as challenging multi-turn tasks.To ensure the data quality, we employ a multi-stage pipeline that integrates a cutting-edge vision-language model, a detection model, a segmentation model, alongside task-specific in-painting procedures and strict post-processing. ImgEdit surpasses existing datasets in both task novelty and data quality.Using ImgEdit, we train **ImgEdit-E1**, an editing model using Vision Language Model to process the reference image and editing prompt, which outperforms existing open-source models on multiple tasks, highlighting the value of ImgEdit and model design.For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce **ImgEdit-Bench**, a benchmark designed to evaluate image editing performance in terms of instruction adherence, editing quality, and detail preservation.It includes a basic testsuite, a challenging single-turn suite, and a dedicated multi-turn suite. We evaluate both open-source and proprietary models, as well as ImgEdit-E1, providing deep analysis and actionable insights into the current behavior of image-editing models.

paragraphs: ImgEdit addresses two obstacles to improving open-source image editing: limited high-quality training data and insufficient evaluation benchmarks. The dataset contains one million curated edit pairs, covering novel and complex single-turn edits as well as multi-turn tasks. This gives models examples of both individual changes and editing across a sequence of instructions.

The data construction pipeline combines a vision-language model, detection, segmentation, task-specific inpainting, and strict post-processing. The authors use the resulting data to train ImgEdit-E1, whose vision-language component processes both the reference image and the editing instruction. It outperforms existing open-source models on multiple tasks, supporting the value of the dataset together with the model design.

The accompanying ImgEdit-Bench evaluates instruction adherence, editing quality, and preservation of details. It includes basic tests, challenging single-turn cases, and a dedicated multi-turn suite. By evaluating proprietary models, open-source models, and ImgEdit-E1 within this structure, the paper connects training resources with a broader assessment of editing behavior. The benchmark separates following the requested change from producing a good-looking result and retaining image details.
summary.tldr: ImgEdit supplies one million editing pairs, a trained editing model, and a benchmark covering instruction following, quality, and detail preservation.

title: ImgEdit: A Unified Image Editing Dataset and Benchmark

abstract: We consider the Tree Alternating Optimization (TAO) algorithm to train regression trees with linear predictors in the leaves. Unlike the traditional, greedy recursive partitioning algorithms such as CART, TAO guarantees a monotonic decrease of the objective function and results in smaller trees of much better accuracy. We modify the TAO algorithm so that it produces exactly the same result but is much faster, particularly for high input dimensionality or deep trees. The idea is based on the fact that, at each iteration of TAO, each leaf receives only a subset of the training instances. Thus, the optimization of the leaf model can be done exactly but faster by using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula. This has the unexpected advantage that, once a tree exceeds a critical depth, then making it deeper makes it faster to train, even though the tree is larger and has more parameters. Indeed, this can make learning a nonlinear model (the tree) asymptotically faster than a regular linear regression model. We analyze the corresponding computational complexity and verify the speedups experimentally in various datasets. The argument can be applied to other types of trees, whenever the optimization of a node can be computed in superlinear time of the number of instances.
originalAbstract: We consider the Tree Alternating Optimization (TAO) algorithm to train regression trees with linear predictors in the leaves. Unlike the traditional, greedy recursive partitioning algorithms such as CART, TAO guarantees a monotonic decrease of the objective function and results in smaller trees of much better accuracy. We modify the TAO algorithm so that it produces exactly the same result but is much faster, particularly for high input dimensionality or deep trees. The idea is based on the fact that, at each iteration of TAO, each leaf receives only a subset of the training instances. Thus, the optimization of the leaf model can be done exactly but faster by using the Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula. This has the unexpected advantage that, once a tree exceeds a critical depth, then making it deeper makes it faster to train, even though the tree is larger and has more parameters. Indeed, this can make learning a nonlinear model (the tree) asymptotically faster than a regular linear regression model. We analyze the corresponding computational complexity and verify the speedups experimentally in various datasets. The argument can be applied to other types of trees, whenever the optimization of a node can be computed in superlinear time of the number of instances.

paragraphs: This paper speeds up training for regression trees whose leaves contain linear predictors. It starts from Tree Alternating Optimization, or TAO, which repeatedly improves a tree rather than constructing it through greedy splits. The abstract describes TAO as guaranteeing a decreasing training objective and producing smaller, more accurate trees than traditional greedy approaches.

The proposed modification preserves TAO’s result while changing how each leaf’s predictor is optimized. At any iteration, a leaf receives only part of the training data. The Sherman-Morrison-Woodbury formula lets the algorithm exploit that smaller subset to solve the same optimization problem more efficiently, with particular benefits for high-dimensional inputs or deep trees.

The complexity analysis yields a surprising conditional result: beyond a critical depth, a larger tree can train faster because individual leaf problems become smaller. This can even make tree training asymptotically faster than ordinary linear regression. Experiments verify speedups across datasets. The reasoning also applies to other trees when node optimization costs grow faster than linearly with the number of assigned examples.
summary.tldr: An exact reformulation accelerates TAO training and explains why sufficiently deep regression trees can become faster to train as they grow.

title: A faster training algorithm for regression trees with linear leaves, and an analysis of its complexity

abstract: Composed Video Retrieval (CoVR) retrieves a target video given a query video and a modification text describing the intended change. Existing CoVR benchmarks emphasize appearance shifts or coarse event changes and therefore do not test the ability to capture subtle, fast-paced temporal differences. We introduce TF-CoVR, the first large-scale benchmark dedicated to temporally fine-grained CoVR. TF-CoVR focuses on gymnastics and diving, and provides 180K triplets drawn from FineGym and FineDiving datasets. Previous CoVR benchmarks, focusing on temporal aspect, link each query to a single target segment taken from the same video, limiting practical usefulness. In TF-CoVR, we instead construct each <query, modification> pair by prompting an LLM with the label differences between clips drawn from different videos; every pair is thus associated with multiple valid target videos (3.9 on average), reflecting real-world tasks such as sports-highlight generation. To model these temporal dynamics, we propose TF-CoVR-Base, a concise two-stage training framework: (i) pre-train a video encoder on fine-grained action classification to obtain temporally discriminative embeddings; (ii) align the composed query with candidate videos using contrastive learning. We conduct the first comprehensive study of image, video, and general multimodal embedding (GME) models on temporally fine-grained composed retrieval in both zero-shot and fine-tuning regimes. On TF-CoVR, TF-CoVR-Base improves zero-shot mAP@50 from 5.92 (LanguageBind) to 7.51, and after fine-tuning raises the state-of-the-art from 19.83 to 27.22.

title: From Play to Replay: Composed Video Retrieval for Temporally Fine-Grained Videos

abstract: Bisimulation metrics are powerful tools for measuring similarities between stochastic processes, and specifically Markov chains. Recent advances have uncovered that bisimulation metrics are, in fact, optimal-transport distances, which has enabled the development of fast algorithms for computing such metrics with provable accuracy and runtime guarantees. However, these recent methods, as well as all previously known methods, assume full knowledge of the transition dynamics. This is often an impractical assumption in most real-world scenarios, where typically only sample trajectories are available. In this work, we propose a stochastic optimization method that addresses this limitation and estimates bisimulation metrics based on sample access, without requiring explicit transition models. Our approach is derived from a new linear programming (LP) formulation of bisimulation metrics, which we solve using a stochastic primal-dual optimization method. We provide theoretical guarantees on the sample complexity of the algorithm and validate its effectiveness through a series of empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: Bisimulation metrics measure similarity between stochastic processes, including Markov chains. Earlier computational methods require full knowledge of the transition dynamics, meaning the probabilities governing movement between states must be available. This paper targets a more practical situation: observations arrive as sample trajectories, without an explicit transition model.

The authors develop a new linear programming formulation of these metrics and solve it using stochastic primal-dual optimization. This provides a way to estimate the distance through sample access. The approach builds on the connection between bisimulation metrics and optimal transport while changing the information needed to carry out the computation.

The paper supplies theoretical sample-complexity guarantees and evaluates the algorithm empirically. Together, these contributions address both the amount of sampled information required and the method’s observed effectiveness. Its significance is the shift from comparing fully specified transition models to estimating process similarity from sampled behavior, making this class of metrics applicable in settings where the dynamics cannot be supplied explicitly.
summary.tldr: A stochastic optimization method estimates bisimulation distances between Markov chains from samples without requiring explicit transition models.

title: Distances for Markov chains from sample streams

abstract: Securing personal identity against deepfake attacks is increasingly critical in the digital age, especially for celebrities and political figures whose faces are easily accessible and frequently targeted. Most existing deepfake detection methods focus on general-purpose scenarios and often ignore the valuable prior knowledge of known facial identities, e.g., "VIP individuals" whose authentic facial data are already available. In this paper, we propose **VIPGuard**, a unified multimodal framework designed to capture fine-grained and comprehensive facial representations of a given identity, compare them against potentially fake or similar-looking faces, and reason over these comparisons to make accurate and explainable predictions. Specifically, our framework consists of three main stages. First, we fine-tune a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to learn detailed and structural facial attributes. Second, we perform identity-level discriminative learning to enable the model to distinguish subtle differences between highly similar faces, including real and fake variations. Finally, we introduce user-specific customization, where we model the unique characteristics of the target face identity and perform semantic reasoning via MLLM to enable personalized and explainable deepfake detection. Our framework shows clear advantages over previous detection works, where traditional detectors mainly rely on low-level visual cues and provide no human-understandable explanations, while other MLLM-based models often lack a detailed understanding of specific face identities. To facilitate the evaluation of our method, we build a comprehensive identity-aware benchmark called **VIPBench** for personalized deepfake detection, involving the latest 7 face-swapping and 7 entire face synthesis techniques for generation. Extensive experiments show that our model outperforms existing methods in both detection and explanation. The code is available at https://github.com/KQL11/VIPGuard .

summary.tldr: VIPGuard uses detailed knowledge of a known person's face to improve personalized deepfake detection and generate understandable explanations.

title: Guard Me If You Know Me: Protecting Specific Face-Identity from Deepfakes

abstract: Maritime object detection is essential for navigation safety, surveillance, and autonomous operations, yet constrained by two key challenges: the scarcity of annotated maritime data and poor generalization across various maritime attributes (e.g., object category, viewpoint, location, and imaging environment). To address these challenges, we propose Neptune-X, a data-centric generative-selection framework that enhances training effectiveness by leveraging synthetic data generation with task-aware sample selection. From the generation perspective, we develop X-to-Maritime, a multi-modality-conditioned generative model that synthesizes diverse and realistic maritime scenes. A key component is the Bidirectional Object-Water Attention module, which captures boundary interactions between objects and their aquatic surroundings to improve visual fidelity. To further improve downstream tasking performance, we propose Attribute-correlated Active Sampling, which dynamically selects synthetic samples based on their task relevance. To support robust benchmarking, we construct the Maritime Generation Dataset, the first dataset tailored for generative maritime learning, encompassing a wide range of semantic conditions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach sets a new benchmark in maritime scene synthesis, significantly improving detection accuracy, particularly in challenging and previously underrepresented settings. The code is available at https://github.com/gy65896/Neptune-X.

It combines synthetic scene generation with selection of examples that are relevant to the detection task, connecting the production of additional data to its usefulness for learning.

A bidirectional attention module models interactions at the boundary between objects and water, aiming to improve visual realism where the two meet. An attribute-correlated active sampling method then dynamically chooses synthetic samples according to their relevance to the downstream task.

The authors also introduce the Maritime Generation Dataset to support generative learning across a broad range of semantic conditions. Experiments report leading maritime synthesis results and significant improvements in detection accuracy, especially in challenging or previously underrepresented settings. The findings support combining realistic generation with task-aware selection, so that expanding a training set also addresses gaps in the conditions it represents.
summary.tldr: Neptune-X combines realistic maritime scene generation with task-aware sample selection to improve object detection, particularly in underrepresented conditions.

title: Neptune-X: Active X-to-Maritime Generation for Universal Maritime Object Detection

abstract: The quadratic complexity of self‑attention prevents transformers from scaling effectively to long input sequences. On the other hand, modern GPUs and other specialized hardware accelerators are well-optimized for processing small input sequences in transformers during both training and inference. A natural question arises: can we take advantage of the efficiency of small transformers to deal with long input sequences? In this paper, we show that transformers with long input sequences (large transformers) can be efficiently simulated by transformers that can only take short input sequences (small transformers). Specifically, we prove that any transformer with input length $N$ can be efficiently simulated by only $O((N/M)^2)$ transformers with input length $M \ll N$, and that this cannot be improved in the worst case. However, we then prove that in various natural scenarios including average-case inputs, sliding window masking and attention sinks, the optimal number $O(N/M)$ of small transformers suffice.

paragraphs: Self-attention becomes costly as input sequences grow because its complexity is quadratic in sequence length. Meanwhile, modern accelerators process short transformer inputs efficiently. This paper asks whether computations over long sequences can be carried out using transformers restricted to shorter sequences. Here, large and small refer to input length, which is central to the question.

The authors prove that a transformer accepting N inputs can be simulated efficiently using on the order of (N/M) squared transformers that accept M inputs, with M much smaller than N. They also prove that the number required cannot be improved in the worst case. Thus, splitting the work into shorter inputs has a precisely characterized general-case requirement.

The result improves under several natural scenarios, including average-case inputs, sliding-window masks, and attention sinks. In those settings, only on the order of N/M small transformers suffice, which the paper establishes as optimal. These are simulation guarantees that distinguish unrestricted attention from favorable cases. They explain when short-input transformer computations can represent long-input behavior with a linear rather than quadratic number of components.
summary.tldr: Short-input transformers can simulate long-input transformers with optimal quadratic worst-case counts and linear counts in several natural settings.

title: Two Heads are Better than One: Simulating Large Transformers with Small Ones

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for teaching robots complex behaviors without reward engineering. However, its effectiveness is often limited by two critical challenges: the reliance on extensive human input and the inherent difficulties in resolving query ambiguity and credit assignment during reward learning. In this paper, we introduce PRIMT, a PbRL framework designed to overcome these challenges by leveraging foundation models (FMs) for multimodal synthetic feedback and trajectory synthesis. Unlike prior approaches that rely on single-modality FM evaluations, PRIMT employs a hierarchical neuro-symbolic fusion strategy, integrating the complementary strengths of vision-language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) in evaluating robot behaviors for more reliable and comprehensive feedback. PRIMT also incorporates foresight trajectory generation to warm-start the trajectory buffer with bootstrapped samples, reducing early-stage query ambiguity, and hindsight trajectory augmentation for counterfactual reasoning with a causal auxiliary loss to improve credit assignment. We evaluate PRIMT on 2 locomotion and 6 manipulation tasks on various benchmarks, demonstrating superior performance over FM-based and scripted baselines. Website at https://primt25.github.io/.

paragraphs: PRIMT uses foundation models to support preference-based reinforcement learning for robot behavior. This learning approach avoids manually engineering rewards, but can require extensive human feedback. It also faces ambiguous comparisons and difficulty assigning credit to the parts of a behavior that deserve reward. PRIMT addresses these issues through synthetic feedback and generated trajectories.

For feedback, the framework combines vision-language models and language models through hierarchical neuro-symbolic fusion. This uses their complementary evaluations of robot behavior to produce more comprehensive judgments. Foresight trajectory generation supplies initial examples to the trajectory buffer, helping reduce ambiguity early in learning when useful comparisons may be difficult to obtain.

PRIMT also augments trajectories in hindsight for counterfactual reasoning, using a causal auxiliary loss to improve credit assignment. This component focuses reward learning on how alternative behavior relates to outcomes. Across two locomotion tasks and six manipulation tasks on various benchmarks, the framework outperforms foundation-model-based and scripted baselines. The results support combining multimodal evaluation with trajectory synthesis to improve preference-based robot learning.
summary.tldr: PRIMT combines multimodal synthetic preferences with generated and counterfactual trajectories to improve robot reward learning.

title: PRIMT: Preference-based Reinforcement Learning with Multimodal Feedback and Trajectory Synthesis from Foundation Models

abstract: The recent success of Shampoo in the AlgoPerf contest has sparked renewed interest in Kronecker-factorization-based optimization algorithms for training neural networks. Despite its success, Shampoo relies heavily on several heuristics such as learning rate grafting and stale preconditioning to achieve performance at-scale. These heuristics increase algorithmic complexity, necessitate further hyperparameter tuning, and lack theoretical justification. This paper investigates these heuristics from the angle of Frobenius norm approximation to full-matrix Adam and decouples the preconditioner's eigenvalues and eigenbasis updates. We show that grafting from Adam mitigates the staleness and mis-scaling of the preconditioner's *eigenvalues* and how correcting the eigenvalues directly eliminates the need for learning rate grafting. To manage the error induced by infrequent *eigenbasis* computations, we propose an adaptive criterion for determining the eigenbasis computation frequency motivated by terminating a warm-started QR algorithm. This criterion decouples the update frequency of different preconditioner matrices and enables us to investigate the impact of approximation error on convergence. These practical techniques offer a principled angle towards removing Shampoo's heuristics and developing improved Kronecker-factorization-based training algorithms.

paragraphs: Shampoo is a neural-network optimizer whose practical success relies on heuristics such as learning-rate grafting and infrequent preconditioner updates. Those choices add complexity and tuning requirements. This paper investigates what these heuristics compensate for by viewing Shampoo’s preconditioner as an approximation to full-matrix Adam and examining its components separately.

The analysis distinguishes the preconditioner’s eigenvalues from its eigenbasis, separating scaling errors from errors associated with the directions of the transformation. The authors show that grafting from Adam helps compensate for stale or incorrectly scaled eigenvalues. Correcting those eigenvalues directly removes the need for learning-rate grafting in their approach, replacing an indirect adjustment with a targeted correction.

Different preconditioner matrices can consequently use different update frequencies. This also enables investigation of how approximation error affects convergence. The contribution is a principled account of specific Shampoo heuristics and practical techniques toward simplifying and improving this family of optimizers.
summary.tldr: Separating Shampoo’s eigenvalue and eigenbasis errors motivates direct scaling corrections and adaptive updates that reduce reliance on optimizer heuristics.

title: Purifying Shampoo: Investigating Shampoo's Heuristics by Decomposing its Preconditioner

abstract: Scaling laws motivate the development of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) that pre-train vast parameters and achieve remarkable zero-shot forecasting performance. Surprisingly, even after fine-tuning, TSFMs cannot consistently outperform smaller, specialized models trained on full-shot downstream data. A key question is how to realize effective adaptation of TSFMs for a target forecasting task. Through empirical studies on various TSFMs, the pre-trained models often exhibit inherent sparsity and redundancy in computation, suggesting that TSFMs have learned to activate task-relevant network substructures to accommodate diverse forecasting tasks. To preserve this valuable prior knowledge, we propose a structured pruning method to regularize the subsequent fine-tuning process by focusing it on a more relevant and compact parameter space. Extensive experiments on seven TSFMs and six benchmarks demonstrate that fine-tuning a smaller, pruned TSFM significantly improves forecasting performance compared to fine-tuning original models. This ``prune-then-finetune'' paradigm often enables TSFMs to achieve state-of-the-art performance and surpass strong specialized baselines. Source code is made publicly available at \url{https://github.com/SJTU-DMTai/Prune-then-Finetune}.
