paragraphs: Large pretrained time series models can forecast well without task-specific training, yet fine-tuning them does not consistently beat smaller models trained specifically for the target task. This paper asks how to adapt those broad forecasting capabilities more effectively. Its empirical starting point is that pretrained models often contain sparse activity patterns and redundant computation.

The authors interpret these patterns as evidence that different forecasting tasks use different parts of the network. They propose structured pruning before fine-tuning, removing network structure so that adaptation happens within a smaller, more relevant parameter space. Pruning acts as a form of regularization intended to preserve useful pretrained knowledge while concentrating subsequent learning on the target task.

Across seven foundation models and six benchmarks, fine-tuning pruned models significantly improves forecasting compared with fine-tuning the original models. The approach often reaches state-of-the-art results and surpasses strong specialized baselines. The finding supports task-focused model reduction as an adaptation strategy, with the reported benefits extending beyond simply having fewer parameters.
summary.tldr: Pruning time series foundation models before fine-tuning improves reported forecasting performance by focusing adaptation on a smaller, task-relevant network.

title: Less is More: Unlocking Specialization of Time Series Foundation Models via Structured Pruning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) for multi-turn conversations suffer from inefficiency: semantically similar queries across different user sessions trigger redundant computation and duplicate memory-intensive Key-Value (KV) caches. Existing optimizations such as prefix caching overlook semantic similarities, while typical semantic caches either ignore conversational context or are not integrated with low-level KV cache management. We propose SmartCache, a system-algorithm co-design framework that tackles this inefficiency by exploiting semantic query similarity across sessions. SmartCache leverages a Semantic Forest structure to hierarchically index conversational turns, enabling efficient retrieval and reuse of responses only when both the semantic query and conversational context match. To maintain accuracy during topic shifts, it leverages internal LLM attention scores—computed during standard prefill—to dynamically detect context changes with minimal computational overhead. Importantly, this semantic understanding is co-designed alongside the memory system: a novel two-level mapping enables transparent cross-session KV cache sharing for semantically equivalent states, complemented by a semantics-aware eviction policy that significantly improves memory utilization. This holistic approach significantly reduces redundant computations and optimizes GPU memory utilization. The evaluation demonstrates SmartCache's effectiveness across multiple benchmarks. On the CoQA and SQuAD datasets, SmartCache reduces KV cache memory usage by up to $59.1\%$ compared to prefix caching and $56.0\%$ over semantic caching, while cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) by $78.0\%$ and $71.7\%$, respectively. It improves answer quality metrics, achieving $39.9\%$ higher F1 and $39.1\%$ higher ROUGE-L for Qwen-2.5-1.5B on CoQA. The Semantic-aware Tiered Eviction Policy (STEP) outperforms LRU/LFU by $29.9\%$ in reuse distance under skewed workloads.

On the CoQA and SQuAD datasets, SmartCache reduces KV cache memory usage by up to $59.1\%$ compared to prefix caching and $56.0\%$ over semantic caching, while cutting Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) by $78.0\%$ and $71.7\%$, respectively. It improves answer quality metrics, achieving $39.9\%$ higher F1 and $39.1\%$ higher ROUGE-L for Qwen-2.5-1.5B on CoQA. The Semantic-aware Tiered Eviction Policy (STEP) outperforms LRU/LFU by $29.9\%$ in reuse distance under skewed workloads.

paragraphs: SmartCache targets duplicated computation and memory use when different conversations ask semantically similar questions. Reusing an answer requires matching the conversational context as well as the current query. The system organizes turns in a Semantic Forest, a hierarchical index that supports retrieval under both conditions.

The framework uses attention scores already computed during standard prefill to detect topic changes with little additional overhead. It connects this semantic processing to memory management through a two-level mapping that shares key-value caches across equivalent conversational states. A semantics-aware eviction policy then decides what cached information to retain, linking answer reuse with GPU memory efficiency.

On CoQA and SQuAD, SmartCache reports memory reductions of up to 59.1% against prefix caching and 56.0% against semantic caching, with time-to-first-token reductions of 78.0% and 71.7%, respectively. It also reports answer-quality improvements for Qwen-2.5-1.5B on CoQA. These results show the benefit of jointly considering conversational meaning and low-level cache management instead of treating them as separate optimization problems.
summary.tldr: SmartCache matches queries together with conversational context to reuse responses and share KV memory, reducing latency and memory use in the reported evaluations.

title: SmartCache: Context-aware Semantic Cache for Efficient Multi-turn LLM Inference

abstract: This paper considers the task of finding a target location by making a limited number of sequential observations. Each observation results from evaluating an imperfect classifier of a chosen cost and accuracy on an interval of chosen length and position. Within a Bayesian framework, we study the problem of minimizing an objective that combines the entropy of the posterior distribution with the cost of the questions asked. In this problem, we show that the one-step lookahead policy is Bayes-optimal for any arbitrary time horizon. Moreover, this one-step lookahead policy is easy to compute and implement. We then use this policy in the context of localizing mitochondria in electron microscope images, and experimentally show that significant speed ups in acquisition can be gained, while maintaining near equal image quality at target locations, when compared to current policies.

paragraphs: Finding a target efficiently requires deciding where to look next and how much to spend on each observation. This paper studies a sequential search problem in which an imperfect classifier examines an interval. The decision includes the interval's location and length, as well as a choice of classifier cost and accuracy.

The authors express the problem in Bayesian terms, updating uncertainty about the target after each observation. Their objective combines the entropy of the resulting probability distribution with the accumulated cost of observations. For this formulation, they prove that choosing the best next observation through one-step lookahead is Bayes-optimal for any time horizon. A decision rule that considers just the immediate next step therefore achieves the full-horizon optimum in the studied problem.

The policy is also straightforward to calculate and implement. Applied to locating mitochondria in electron microscope images, it substantially speeds image acquisition relative to existing policies while preserving nearly equal image quality at target locations. This connects the optimality result to a practical allocation problem: concentrating acquisition effort where the desired structures are located.
summary.tldr: For a Bayesian target-search formulation, a simple one-step policy is optimal and speeds microscopy acquisition while preserving target-region image quality.

title: An Optimal Policy for Target Localization with Application to Electron Microscopy

abstract: We consider stochastic multi-armed bandits where the expected reward is a unimodal function over partially ordered arms. This important class of problems has been recently investigated in (Cope 2009, Yu 2011). The set of arms is either discrete, in which case arms correspond to the vertices of a finite graph whose structure represents similarity in rewards, or continuous, in which case arms belong to a bounded interval. For discrete unimodal bandits, we derive asymptotic lower bounds for the regret achieved under any algorithm, and propose OSUB, an algorithm whose regret matches this lower bound. Our algorithm optimally exploits the unimodal structure of the problem, and surprisingly, its asymptotic regret does not depend on the number of arms. We also provide a regret upper bound for OSUB in non-stationary environments where the expected rewards smoothly evolve over time. The analytical results are supported by numerical experiments showing that OSUB performs significantly better than the state-of-the-art algorithms. For continuous sets of arms, we provide a brief discussion. We show that combining an appropriate discretization of the set of arms with the UCB algorithm yields an order-optimal regret, and in practice, outperforms recently proposed algorithms designed to exploit the unimodal structure.

paragraphs: This paper studies bandit problems whose expected rewards have a unimodal structure over related choices. In the discrete case, the choices are vertices of a finite graph representing reward similarity. The authors derive asymptotic lower bounds on regret and introduce OSUB, an algorithm that matches those bounds.

OSUB's asymptotic regret does not depend on the total number of arms, showing how effectively it can exploit the specified structure. The paper also provides an upper bound for environments where expected rewards change smoothly over time. Numerical experiments support the analysis and report substantially better performance than the state-of-the-art algorithms considered.

For choices drawn from a bounded continuous interval, the authors briefly examine a different construction: discretize the interval appropriately and apply UCB. They show that this combination achieves order-optimal regret and empirically outperforms recently proposed methods designed for unimodal rewards. The results distinguish exact asymptotic matching in the discrete setting from order optimality in the continuous setting, while showing the value of using unimodal structure.
summary.tldr: OSUB matches asymptotic regret lower bounds for discrete unimodal bandits, with regret independent of the total number of arms.

title: Unimodal Bandits: Regret Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms

abstract: Many machine learning algorithms require the input to be represented as a fixed length feature vector. When it comes to texts, one of the most common representations is bag-of-words. Despite their popularity, bag-of-words models have two major weaknesses: they lose the ordering of the words and they also ignore semantics of the words. For example, "powerful," "strong" and "Paris" are equally distant. In this paper, we propose an unsupervised algorithm that learns vector representations of sentences and text documents. This algorithm represents each document by a dense vector which is trained to predict words in the document. Its construction gives our algorithm the potential to overcome the weaknesses of bag-of-words models. Empirical results show that our technique outperforms bag-of-words models as well as other techniques for text representations. Finally, we achieve new state-of-the-art results on several text classification and sentiment analysis tasks.

paragraphs: Many learning algorithms need every input to have a fixed number of features, even when the inputs are sentences or documents of different lengths. Bag-of-words representations provide one solution, but discard word order and fail to represent semantic relationships between words. These weaknesses motivate learning a richer representation of whole texts.

The proposed unsupervised algorithm assigns each document a dense vector and trains that vector to predict words appearing in the document. Prediction supplies the learning signal, allowing the representation to be learned without task labels. The construction gives the method the potential to address the weaknesses identified in bag-of-words representations.

The empirical results show better performance than bag-of-words models and other text representation methods. The authors also report new state-of-the-art results on several text classification and sentiment analysis tasks. These findings connect the word-prediction training objective to useful document features: vectors learned without task labels can support subsequent prediction tasks that depend on the content of a sentence or document.
summary.tldr: An unsupervised word-prediction objective learns dense document vectors that outperform several text representations in the reported experiments.

title: Distributed Representations of Sentences and Documents

abstract: We introduce a deep, generative autoencoder capable of learning hierarchies of distributed representations from data. Successive deep stochastic hidden layers are equipped with autoregressive connections, which enable the model to be sampled from quickly and exactly via ancestral sampling. We derive an efficient approximate parameter estimation method based on the minimum description length (MDL) principle, which can be seen as maximising a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood, with a feedforward neural network implementing approximate inference. We demonstrate state-of-the-art generative performance on a number of classic data sets: several UCI data sets, MNIST and Atari 2600 games.
originalAbstract: We introduce a deep, generative autoencoder capable of learning hierarchies of distributed representations from data. Successive deep stochastic hidden layers are equipped with autoregressive connections, which enable the model to be sampled from quickly and exactly via ancestral sampling. We derive an efficient approximate parameter estimation method based on the minimum description length (MDL) principle, which can be seen as maximising a variational lower bound on the log-likelihood, with a feedforward neural network implementing approximate inference. We demonstrate state-of-the-art generative performance on a number of classic data sets: several UCI data sets, MNIST and Atari 2600 games.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a generative autoencoder that learns multiple levels of distributed representations. Its hidden layers are stochastic, so they describe uncertain internal variables rather than only deterministic transformations. Autoregressive connections organize dependencies within successive hidden layers, providing a structure for generating values in a defined sequence.

That structure allows fast, exact ancestral sampling from the model. Sampling and learning have different computational properties here: although generation is exact, parameter estimation uses an efficient approximation. The training method follows the minimum description length principle and can also be understood as maximizing a variational lower bound on log-likelihood.

A feedforward neural network supplies approximate inference, helping estimate hidden representations from observed data during learning. Together, these components connect hierarchical representation learning, tractable generation, and approximate training within one model. The authors report state-of-the-art generative performance on several UCI datasets, MNIST, and Atari 2600 games. These findings support the model’s effectiveness across the evaluated datasets while preserving the distinction between exact sampling and approximate inference.
summary.tldr: Deep autoregressive networks combine hierarchical stochastic representations, exact sampling, and approximate training, with strong reported generative performance.

title: Deep AutoRegressive Networks

abstract: Given a dictionary \Pi and a signal ξ= \Pi \mathbf x generated by a few \textitlinearly independent columns of \Pi, classical sparse recovery theory deals with the problem of uniquely recovering the sparse representation \mathbf x of ξ. In this work, we consider the more general case where ξlies in a low-dimensional subspace spanned by a few columns of \Pi, which are possibly \textitlinearly dependent. In this case, \mathbf x may not unique, and the goal is to recover any subset of the columns of \Pi that spans the subspace containing ξ. We call such a representation \mathbf x \textitsubspace-sparse. We study conditions under which existing pursuit methods recover a subspace-sparse representation. Such conditions reveal important geometric insights and have implications for the theory of classical sparse recovery as well as subspace clustering.

In this work, we consider the more general case where ξlies in a low-dimensional subspace spanned by a few columns of \Pi, which are possibly \textitlinearly dependent. paragraphs: Classical sparse recovery seeks a unique sparse set of coefficients representing a signal using columns of a dictionary. This paper studies a broader setting in which the relevant columns can be linearly dependent. In that setting, several coefficient choices may represent the same signal, so unique coefficient recovery is no longer the appropriate goal.

The authors instead define a subspace-sparse representation. The objective is to recover a subset of dictionary columns that spans the low-dimensional subspace containing the signal. This shifts attention from identifying one particular coefficient vector to identifying the subspace structure that accounts for the observation.

The paper studies conditions under which existing pursuit methods can recover such representations. These conditions provide geometric insight into why recovery can work even when the relevant dictionary columns are dependent. The contribution is therefore a recovery framework and analysis, rather than simply a new algorithm. The authors also identify implications for classical sparse-recovery theory and subspace clustering, connecting coefficient-based reconstruction with the problem of finding the underlying low-dimensional spaces.
summary.tldr: The paper gives geometric conditions for recovering a signal's supporting subspace when its dictionary coefficients need not be unique.

title: Geometric Conditions for Subspace-Sparse Recovery

abstract: Existing methods for retrieving k-nearest neighbours suffer from the curse of dimensionality. We argue this is caused in part by inherent deficiencies of space partitioning, which is the underlying strategy used by most existing methods. We devise a new strategy that avoids partitioning the vector space and present a novel randomized algorithm that runs in time linear in dimensionality of the space and sub-linear in the intrinsic dimensionality and the size of the dataset and takes space constant in dimensionality of the space and linear in the size of the dataset. The proposed algorithm allows fine-grained control over accuracy and speed on a per-query basis, automatically adapts to variations in data density, supports dynamic updates to the dataset and is easy-to-implement. We show appealing theoretical properties and demonstrate empirically that the proposed algorithm outperforms locality-sensitivity hashing (LSH) in terms of approximation quality, speed and space efficiency.
originalAbstract: Existing methods for retrieving k-nearest neighbours suffer from the curse of dimensionality. We argue this is caused in part by inherent deficiencies of space partitioning, which is the underlying strategy used by most existing methods. We devise a new strategy that avoids partitioning the vector space and present a novel randomized algorithm that runs in time linear in dimensionality of the space and sub-linear in the intrinsic dimensionality and the size of the dataset and takes space constant in dimensionality of the space and linear in the size of the dataset. The proposed algorithm allows fine-grained control over accuracy and speed on a per-query basis, automatically adapts to variations in data density, supports dynamic updates to the dataset and is easy-to-implement. We show appealing theoretical properties and demonstrate empirically that the proposed algorithm outperforms locality-sensitivity hashing (LSH) in terms of approximation quality, speed and space efficiency.

paragraphs: Finding the nearest data points becomes difficult in high-dimensional spaces. This paper argues that part of this difficulty comes from partitioning space, the strategy underlying many search methods. It introduces a randomized alternative that avoids dividing the vector space into regions and supports retrieval of k nearest neighbors.

The algorithm has stated running-time dependence that is linear in ambient dimensionality and sublinear in both intrinsic dimensionality and dataset size. Its space usage is independent of ambient dimensionality and linear in dataset size. These properties address different aspects of scalability: the cost of answering a query and the storage needed by the search method.

The approach also allows accuracy and speed to be adjusted separately for each query, adapts automatically to changes in data density, and supports updates to the dataset. The authors provide theoretical properties and empirical comparisons against locality-sensitive hashing. In those comparisons, the method improves approximation quality, speed, and space efficiency, supporting its practical appeal alongside its stated computational guarantees.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Continuous Indexing avoids space partitioning and offers efficient, adjustable nearest-neighbor search with support for dataset updates.

title: Fast k-Nearest Neighbour Search via Dynamic Continuous Indexing

abstract: This paper introduces a new technique for mapping Deep Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN) efficiently onto GPUs. We show how it is possi- ble to achieve substantially higher computational throughput at low mini-batch sizes than direct implementations of RNNs based on matrix multiplications. The key to our approach is the use of persistent computational kernels that exploit the GPU’s inverted memory hierarchy to reuse network weights over multiple timesteps. Our initial implementation sustains 2.8 TFLOP/s at a mini-batch size of 4 on an NVIDIA TitanX GPU. This provides a 16x reduction in activation memory footprint, enables model training with 12x more parameters on the same hardware, allows us to strongly scale RNN training to 128 GPUs, and allows us to efficiently explore end-to-end speech recognition models with over 100 layers.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a GPU implementation technique for recurrent neural networks, focusing on high computational throughput at small minibatch sizes. Its key idea is to keep recurrent weights on-chip and reuse them across multiple time steps through persistent computational kernels. This uses the GPU’s memory hierarchy to improve how the recurrent computation is mapped onto hardware.

The initial implementation sustains 2.8 TFLOP/s with a minibatch size of four on an NVIDIA TitanX. The authors report substantially higher throughput at small minibatch sizes than direct implementations based on matrix multiplication. The result shows that the implementation strategy can make small-batch recurrent computation efficient on the evaluated hardware.

The paper reports a sixteenfold reduction in activation memory and the ability to train models with twelve times as many parameters on the same hardware. It also enables strong scaling to 128 GPUs and efficient exploration of end-to-end speech recognition models exceeding 100 layers. These outcomes connect weight reuse to practical gains in memory use, model capacity, and distributed training.
summary.tldr: Persistent GPU kernels reuse recurrent weights across time steps, improving small-batch throughput and enabling larger and deeper RNN training.

title: Persistent RNNs: Stashing Recurrent Weights On-Chip

abstract: We introduce the Dynamic Capacity Network (DCN), a neural network that can adaptively assign its capacity across different portions of the input data. This is achieved by combining modules of two types: low-capacity sub-networks and high-capacity sub-networks. The low-capacity sub-networks are applied across most of the input, but also provide a guide to select a few portions of the input on which to apply the high-capacity sub-networks. The selection is made using a novel gradient-based attention mechanism, that efficiently identifies input regions for which the DCN’s output is most sensitive and to which we should devote more capacity. We focus our empirical evaluation on the Cluttered MNIST and SVHN image datasets. Our findings indicate that DCNs are able to drastically reduce the number of computations, compared to traditional convolutional neural networks, while maintaining similar or even better performance.

Our findings indicate that DCNs are able to drastically reduce the number of computations, compared to traditional convolutional neural networks, while maintaining similar or even better performance.

paragraphs: Dynamic Capacity Networks address how a neural network distributes computation across an input. Different portions may benefit from different amounts of processing, so the architecture combines low-capacity and high-capacity subnetworks. The smaller subnetworks operate over most of the input and help decide where the larger subnetworks should be applied.

The selection mechanism uses gradients to identify regions where the network’s output is most sensitive to the input. It then allocates additional capacity to a few selected regions. This makes attention a way to direct computation: the initial processing both contributes to the prediction and guides where more expensive processing should occur.

Experiments on Cluttered MNIST and SVHN indicate that this adaptive allocation can drastically reduce computation compared with traditional convolutional neural networks while maintaining similar or better performance. The finding is empirical and tied to those evaluations. Its significance is that substantial computational savings can come from choosing where to use capacity within an input, rather than applying the same amount of processing everywhere.
summary.tldr: Dynamic Capacity Networks use gradient-based attention to concentrate expensive processing on selected input regions, reducing computation in image experiments.

title: Dynamic Capacity Networks

abstract: Multi-label classification is a generalization of binary classification where the task consists in predicting \emphsets of labels. With the availability of ever larger datasets, the multi-label setting has become a natural one in many applications, and the interest in solving multi-label problems has grown significantly. As expected, deep learning approaches are now yielding state-of-the-art performance for this class of problems. Unfortunately, they usually do not take into account the often unknown but nevertheless rich relationships between labels. In this paper, we propose to make use of this underlying structure by learning to partition the labels into a Markov Blanket Chain and then applying a novel deep architecture that exploits the partition. Experiments on several popular and large multi-label datasets demonstrate that our approach not only yields significant improvements, but also helps to overcome trade-offs specific to the multi-label classification setting.

paragraphs: Multilabel classification predicts a set of labels for each example. The paper focuses on the relationships among those labels, which can contain useful structure even when that structure is unknown beforehand. It argues that deep learning approaches can achieve strong results while still leaving these relationships insufficiently represented.

ADIOS first learns to partition the labels into a structure called a Markov Blanket Chain. It then uses a new deep architecture designed to exploit that partition. The output organization is therefore learned as part of the approach, giving the network a way to use relationships among labels when making its predictions.

Experiments on several popular, large multilabel datasets report significant improvements and benefits for trade-offs specific to multilabel classification. These findings support the usefulness of explicitly organizing the output space in the evaluated settings. The central contribution is the combination of learning label structure and constructing an architecture around it, so that prediction can draw on more than the information used to distinguish each label separately.
summary.tldr: ADIOS learns a structured partition of labels and uses it in a deep architecture to improve multilabel prediction.

title: ADIOS: Architectures Deep In Output Space

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of Robust Matrix Completion (RMC) where the goal is to recover a low-rank matrix by observing a small number of its entries out of which a few can be arbitrarily corrupted. We propose a simple projected gradient descent-based method to estimate the low-rank matrix that alternately performs a projected gradient descent step and cleans up a few of the corrupted entries using hard-thresholding. Our algorithm solves RMC using nearly optimal number of observations while tolerating a nearly optimal number of corruptions. Our result also implies significant improvement over the existing time complexity bounds for the low-rank matrix completion problem. Finally, an application of our result to the robust PCA problem (low-rank+sparse matrix separation) leads to nearly linear time (in matrix dimensions) algorithm for the same; existing state-of-the-art methods require quadratic time. Our empirical results corroborate our theoretical results and show that even for moderate sized problems, our method for robust PCA is an order of magnitude faster than the existing methods.

Our algorithm solves RMC using nearly optimal number of observations while tolerating a nearly optimal number of corruptions. Our result also implies significant improvement over the existing time complexity bounds for the low-rank matrix completion problem. paragraphs: Robust matrix completion seeks to reconstruct a low-rank matrix from a small set of observed entries when some observations may be arbitrarily corrupted. The task combines missing information with unreliable information. This paper proposes a simple iterative method that alternates between a projected gradient descent step and a hard-thresholding step that cleans up some corrupted entries.

The theoretical result addresses both demands of the problem: the method uses a nearly optimal number of observations while tolerating a nearly optimal number of corruptions. The authors also derive a significant improvement over existing runtime bounds for low-rank matrix completion. These results connect efficient computation with recovery from incomplete and corrupted observations.

Applied to robust principal component analysis, which separates a matrix into low-rank and sparse components, the result yields nearly linear runtime in matrix dimensions, compared with quadratic time for the cited leading methods. Empirical results support the theory, and the robust PCA implementation is an order of magnitude faster than existing methods even on moderately sized problems.
summary.tldr: Alternating projected gradient descent with hard-thresholding enables nearly optimal robust matrix completion and a nearly linear-time robust PCA algorithm.

title: Nearly Optimal Robust Matrix Completion

abstract: Determinantal point processes (DPPs) are popular probabilistic models that arise in many machine learning tasks, where distributions of diverse sets are characterized by determinants of their features. In this paper, we develop fast algorithms to find the most likely configuration (MAP) of large-scale DPPs, which is NP-hard in general. Due to the submodular nature of the MAP objective, greedy algorithms have been used with empirical success. Greedy implementations require computation of log-determinants, matrix inverses or solving linear systems at each iteration. We present faster implementations of the greedy algorithms by utilizing the orthogonal benefits of two log-determinant approximation schemes: (a) first-order expansions to the matrix log-determinant function and (b) high-order expansions to the scalar log function with stochastic trace estimators. In our experiments, our algorithms are orders of magnitude faster than their competitors, while sacrificing marginal accuracy.

In this paper, we develop fast algorithms to find the most likely configuration (MAP) of large-scale DPPs, which is NP-hard in general. Due to the submodular nature of the MAP objective, greedy algorithms have been used with empirical success. Greedy implementations require computation of log-determinants, matrix inverses or solving linear systems at each iteration. We present faster implementations of the greedy algorithms by utilizing the orthogonal benefits of two log-determinant approximation schemes: (a) first-order expansions to the matrix log-determinant function and (b) high-order expansions to the scalar log function with stochastic trace estimators. In our experiments, our algorithms are orders of magnitude faster than their competitors, while sacrificing marginal accuracy.

paragraphs: Determinantal point processes model distributions over diverse sets using determinants of their features. Finding the most likely set, known as MAP inference, is NP-hard in general. Greedy algorithms have nevertheless worked well empirically, drawing on the submodular structure of the objective to build a solution through successive choices.

The paper accelerates these greedy procedures by reducing the cost of their matrix calculations. Existing implementations repeatedly compute log-determinants, matrix inverses, or solutions to linear systems. The proposed implementations exploit two complementary approximations: first-order expansions of the matrix log-determinant and higher-order expansions of the scalar logarithm combined with stochastic trace estimation.

In the reported experiments, these algorithms run orders of magnitude faster than competitors while giving up only marginal accuracy. The result concerns faster approximate greedy inference; the underlying general MAP problem remains hard. Its practical importance is that expensive calculations inside an empirically useful search procedure can be approximated with a favorable observed speed–accuracy tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Complementary log-determinant approximations greatly accelerate greedy DPP inference with only marginal accuracy loss in the reported experiments.

title: Faster Greedy MAP Inference for Determinantal Point Processes

abstract: Whitened Neural Network (WNN) is a recent advanced deep architecture, which improves convergence and generalization of canonical neural networks by whitening their internal hidden representation. However, the whitening transformation increases computation time. Unlike WNN that reduced runtime by performing whitening every thousand iterations, which degenerates convergence due to the ill conditioning, we present generalized WNN (GWNN), which has three appealing properties. First, GWNN is able to learn compact representation to reduce computations. Second, it enables whitening transformation to be performed in a short period, preserving good conditioning. Third, we propose a data-independent estimation of the covariance matrix to further improve computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the benefits of GWNN.

However, the whitening transformation increases computation time. Unlike WNN that reduced runtime by performing whitening every thousand iterations, which degenerates convergence due to the ill conditioning, we present generalized WNN (GWNN), which has three appealing properties. First, GWNN is able to learn compact representation to reduce computations. Second, it enables whitening transformation to be performed in a short period, preserving good conditioning. Third, we propose a data-independent estimation of the covariance matrix to further improve computational efficiency. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate the benefits of GWNN.

paragraphs: Whitened neural networks transform their internal representations to improve convergence and generalization. The transformation also adds computational cost. An earlier workaround performs whitening only every thousand iterations, but the abstract reports that this allows poor conditioning to harm convergence. This paper develops generalized whitened neural networks to address that tension.

The proposed architecture learns compact representations, reducing the amount of computation required. It also allows whitening to occur at shorter intervals, preserving good conditioning instead of letting the transformation become too infrequent. These two changes connect representation size with the practical ability to keep the network’s internal representations well conditioned during training.

A further contribution estimates the covariance matrix independently of the data to improve computational efficiency. Experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate benefits of the generalized approach. The overall contribution is a way to make whitening more affordable while retaining the conditioning benefit that motivates it, addressing both the size of the representation and the cost of the transformation.
summary.tldr: Generalized whitened neural networks reduce whitening costs through compact representations and data-independent covariance estimation.

title: Learning Deep Architectures via Generalized Whitened Neural Networks

abstract: Sparse support vector machine (SVM) is a popular classification technique that can simultaneously learn a small set of the most interpretable features and identify the support vectors. It has achieved great successes in many real-world applications. However, for large-scale problems involving a huge number of samples and extremely high-dimensional features, solving sparse SVMs remains challenging. By noting that sparse SVMs induce sparsities in both feature and sample spaces, we propose a novel approach, which is based on accurate estimations of the primal and dual optima of sparse SVMs, to simultaneously identify the features and samples that are guaranteed to be irrelevant to the outputs. Thus, we can remove the identified inactive samples and features from the training phase, leading to substantial savings in both the memory usage and computational cost without sacrificing accuracy. To the best of our knowledge, the proposed method is the first static feature and sample reduction method for sparse SVMs. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets (e.g., the kddb dataset with about 20 million samples and 30 million features) demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods and the speedup gained by our approach can be orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Sparse support vector machines can select a small set of useful features while identifying the training examples that act as support vectors. Yet training remains difficult when both the number of examples and the feature dimension are enormous. This paper uses sparsity in both spaces to reduce the problem before training.

The method estimates the primal and dual optima accurately enough to identify features and samples guaranteed to be irrelevant to the resulting outputs. Those inactive elements can then be removed from training. The guarantee is central: the reduction is designed to save memory and computation without sacrificing the accuracy of the sparse SVM solution.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with speedups that can reach orders of magnitude. The evaluated data includes kddb, with about 20 million samples and 30 million features. The contribution combines feature screening and sample screening in one static reduction procedure, addressing both major sources of scale in a large sparse classification problem.
summary.tldr: Jointly screening guaranteed-irrelevant features and samples speeds sparse SVM training without sacrificing accuracy.

title: Scaling Up Sparse Support Vector Machines by Simultaneous Feature and Sample Reduction

abstract: Minimax optimization plays a key role in adversarial training of machine learning algorithms, such as learning generative models, domain adaptation, privacy preservation, and robust learning. In this paper, we demonstrate the failure of alternating gradient descent in minimax optimization problems due to the discontinuity of solutions of the inner maximization. To address this, we propose a new $\epsilon$-subgradient descent algorithm that addresses this problem by simultaneously tracking $K$ candidate solutions. Practically, the algorithm can find solutions that previous saddle-point algorithms cannot find, with only a sublinear increase of complexity in $K$. We analyze the conditions under which the algorithm converges to the true solution in detail. A significant improvement in stability and convergence speed of the algorithm is observed in simple representative problems, GAN training, and domain-adaptation problems.

paragraphs: Minimax learning combines two opposing optimization problems: one component minimizes an objective while another maximizes it. This paper identifies a failure mode of alternating gradient updates. The solution to the inner maximization can change discontinuously, making it difficult for an alternating method to follow the relevant maximizing solution as the outer variables move.

The proposed K-Beam method addresses this issue by tracking K candidate inner solutions simultaneously. It uses an approximate-subgradient descent algorithm to support the outer optimization. Keeping multiple candidates gives the procedure alternatives when the relevant inner solution changes. The authors report that this can reach solutions missed by previous saddle-point algorithms, with complexity increasing only sublinearly in K.

The paper analyzes conditions under which the algorithm converges to the true solution. Experiments on representative problems, generative adversarial network training, and domain adaptation show substantial improvements in stability and convergence speed. These results support maintaining several competing inner solutions as a practical response to the discontinuities identified in the analysis.
summary.tldr: K-Beam tracks multiple inner maximizers to address discontinuities that can derail alternating minimax optimization.

title: K-Beam Minimax: Efficient Optimization for Deep Adversarial Learning

abstract: Generative flows are attractive because they admit exact likelihood optimization and efficient image synthesis. Recently, Kingma & Dhariwal (2018) demonstrated with Glow that generative flows are capable of generating high quality images. We generalize the 1 {\texttimes} 1 convolutions proposed in Glow to invertible d {\texttimes} d convolutions, which are more flexible since they operate on both channel and spatial axes. We propose two methods to produce invertible convolutions, that have receptive fields identical to standard convolutions: Emerging convolutions are obtained by chaining specific autoregressive convolutions, and periodic convolutions are decoupled in the frequency domain. Our experiments show that the flexibility of d {\texttimes} d convolutions significantly improves the performance of generative flow models on galaxy images, CIFAR10 and ImageNet.

paragraphs: Generative flow models support exact likelihood optimization and efficient image generation. This paper focuses on making their convolutional transformations more flexible. It extends the invertible 1-by-1 convolutions used in Glow to invertible d-by-d convolutions, enabling a transformation to operate across spatial positions as well as image channels.

The authors propose two constructions that preserve invertibility while giving the transformations receptive fields like those of standard convolutions. Emerging convolutions chain together particular autoregressive convolutions. Periodic convolutions use a frequency-domain representation in which the convolution can be decoupled. These provide different routes to introducing spatial interactions into an invertible flow component.

Experiments on galaxy images, CIFAR10, and ImageNet show significant improvements in generative-flow performance from the added flexibility. The findings support the value of expanding the spatial reach of invertible convolutions within these models. The contribution connects a concrete architectural change with observed improvements while retaining the invertible transformation structure needed by the flow framework.
summary.tldr: Two constructions extend invertible flow convolutions across spatial positions and channels, improving performance on the tested image datasets.

title: Emerging Convolutions for Generative Normalizing Flows

abstract: Reinforcement learning algorithms struggle when the reward signal is very sparse. In these cases, naive random exploration methods essentially rely on a random walk to stumble onto a rewarding state. Recent works utilize intrinsic motivation to guide the exploration via generative models, predictive forward models, or discriminative modeling of novelty. We propose EMI, which is an exploration method that constructs embedding representation of states and actions that does not rely on generative decoding of the full observation but extracts predictive signals that can be used to guide exploration based on forward prediction in the representation space. Our experiments show competitive results on challenging locomotion tasks with continuous control and on image-based exploration tasks with discrete actions on Atari. The source code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/EMI.

paragraphs: When rewards are sparse, random exploration may require an agent to stumble onto a useful state before it receives meaningful feedback. Intrinsic motivation methods try to supply another signal for deciding where to explore. EMI develops such a signal using learned representations of states and actions and predictions made within that representation space.

The approach extracts predictive information without requiring a generative decoder to reconstruct the complete observation. This places the emphasis on representing information useful for forward prediction rather than reproducing every detail of what the agent sees. The learned state and action embeddings provide the space in which those predictions can guide exploration.

The authors report competitive performance on challenging locomotion tasks with continuous control and on Atari exploration tasks with image observations and discrete actions. These evaluations cover different observation and action settings, supporting the approach's usefulness across the tested tasks. The result is a representation-based exploration method with competitive empirical evidence; the abstract does not claim that it uniformly surpasses other exploration approaches.
summary.tldr: EMI guides exploration through forward prediction in learned state and action representations without reconstructing full observations.

title: EMI: Exploration with Mutual Information

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) are a class of deep generative models which aim to learn a target distribution in an unsupervised fashion. While they were successfully applied to many problems, training a GAN is a notoriously challenging task and requires a significant number of hyperparameter tuning, neural architecture engineering, and a non-trivial amount of “tricks". The success in many practical applications coupled with the lack of a measure to quantify the failure modes of GANs resulted in a plethora of proposed losses, regularization and normalization schemes, as well as neural architectures. In this work we take a sober view of the current state of GANs from a practical perspective. We discuss and evaluate common pitfalls and reproducibility issues, open-source our code on Github, and provide pre-trained models on TensorFlow Hub.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial networks aim to learn a target distribution without supervision, but getting them to train successfully can require substantial practical effort. Choices about hyperparameters, network architecture, and training adjustments all enter the process. This paper examines that practical situation through a large-scale study of regularization and normalization in GANs.

The motivation is that successful applications have appeared alongside many competing losses, regularization schemes, normalization methods, and architectures. The authors connect this proliferation to the difficulty of measuring GAN failure modes. Their study therefore addresses how these methods are evaluated and reproduced, as well as the training choices themselves.

The contribution described is a practical assessment of common pitfalls and reproducibility problems, accompanied by publicly released code and pretrained models. These resources make the study's implementations available for inspection and reuse. Its stated emphasis is understanding and evaluating the existing training landscape; the abstract does not identify a particular regularizer or normalization scheme as the overall winner.
summary.tldr: This study examines practical GAN training choices, common evaluation pitfalls, and reproducibility issues, and releases code and pretrained models.

title: A Large-Scale Study on Regularization and Normalization in GANs

abstract: In many finite horizon episodic reinforcement learning (RL) settings, it is desirable to optimize for the undiscounted return - in settings like Atari, for instance, the goal is to collect the most points while staying alive in the long run. Yet, it may be difficult (or even intractable) mathematically to learn with this target. As such, temporal discounting is often applied to optimize over a shorter effective planning horizon. This comes at the cost of potentially biasing the optimization target away from the undiscounted goal. In settings where this bias is unacceptable - where the system must optimize for longer horizons at higher discounts - the target of the value function approximator may increase in variance leading to difficulties in learning. We present an extension of temporal difference (TD) learning, which we call TD($\Delta$), that breaks down a value function into a series of components based on the differences between value functions with smaller discount factors. The separation of a longer horizon value function into these components has useful properties in scalability and performance. We discuss these properties and show theoretic and empirical improvements over standard TD learning in certain settings.

paragraphs: In finite-horizon episodic reinforcement learning, the desired objective may be total undiscounted reward. Discounting makes learning focus on a shorter effective horizon, but can shift the objective away from that goal. Using a higher discount factor preserves more long-term influence, while potentially increasing the variance of value-learning targets and making training harder.

The paper introduces TD(Delta), an extension of temporal-difference learning that decomposes a value function across time scales. Its components are based on differences between value functions with smaller discount factors. This represents a longer-horizon value through a sequence of related pieces, giving the learning procedure a structured way to handle contributions associated with different horizons.

The authors analyze useful scalability and performance properties of this decomposition and report theoretical and empirical improvements over standard TD learning in certain settings. The result offers a way to organize long-horizon value estimation without simply replacing the desired horizon with a shorter one. Its improvement claims are qualified by the settings studied, rather than establishing a universal advantage for all reinforcement-learning problems.
summary.tldr: TD(Delta) decomposes long-horizon value functions across discount scales, improving on standard TD learning in certain theoretical and empirical settings.

title: Separating value functions across time-scales

abstract: We study Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with diminishing step sizes for convex objective functions. We introduce a definitional framework and theory that defines and characterizes a core property, called curvature, of convex objective functions. In terms of curvature we can derive a new inequality that can be used to compute an optimal sequence of diminishing step sizes by solving a differential equation. Our exact solutions confirm known results in literature and allows us to fully characterize a new regularizer with its corresponding expected convergence rates.
originalAbstract: We study Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with diminishing step sizes for convex objective functions. We introduce a definitional framework and theory that defines and characterizes a core property, called curvature, of convex objective functions. In terms of curvature we can derive a new inequality that can be used to compute an optimal sequence of diminishing step sizes by solving a differential equation. Our exact solutions confirm known results in literature and allows us to fully characterize a new regularizer with its corresponding expected convergence rates.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to reduce the step size in stochastic gradient descent when optimizing a convex objective. The step size controls how far each update moves. Rather than treating its schedule as a separate tuning choice, the authors connect the schedule to a property of the objective that they formally define as curvature.

The main contribution is a framework for characterizing that curvature and deriving an inequality from it. This inequality makes it possible to compute an optimal sequence of diminishing step sizes by solving a differential equation. The approach therefore connects the shape of the optimization problem, the choice of updates, and the expected rate of progress within one theoretical analysis.

The exact solutions recover results already known in the literature, while also allowing the authors to characterize a new regularizer and its expected convergence rates. These findings concern convex objectives and diminishing step sizes; they explain how the proposed curvature framework organizes convergence behavior in that setting.
summary.tldr: A formal notion of convex-objective curvature connects diminishing SGD step sizes to optimal expected convergence rates.

title: Characterization of Convex Objective Functions and Optimal Expected Convergence Rates for SGD

abstract: Difference of convex (DC) functions cover a broad family of non-convex and possibly non-smooth and non-differentiable functions, and have wide applications in machine learning and statistics. Although deterministic algorithms for DC functions have been extensively studied, stochastic optimization that is more suitable for learning with big data remains under-explored. In this paper, we propose new stochastic optimization algorithms and study their first-order convergence theories for solving a broad family of DC functions. We improve the existing algorithms and theories of stochastic optimization for DC functions from both practical and theoretical perspectives. Moreover, we extend the proposed stochastic algorithms for DC functions to solve problems with a general non-convex non-differentiable regularizer, which does not necessarily have a DC decomposition but enjoys an efficient proximal mapping. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that gives the first non-asymptotic convergence for solving non-convex optimization whose objective has a general non-convex non-differentiable regularizer.

paragraphs: A difference-of-convex function expresses an objective as one convex function minus another. This representation covers a broad range of nonconvex objectives, including ones that are nonsmooth or nondifferentiable. Although deterministic methods for these problems have received extensive attention, this paper focuses on stochastic optimization, which is better suited to learning with large datasets.

The authors propose stochastic algorithms and analyze their first-order convergence for a broad family of difference-of-convex problems. They report improvements over existing algorithms and theory from both practical and theoretical perspectives. The contribution therefore addresses how to optimize these objectives and how to characterize the progress that the stochastic procedures make.

The methods are also extended to objectives with general nonconvex, nondifferentiable regularizers. Such regularizers need not admit a difference-of-convex decomposition, but they must have an efficient proximal mapping. For this broader setting, the paper provides non-asymptotic convergence results, describing behavior over finite computation rather than only in the limit. This expands the analyzed class beyond objectives directly covered by the original decomposition.
summary.tldr: The paper develops stochastic optimization methods with finite-time convergence analysis for difference-of-convex objectives and broader proximally tractable nonconvex regularizers.

title: Stochastic Optimization for DC Functions and Non-smooth Non-convex Regularizers with Non-asymptotic Convergence

abstract: Frank-Wolfe algorithm is an efficient method for optimizing non-convex constrained problems. However, most of existing methods focus on the first-order case. In real-world applications, the gradient is not always available. To address the problem of lacking gradient in many applications, we propose two new stochastic zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe algorithms and theoretically proved that they have a faster convergence rate than existing methods for non-convex problems. Specifically, the function queries oracle of the proposed faster zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe (FZFW) method is $O(\frac{n^{1/2}d}{\epsilon^2})$ which can match the iteration complexity of the first-order counterpart approximately. As for the proposed faster zeroth-order conditional gradient sliding (FZCGS) method, its function queries oracle is improved to $O(\frac{n^{1/2}d}{\epsilon})$, indicating that its iteration complexity is even better than that of its first-order counterpart NCGS-VR. In other words, the iteration complelxity of the accelerated first-order Frank-Wolfe method NCGS-VR is suboptimal. Then, we proposed a new algorithm to improve its IFO (incremental first-order oracle) to $O(\frac{n^{1/2}}{\epsilon})$. At last, the empirical studies on benchmark datasets validate our theoretical results.

paragraphs: This paper studies constrained, non-convex optimization when gradients are unavailable. Frank-Wolfe methods are useful for constrained problems, but much of the existing work assumes access to first-order information. The authors develop two stochastic zeroth-order variants, which work with function evaluations, and prove faster convergence rates than existing methods for the problems considered.

The first method, FZFW, has function-query complexity O(n^(1/2)d/epsilon^2). The second, FZCGS, improves this to O(n^(1/2)d/epsilon). These expressions describe how the required function queries scale with the quantities appearing in the analysis. The authors relate the results to first-order counterparts, finding an approximate match for FZFW and an improved iteration comparison for FZCGS.

The comparison also reveals that the iteration complexity of the accelerated first-order method NCGS-VR is suboptimal. The authors consequently propose a new algorithm with incremental first-order oracle complexity O(n^(1/2)/epsilon). Benchmark experiments support the theoretical findings. The contribution therefore includes both faster methods without direct gradients and an improvement prompted by reexamining the corresponding first-order approach.
summary.tldr: Two zeroth-order Frank-Wolfe methods improve convergence guarantees and motivate a faster first-order algorithm for non-convex constrained optimization.

title: Can Stochastic Zeroth-Order Frank-Wolfe Method Converge Faster for Non-Convex Problems?

abstract: Entropy is ubiquitous in machine learning, but it is in general intractable to compute the entropy of the distribution of an arbitrary continuous random variable. In this paper, we propose the amortized residual denoising autoencoder (AR-DAE) to approximate the gradient of the log density function, which can be used to estimate the gradient of entropy. Amortization allows us to significantly reduce the error of the gradient approximator by approaching asymptotic optimality of a regular DAE, in which case the estimation is in theory unbiased. We conduct theoretical and experimental analyses on the approximation error of the proposed method, as well as extensive studies on heuristics to ensure its robustness. Finally, using the proposed gradient approximator to estimate the gradient of entropy, we demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on density estimation with variational autoencoders and continuous control with soft actor-critic.

paragraphs: Entropy describes uncertainty in a distribution, but computing it for an arbitrary continuous random variable is generally intractable. For learning algorithms, the useful quantity can instead be the gradient of entropy: how that uncertainty changes as the model changes. This paper develops a neural approximation that makes this gradient more accessible.

The proposed amortized residual denoising autoencoder, or AR-DAE, approximates the gradient of the log density. That approximation can then be used to estimate an entropy gradient. The authors explain that amortization reduces approximation error by approaching the asymptotic optimum of a regular denoising autoencoder. Unbiasedness is a theoretical property at that optimum, so the claim concerns a limiting condition rather than an unconditional guarantee for every trained estimator.

The paper examines approximation error through both theory and experiments and studies practical heuristics intended to improve robustness. It also applies the estimator to variational autoencoders for density estimation and soft actor-critic for continuous control, reporting state-of-the-art performance. These applications show how improving an intermediate gradient estimate can benefit broader learning procedures.
summary.tldr: AR-DAE estimates entropy gradients through learned log-density gradients, approaching theoretical unbiasedness under an asymptotic optimality condition.

title: AR-DAE: Towards Unbiased Neural Entropy Gradient Estimation

abstract: Collective Inference (CI) is a procedure designed to boost weak relational classifiers, specially for node classification tasks. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are strong classifiers that have been used with great success. Unfortunately, most existing practical GNNs are not most-expressive (universal). Thus, it is an open question whether one can improve strong relational node classifiers, such as GNNs, with CI. In this work, we investigate this question and propose {\em collective learning} for GNNs —a general collective classification approach for node representation learning that increases their representation power. We show that previous attempts to incorporate CI into GNNs fail to boost their expressiveness because they do not adapt CI’s Monte Carlo sampling to representation learning. We evaluate our proposed framework with a variety of state-of-the-art GNNs. Our experiments show a consistent, significant boost in node classification accuracy —regardless of the choice of underlying GNN— for inductive node classification in partially-labeled graphs, across five real-world network datasets.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can classify nodes effectively while still having limits on the representations they can learn. This paper asks whether collective inference, a procedure originally intended to improve weaker relational classifiers, can also strengthen these already capable models. The goal is to increase representation power and thereby improve node classification.

The proposed framework, collective learning, adapts collective classification to learning node representations. The authors identify a specific obstacle in earlier combinations of collective inference and graph neural networks: their Monte Carlo sampling was not adapted to representation learning. They show that those earlier approaches consequently fail to increase expressiveness, and design their framework to address that issue.

Experiments combine collective learning with several leading graph neural networks on five real-world network datasets. For inductive node classification in partially labeled graphs, the authors report consistent, significant accuracy improvements across the underlying networks tested. These findings support collective learning as a broadly usable enhancement within that evaluated setting, alongside its contribution to representation power.
summary.tldr: Collective learning adapts collective inference to strengthen GNN representations and improves node classification across five evaluated network datasets.

title: A Collective Learning Framework to Boost GNN Expressiveness for Node Classification

abstract: We show that the gradient estimates used in training Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) with importance-weighted variational inference are susceptible to signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) issues. Specifically, we show both theoretically and via an extensive empirical evaluation that the SNR of the gradient estimates for the latent variable’s variational parameters decreases as the number of importance samples increases. As a result, these gradient estimates degrade to pure noise if the number of importance samples is too large. To address this pathology, we show how doubly-reparameterized gradient estimators, originally proposed for training variational autoencoders, can be adapted to the DGP setting and that the resultant estimators completely remedy the SNR issue, thereby providing more reliable training. Finally, we demonstrate that our fix can lead to consistent improvements in the predictive performance of DGP models.

Finally, we demonstrate that our fix can lead to consistent improvements in the predictive performance of DGP models.

paragraphs: This paper identifies a training problem in deep Gaussian processes using importance-weighted variational inference. Increasing the number of importance samples can make certain gradient estimates less informative. Specifically, the affected gradients are those for the latent variable’s variational parameters, whose signal-to-noise ratio decreases as more importance samples are used.

The authors establish this effect theoretically and through extensive empirical evaluation. With too many samples, the relevant estimates degrade to pure noise, undermining the training signal. The finding is specific about which gradients suffer and connects the sampling choice directly to the reliability of the updates used to learn those parameters.

To address the issue, the paper adapts doubly-reparameterized gradient estimators previously proposed for variational autoencoders. The authors show that the adapted estimators completely remedy the identified signal-to-noise problem in the DGP setting. They also demonstrate that the fix can produce consistent predictive improvements. The method therefore addresses a diagnosed training pathology with both analytical support and evidence of downstream benefits.
summary.tldr: Adapted doubly-reparameterized gradients fix a signal-to-noise failure in importance-weighted deep Gaussian process training.

title: On Signal-to-Noise Ratio Issues in Variational Inference for Deep Gaussian Processes

abstract: Actor-critic (AC) methods are ubiquitous in reinforcement learning. Although it is understood that AC methods are closely related to policy gradient (PG), their precise connection has not been fully characterized previously. In this paper, we explain the gap between AC and PG methods by identifying the exact adjustment to the AC objective/gradient that recovers the true policy gradient of the cumulative reward objective (PG). Furthermore, by viewing the AC method as a two-player Stackelberg game between the actor and critic, we show that the Stackelberg policy gradient can be recovered as a special case of our more general analysis. Based on these results, we develop practical algorithms, Residual Actor-Critic and Stackelberg Actor-Critic, for estimating the correction between AC and PG and use these to modify the standard AC algorithm. Experiments on popular tabular and continuous environments show the proposed corrections can improve both the sample efficiency and final performance of existing AC methods.

paragraphs: Actor–critic algorithms learn a policy with the help of a value-estimating critic, but their updates need not equal the true policy gradient of cumulative reward. This paper characterizes that difference precisely. The aim is to explain what standard actor–critic updates omit and turn that explanation into practical improvements.

The authors identify the exact adjustment to the actor–critic objective or gradient that recovers the policy gradient. They also interpret actor and critic as players in a Stackelberg game, showing that a corresponding Stackelberg policy gradient is a special case of their broader analysis. These connections motivate Residual Actor-Critic and Stackelberg Actor-Critic algorithms that estimate the correction.

Experiments in tabular and continuous environments show that the corrections can improve sample efficiency and final performance of existing methods. The contribution links an analytical distinction to implementable update rules. The empirical wording matters: the reported corrections can help in the evaluated settings, rather than establishing an unconditional improvement for every actor–critic implementation.
summary.tldr: An exact characterization of the actor–critic gradient gap leads to corrective algorithms with improved reported learning performance.

title: Characterizing the Gap Between Actor-Critic and Policy Gradient

abstract: The focus of the paper is functional output regression (FOR) with convoluted losses. While most existing work consider the square loss setting, we leverage extensions of the Huber and the $\epsilon$-insensitive loss (induced by infimal convolution) and propose a flexible framework capable of handling various forms of outliers and sparsity in the FOR family. We derive computationally tractable algorithms relying on duality to tackle the resulting tasks in the context of vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The efficiency of the approach is demonstrated and contrasted with the classical squared loss setting on both synthetic and real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: Functional output regression predicts an output that is itself a function. This paper examines how the choice of loss can make such regression more flexible in dealing with outliers and sparsity. Much of the existing work uses squared loss, while the authors develop alternatives based on extensions of Huber and epsilon-insensitive losses.

These losses are constructed through infimal convolution, which supplies the mathematical foundation for the proposed framework. The aim is to accommodate different forms of outliers and sparsity within functional output regression. This places the treatment of those properties inside the regression objective, making loss design a central part of how the prediction problem is formulated.

The authors derive computationally tractable algorithms using duality in vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. They demonstrate the approach’s efficiency on synthetic and real-world benchmarks and compare it with the conventional squared-loss formulation. The contribution joins a flexible family of objectives with algorithms for solving them, showing how alternatives to squared loss can be used in the functional-output setting.
summary.tldr: The paper develops tractable functional-output regression methods using extended Huber and epsilon-insensitive losses to handle outliers and sparsity.

title: Functional Output Regression with Infimal Convolution: Exploring the Huber and $ε$-insensitive Losses

abstract: In Multi-task learning (MTL), a joint model is trained to simultaneously make predictions for several tasks. Joint training reduces computation costs and improves data efficiency; however, since the gradients of these different tasks may conflict, training a joint model for MTL often yields lower performance than its corresponding single-task counterparts. A common method for alleviating this issue is to combine per-task gradients into a joint update direction using a particular heuristic. In this paper, we propose viewing the gradients combination step as a bargaining game, where tasks negotiate to reach an agreement on a joint direction of parameter update. Under certain assumptions, the bargaining problem has a unique solution, known as the Nash Bargaining Solution , which we propose to use as a principled approach to multi-task learning. We describe a new MTL optimization procedure, Nash-MTL, and derive theoretical guarantees for its convergence. Empirically, we show that Nash-MTL achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple MTL benchmarks in various domains.

paragraphs: Training one model for several tasks can save computation and improve data efficiency, but tasks can disagree about how shared parameters should change. Their gradients may conflict, leaving joint training worse than training separate models. This paper focuses on the step that combines those gradients into a single update direction.

The authors formulate that combination as a bargaining game in which the tasks negotiate a shared direction. Under certain assumptions, the game has a unique Nash Bargaining Solution. They use this solution to define Nash-MTL, replacing a heuristic choice of gradient combination with one grounded in the stated bargaining formulation and its assumptions.

The paper develops the resulting optimization procedure and provides theoretical convergence guarantees. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across multiple multi-task benchmarks in different domains. Together, these contributions connect a formal model of agreement between tasks to an operational training method. The uniqueness claim remains conditional on the bargaining assumptions, while the reported benchmark results provide empirical support for using that solution in multi-task optimization.
summary.tldr: Nash-MTL combines task gradients through a bargaining solution, with convergence guarantees and strong reported multi-task benchmark performance.

title: Multi-Task Learning as a Bargaining Game

abstract: Graph neural architecture search has shown great potentials for automatically designing graph neural network (GNN) architectures for graph classification tasks. However, when there is a distribution shift between training and testing graphs, the existing approaches fail to deal with the problem of adapting to unknown test graph structures since they only search for a fixed architecture for all graphs. To solve this problem, we propose a novel GRACES model which is able to generalize under distribution shifts through tailoring a customized GNN architecture suitable for each graph instance with unknown distribution. Specifically, we design a self-supervised disentangled graph encoder to characterize invariant factors hidden in diverse graph structures. Then, we propose a prototype-based architecture customization strategy to generate the most suitable GNN architecture weights in a continuous space for each graph instance. We further propose a customized super-network to share weights among different architectures for the sake of efficient training. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed GRACES model can adapt to diverse graph structures and achieve state-of-the-art performance for graph classification tasks under distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Graph neural architecture search usually selects a single architecture to classify all graphs. This paper argues that such a fixed choice is poorly suited to changes between training and test graph structures. GRACES addresses that problem by customizing the graph neural network architecture for each graph instance, including graphs from an unknown distribution.

The method first uses a self-supervised, disentangled graph encoder to characterize factors that remain invariant across diverse graph structures. A prototype-based customization strategy then produces architecture weights in a continuous space for each graph. A shared super-network allows different architectures to reuse weights, making the training of these customized choices more efficient.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show adaptation to diverse structures and reported state-of-the-art graph classification performance under distribution shifts. The approach matters because architecture selection becomes responsive to the individual input instead of being a single decision made for the whole dataset. The empirical findings support that strategy in the evaluated settings, while the shared network provides a practical means of training the collection of architectural choices.
summary.tldr: GRACES customizes a GNN architecture for each graph and shares weights across choices, improving graph classification under evaluated distribution shifts.

title: Graph Neural Architecture Search Under Distribution Shifts

abstract: Providing privacy protection has been one of the primary motivations of Federated Learning (FL). Recently, there has been a line of work on incorporating the formal privacy notion of differential privacy with FL. To guarantee the client-level differential privacy in FL algorithms, the clients’ transmitted model updates have to be clipped before adding privacy noise. Such clipping operation is substantially different from its counterpart of gradient clipping in the centralized differentially private SGD and has not been well-understood. In this paper, we first empirically demonstrate that the clipped FedAvg can perform surprisingly well even with substantial data heterogeneity when training neural networks, which is partly because the clients’ updates become similar for several popular deep architectures. Based on this key observation, we provide the convergence analysis of a differential private (DP) FedAvg algorithm and highlight the relationship between clipping bias and the distribution of the clients’ updates. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that rigorously investigates theoretical and empirical issues regarding the clipping operation in FL algorithms.
