paragraphs: Client-level differential privacy in the federated algorithms considered here involves clipping transmitted model updates before adding privacy noise. Clipping limits the magnitude of an update, but it also changes the information used for learning. This paper studies that effect, emphasizing that clipping client updates differs substantially from clipping gradients in centralized private training.

The authors first show empirically that clipped federated averaging can perform surprisingly well when neural networks are trained on highly heterogeneous client data. They partly explain this through an observation that client updates become similar for several popular deep architectures. Thus, differing local datasets do not necessarily translate into equally disparate updates throughout training.

Building on that observation, the paper analyzes convergence of differentially private FedAvg and relates clipping bias to the distribution of client updates. This connects the practical behavior of clipping to the geometry of the information clients transmit. The contribution combines empirical evidence with theoretical analysis to clarify when clipping can be less damaging than data heterogeneity alone might suggest.
summary.tldr: An empirical and theoretical study links the effects of clipping in private federated averaging to the distribution of client updates.

title: Understanding Clipping for Federated Learning: Convergence and Client-Level Differential Privacy

abstract: Two different approaches exist to handle missing values for prediction: either imputation, prior to fitting any predictive algorithms, or dedicated methods able to natively incorporate missing values. While imputation is widely (and easily) use, it is unfortunately biased when low-capacity predictors (such as linear models) are applied afterward. However, in practice, naive imputation exhibits good predictive performance. In this paper, we study the impact of imputation in a high-dimensional linear model with MCAR missing data. We prove that zero imputation performs an implicit regularization closely related to the ridge method, often used in high-dimensional problems. Leveraging on this connection, we establish that the imputation bias is controlled by a ridge bias, which vanishes in high dimension. As a predictor, we argue in favor of the averaged SGD strategy, applied to zero-imputed data. We establish an upper bound on its generalization error, highlighting that imputation is benign in the $d \gg \sqrt{n}$ regime. Experiments illustrate our findings.

paragraphs: Replacing missing entries with zeros is easy, but fitting a linear predictor afterward can introduce bias. This paper examines why such a simple procedure can nevertheless predict well in high-dimensional settings. Its analysis assumes data are missing completely at random, so the result is tied to that specified missingness setting.

The authors prove that zero imputation creates an implicit regularization effect closely related to ridge regression. This connection lets them bound the bias introduced by imputation using a ridge-related bias that vanishes in high dimension within their analysis. The missing-value replacement therefore changes more than the completed dataset: it also has a mathematically identifiable effect on the fitted predictor.

The paper favors averaged stochastic gradient descent applied directly to the zero-filled data and establishes an upper bound on its generalization error. That bound identifies a benign regime where the number of features d is much larger than the square root of the sample count n. Experiments illustrate the theory, supporting a conditional explanation for strong predictive performance from naive imputation.
summary.tldr: Under completely random missingness, zero imputation implicitly regularizes high-dimensional linear prediction in a way closely related to ridge regression.

title: Naive imputation implicitly regularizes high-dimensional linear models

abstract: Directed Exploration is a crucial challenge in reinforcement learning (RL), especially when rewards are sparse. Information-directed sampling (IDS), which optimizes the information ratio, seeks to do so by augmenting regret with information gain. However, estimating information gain is computationally intractable or relies on restrictive assumptions which prohibit its use in many practical instances. In this work, we posit an alternative exploration incentive in terms of the integral probability metric (IPM) between a current estimate of the transition model and the unknown optimal, which under suitable conditions, can be computed in closed form with the kernelized Stein discrepancy (KSD). Based on KSD, we develop a novel algorithm STEERING: STEin information dirEcted exploration for model-based Reinforcement LearnING. To enable its derivation, we develop fundamentally new variants of KSD for discrete conditional distributions. We further establish that STEERING archives sublinear Bayesian regret, improving upon prior learning rates of information-augmented MBRL, IDS included. Experimentally, we show that the proposed algorithm is computationally affordable and outperforms several prior approaches.

paragraphs: Exploration is difficult when rewards are sparse because an agent has little direct feedback about promising actions. Information-directed sampling addresses exploration by balancing regret with information gain. However, computing that gain can be intractable or require restrictive assumptions, limiting the practicality of the approach.

STEERING replaces this exploration incentive with an integral probability metric comparing the current transition-model estimate with the unknown optimal model. Under suitable conditions, the metric can be computed in closed form using kernelized Stein discrepancy. To build the algorithm, the authors develop new versions of that discrepancy for discrete conditional distributions, adapting the mathematical tool to the transition models involved in reinforcement learning.

The theory establishes sublinear Bayesian regret and improves on prior learning rates for information-augmented model-based reinforcement learning, including information-directed sampling. Experiments also report affordable computation and better performance than several earlier approaches. Together, these results support the proposed discrepancy as a useful exploration signal, with its closed-form computability depending on the suitable conditions identified by the method.
summary.tldr: STEERING uses a Stein-discrepancy exploration incentive to obtain improved regret guarantees and practical performance in model-based reinforcement learning.

title: STEERING : Stein Information Directed Exploration for Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Various optimal gradient-based algorithms have been developed for smooth nonconvex optimization. However, many nonconvex machine learning problems do not belong to the class of smooth functions and therefore the existing algorithms are sub-optimal. Instead, these problems have been shown to satisfy certain generalized-smooth conditions, which have not been well understood in the existing literature. In this paper, we propose a notion of $\alpha$-symmetric generalized-smoothness that substantially extends the existing notions and covers many important functions such as high-order polynomials and exponential functions. We study the fundamental properties and establish descent lemmas for the functions in this class. Then, to solve such a large class of nonconvex problems, we design a special deterministic normalized gradient descent algorithm that achieves the optimal iteration complexity $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-2})$, and also prove that the popular SPIDER variance reduction algorithm achieves the optimal sample complexity $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{-3})$. Our results show that solving generalized-smooth nonconvex problems is as efficient as solving smooth nonconvex problems.

paragraphs: Many optimization guarantees rely on smoothness assumptions that do not cover important nonconvex machine learning problems. Applying algorithms designed around those assumptions can be suboptimal. This paper asks whether a broader class of functions can still be optimized with the efficiency established for smooth problems.

The authors introduce α-symmetric generalized smoothness, extending earlier definitions and covering important functions including high-order polynomials and exponentials. They establish basic properties and descent lemmas for this class. These lemmas provide the mathematical connection between taking an optimization step and making progress, supporting algorithm design under the broader condition.

A specially designed deterministic normalized gradient descent method achieves optimal iteration complexity O(ε⁻²). The authors also prove optimal sample complexity O(ε⁻³) for the SPIDER variance-reduction algorithm. These are different measures of computational effort: one counts iterations and the other samples. The results show that, for the generalized-smooth problems covered by the analysis, broadening the function class need not worsen these optimal complexity rates.
summary.tldr: A broader generalized-smooth function class admits optimization algorithms with the same optimal complexity rates as smooth nonconvex problems.

title: Generalized-Smooth Nonconvex Optimization is As Efficient As Smooth Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: Medical studies frequently require to extract the relationship between each covariate and the outcome with statistical confidence measures. To do this, simple parametric models are frequently used (e.g. coefficients of linear regression) but always fitted on the whole dataset. However, it is common that the covariates may not have a uniform effect over the whole population and thus a unified simple model can miss the heterogeneous signal. For example, a linear model may be able to explain a subset of the data but fail on the rest due to the nonlinearity and heterogeneity in the data. In this paper, we propose DDGroup (data-driven group discovery), a data-driven method to effectively identify subgroups in the data with a uniform linear relationship between the features and the label. DDGroup outputs an interpretable region in which the linear model is expected to hold. It is simple to implement and computationally tractable for use. We show theoretically that, given a large enough sample, DDGroup recovers a region where a single linear model with low variance is well-specified (if one exists), and experiments on real-world medical datasets confirm that it can discover regions where a local linear model has improved performance. Our experiments also show that DDGroup can uncover subgroups with qualitatively different relationships which are missed by simply applying parametric approaches to the whole dataset.

paragraphs: A single linear regression can obscure relationships that differ across a population. In medical data, for example, a feature may have a consistent relationship with an outcome within one subgroup while behaving differently elsewhere. DDGroup searches for interpretable regions of the data in which one linear relationship is appropriate, making subgroup discovery part of the modeling process.

The method identifies groups whose features and labels follow a uniform linear relationship. Its output describes a region where the fitted linear model is expected to hold, giving the model an interpretable scope. The authors characterize the procedure as simple to implement and computationally tractable. Their theoretical result is conditional: with enough samples, it recovers a region supporting a well-specified, low-variance linear model if such a region exists.

Experiments on real medical datasets show regions where local linear models perform better. They also reveal subgroups with qualitatively different relationships that whole-dataset parametric models miss. The findings show how identifying where a simple model applies can expose meaningful heterogeneity without requiring one relationship to describe everyone.
summary.tldr: DDGroup discovers interpretable subgroups where linear regression fits well and can reveal relationships hidden by whole-population models.

title: Data-Driven Subgroup Identification for Linear Regression

abstract: Learning to predict reliable characteristic orientations of 3D point clouds is an important yet challenging problem, as different point clouds of the same class may have largely varying appearances. In this work, we introduce a novel method to decouple the shape geometry and semantics of the input point cloud to achieve both stability and consistency. The proposed method integrates shape-geometry-based SO(3)-equivariant learning and shape-semantics-based SO(3)-invariant residual learning, where a final characteristic orientation is obtained by calibrating an SO(3)-equivariant orientation hypothesis using an SO(3)-invariant residual rotation. In experiments, the proposed method not only demonstrates superior stability and consistency but also exhibits state-of-the-art performances when applied to point cloud part segmentation, given randomly rotated inputs.

In experiments, the proposed method not only demonstrates superior stability and consistency but also exhibits state-of-the-art performances when applied to point cloud part segmentation, given randomly rotated inputs.

paragraphs: Predicting a reliable characteristic orientation for a three-dimensional point cloud is difficult because shapes in the same class can look very different. This paper aims to obtain orientations that are both stable and consistent by separating the roles of shape geometry and shape semantics in the prediction process.

The method first produces an orientation hypothesis through SO(3)-equivariant learning based on geometry. Equivariance means that the hypothesis responds predictably when the input is rotated. A second component uses shape semantics to predict an SO(3)-invariant residual rotation, which calibrates the initial hypothesis. The residual is invariant to input rotation, allowing the two components to contribute different kinds of information to the final orientation.

Experiments report superior stability and consistency for the resulting predictions. The method also achieves state-of-the-art performance when used for point-cloud part segmentation with randomly rotated inputs. This downstream result shows that the orientation procedure can benefit a task beyond orientation prediction itself. The contribution is the coordinated use of rotation-responsive geometric reasoning and rotation-invariant semantic correction.
summary.tldr: Combining a rotation-equivariant geometric hypothesis with an invariant semantic correction improves 3D orientation stability, consistency, and rotated-input segmentation.

title: Stable and Consistent Prediction of 3D Characteristic Orientation via Invariant Residual Learning

abstract: The gap between speech and text modalities is a major challenge in speech-to-text translation (ST). Different methods have been proposed to reduce this gap, but most of them require architectural changes in ST training. In this work, we propose to mitigate this issue at the pre-training stage, requiring no change in the ST model. First, we show that the connectionist temporal classification (CTC) loss can reduce the modality gap by design. We provide a quantitative comparison with the more common cross-entropy loss, showing that pre-training with CTC consistently achieves better final ST accuracy. Nevertheless, CTC is only a partial solution and thus, in our second contribution, we propose a novel pre-training method combining CTC and optimal transport to further reduce this gap. Our method pre-trains a Siamese-like model composed of two encoders, one for acoustic inputs and the other for textual inputs, such that they produce representations that are close to each other in the Wasserstein space. Extensive experiments on the standard CoVoST-2 and MuST-C datasets show that our pre-training method applied to the vanilla encoder-decoder Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance under the no-external-data setting, and performs on par with recent strong multi-task learning systems trained with external data. Finally, our method can also be applied on top of these multi-task systems, leading to further improvements for these models.

paragraphs: Speech translation must connect acoustic inputs with textual outputs, despite the gap between those modalities. This paper addresses that gap during pretraining, allowing the translation model's architecture to remain unchanged. The authors first show that connectionist temporal classification, or CTC, reduces the modality gap by design and consistently improves final translation accuracy over cross-entropy pretraining in their comparisons.

Because CTC addresses only part of the gap, the proposed method combines it with optimal transport. A paired-encoder model processes acoustic and textual inputs separately while learning representations that are close in Wasserstein space. This gives pretraining an explicit way to bring the two modalities' representations together before speech translation training.

On CoVoST-2 and MuST-C, the method applied to a standard encoder-decoder Transformer achieves state-of-the-art performance in the no-external-data setting. It also performs on par with strong multitask systems trained with external data. Applying the pretraining method to those multitask systems brings further improvements. The findings show that alignment during pretraining can benefit both a standard translation architecture and more elaborate training systems.
summary.tldr: Combining CTC and optimal transport during pretraining aligns speech and text representations and improves translation without changing the translation architecture.

title: Pre-training for Speech Translation: CTC Meets Optimal Transport

abstract: Machine learning models can make critical errors that are easily hidden within vast amounts of data. Such errors often run counter to rules based on human intuition. However, rules based on human knowledge are challenging to scale or to even formalize. We thereby seek to infer statistical rules from the data and quantify the extent to which a model has learned them. We propose a framework SQRL that integrates logic-based methods with statistical inference to derive these rules from a model’s training data without supervision. We further show how to adapt models at test time to reduce rule violations and produce more coherent predictions. SQRL generates up to 300K rules over datasets from vision, tabular, and language settings. We uncover up to 158K violations of those rules by state-of-the-art models for classification, object detection, and data imputation. Test-time adaptation reduces these violations by up to 68.7% with relative performance improvement up to 32%. SQRL is available at https://github.com/DebugML/sqrl.

Human-written rules can expose some errors, but they are hard to formalize and scale. SQRL instead derives statistical rules from the data and checks how well a model follows them.

The framework combines logic-based methods with statistical inference to discover rules without supervision. It then uses these rules to quantify violations in model predictions. The paper also introduces test-time adaptation that reduces violations, allowing the discovered relationships to guide more coherent predictions as well as serve as a diagnostic tool.

Across vision, tabular, and language settings, SQRL generates up to 300,000 rules and uncovers up to 158,000 violations by state-of-the-art classification, object detection, and imputation models. They show that data-derived rules can reveal substantial inconsistencies and can also help improve predictions.
summary.tldr: SQRL discovers statistical rules from training data, exposes model violations, and uses test-time adaptation to improve prediction coherence.

title: Do Machine Learning Models Learn Statistical Rules Inferred from Data?

abstract: Neural networks constitute a class of functions that are typically non-surjective, with high-dimensional fibers and complicated image. We prove two main results concerning the geometry of the loss landscape of a neural network. First, we provide an explicit effective bound on the sizes of the hidden layers so that the loss landscape has no spurious valleys, which guarantees the success of gradient descent methods. Second, we present a novel method for analyzing whether a given neural network architecture with monomial activation function can represent a target function of interest. The core of our analysis method is the study of a specific set of error values, and its behavior depending on different training datasets.

paragraphs: This paper examines the geometry behind neural-network optimization and representation. Neural networks can have many parameter settings corresponding to the same output, while the collection of outputs they can produce has a complicated shape. These properties motivate studying the loss landscape and the functions an architecture can represent as related mathematical questions.

The first result gives an explicit bound on hidden-layer sizes sufficient to rule out spurious valleys in the loss landscape. The authors connect this condition to the success of gradient descent methods. The result supplies a concrete architectural condition for favorable optimization geometry; it is a sufficient width bound rather than a claim that every smaller architecture must fail.

The second result introduces a method for determining whether an architecture with monomial activations can represent a target function. It studies a particular set of error values and how that set changes with training datasets. Together, the results address both reaching good solutions through optimization and determining whether the desired function lies within an architecture's representational possibilities.
summary.tldr: The paper gives sufficient layer-width bounds for eliminating spurious valleys and a representability analysis for networks with monomial activations.

title: Spurious Valleys and Clustering Behavior of Neural Networks

abstract: Temperature scaling is a popular technique for tuning the sharpness of a model distribution. It is used extensively for sampling likely generations and calibrating model uncertainty, and even features as a controllable parameter to many large language models in deployment. However, autoregressive models rely on myopic temperature scaling that greedily optimizes the next token. To address this, we propose Long Horizon Temperature Scaling (LHTS), a novel approach for sampling from temperature-scaled joint distributions. LHTS is compatible with all likelihood-based models, and optimizes for the long-horizon likelihood of samples. We derive a temperature-dependent LHTS objective, and show that fine-tuning a model on a range of temperatures produces a single model capable of generation with a controllable long-horizon temperature parameter. We experiment with LHTS on image diffusion models and character/language autoregressive models, demonstrating its advantages over myopic temperature scaling in likelihood and sample quality, and showing improvements in accuracy of a multiple choice analogy by $10$%.

paragraphs: Temperature scaling changes how sharply a model concentrates probability on its preferred outputs. In autoregressive generation, the usual procedure applies this adjustment to the next token at each step. The paper argues that this local procedure is myopic and introduces Long Horizon Temperature Scaling to target the temperature-scaled joint distribution of complete samples.

The authors derive a temperature-dependent training objective that optimizes long-horizon sample likelihood. Fine-tuning across a range of temperatures produces a single model whose long-horizon temperature remains controllable during generation. The proposed approach is compatible with likelihood-based models generally, and its evaluation includes both image diffusion models and autoregressive character and language models.

The experiments demonstrate advantages over myopic temperature scaling in likelihood and sample quality, along with a reported 10% accuracy improvement on a multiple-choice analogy task. These findings suggest that controlling the probability distribution over whole outputs can change generation behavior in useful ways. The contribution includes both the joint-distribution objective and a practical method for supporting multiple temperatures within one model.
summary.tldr: Long Horizon Temperature Scaling trains models to control temperature over complete samples, improving tested likelihood and generation quality.

title: Long Horizon Temperature Scaling

abstract: We study offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL) in Markov games, where the goal is to learn an approximate equilibrium—such as Nash equilibrium and (Coarse) Correlated Equilibrium—from an offline dataset pre-collected from the game. Existing works consider relatively restricted tabular or linear models and handle each equilibria separately. In this work, we provide the first framework for sample-efficient offline learning in Markov games under general function approximation, handling all 3 equilibria in a unified manner. By using Bellman-consistent pessimism, we obtain interval estimation for policies’ returns, and use both the upper and the lower bounds to obtain a relaxation on the gap of a candidate policy, which becomes our optimization objective. Our results generalize prior works and provide several additional insights. Importantly, we require a data coverage condition that improves over the recently proposed “unilateral concentrability”. Our condition allows selective coverage of deviation policies that optimally trade-off between their greediness (as approximate best responses) and coverage, and we show scenarios where this leads to significantly better guarantees. As a new connection, we also show how our algorithmic framework can subsume seemingly different solution concepts designed for the special case of two-player zero-sum games.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning aims to learn stable joint behavior from previously collected game data. This paper provides a unified framework for approximating Nash, correlated, and coarse correlated equilibria in Markov games. It accommodates general function approximation, extending beyond the tabular and linear models emphasized in earlier work.

The framework uses Bellman-consistent pessimism to construct intervals for policy returns. Both ends of those intervals help form a relaxed measure of a candidate policy's equilibrium gap, which becomes the optimization objective. This turns uncertainty about returns into a quantity the learning procedure can use when comparing candidate solutions.

The guarantees require data coverage, but the proposed condition improves on unilateral concentrability. It permits selective coverage of deviation policies that balance being close to best responses with being supported by the available data. The authors identify scenarios where this gives substantially better guarantees. They also show that the framework encompasses apparently different solution concepts for two-player zero-sum games, connecting those special cases to the broader treatment.
summary.tldr: A unified offline Markov-game framework learns three equilibrium types with general function approximation under an improved data-coverage condition.

title: Offline Learning in Markov Games with General Function Approximation

abstract: We investigate coresets for approximating the cost with respect to median queries. In this problem, we are given a set of points $P\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and median queries are $\sum_{p\in P} ||p-c||$ for any point $c\in \mathbb{R}^d$. Our goal is to compute a small weighted summary $S\subset P$ such that the cost of any median query is approximated within a multiplicative $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ factor. We provide matching upper and lower bounds on the number of points contained in $S$ of the order $\tilde{\Theta}\left(\varepsilon^{-d/(d+1)}\right)$.

In this problem, we are given a set of points $P\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and median queries are $\sum_{p\in P} ||p-c||$ for any point $c\in \mathbb{R}^d$. paragraphs: For a collection of points, a median query asks for the sum of distances from every point to a proposed center. Computing this quantity repeatedly involves the full collection. This paper studies how much of that collection must be retained in a weighted summary so that such costs remain approximately correct.

The summary is a coreset: a subset of the original points with weights attached. Its requirement is stronger than accurately evaluating one chosen center. It must approximate the cost for every possible center within a multiplicative factor of one plus or minus epsilon. Epsilon therefore specifies the permitted relative error across the entire family of median queries.

The authors establish matching upper and lower bounds on coreset size of order epsilon raised to minus d divided by d plus one, up to logarithmic factors. Here d is the dimension. The upper bound shows that summaries of this size suffice; the lower bound establishes the corresponding size requirement in general. Together, they characterize the accuracy-versus-summary-size tradeoff for this geometric problem.
summary.tldr: Matching bounds characterize how many weighted points are needed to approximate every geometric-median cost within a chosen relative error.

title: Optimal Coresets for Low-Dimensional Geometric Median

abstract: Most transformer-based video encoders are limited to short temporal contexts due to their quadratic complexity. While various attempts have been made to extend this context, this has often come at the cost of both conceptual and computational complexity. We propose to instead re-purpose existing pre-trained video transformers by simply fine-tuning them to attend to memories derived non-parametrically from past activations. By leveraging redundancy reduction, our memory-consolidated vision transformer (MC-ViT) effortlessly extends its context far into the past and exhibits excellent scaling behavior when learning from longer videos. In doing so, MC-ViT sets a new state-of-the-art in long-context video understanding on EgoSchema, Perception Test, and Diving48, outperforming methods that benefit from orders of magnitude more parameters.

paragraphs: Video transformers often process only short time spans because their quadratic complexity makes longer contexts expensive. Extending those contexts can introduce additional computational and conceptual complexity. This paper proposes adapting existing pretrained video transformers so they can use information retained from earlier portions of a video.

The method, MC-ViT, fine-tunes a transformer to attend to memories derived non-parametrically from past activations. Redundancy reduction consolidates those memories, allowing the model to draw on a more distant past. This connects current processing to earlier internal representations while reusing an existing pretrained video encoder.

The authors report strong scaling when learning from longer videos and new state-of-the-art results on EgoSchema, Perception Test, and Diving48. MC-ViT also outperforms methods with orders of magnitude more parameters. These findings indicate that retaining and consolidating past activations can be an effective route to longer-context video understanding, and that access to relevant history can deliver gains without relying on a much larger model.
summary.tldr: MC-ViT extends pretrained video transformers with consolidated memories of past activations, achieving leading results on three long-context video benchmarks.

title: Memory Consolidation Enables Long-Context Video Understanding

abstract: One-shot imitation learning (OSIL) is to learn an imitator agent that can execute multiple tasks with only a single demonstration. In real-world scenario, the environment is dynamic, e.g., unexpected changes can occur after demonstration. Thus, achieving generalization of the imitator agent is crucial as agents would inevitably face situations unseen in the provided demonstrations. While traditional OSIL methods excel in relatively stationary settings, their adaptability to such unforeseen changes, which asking for a higher level of generalization ability for the imitator agents, is limited and rarely discussed. In this work, we present a new algorithm called Deep Demonstration Tracing (DDT). In DDT, we propose a demonstration transformer architecture to encourage agents to adaptively trace suitable states in demonstrations. Besides, it integrates OSIL into a meta-reinforcement-learning training paradigm, providing regularization for policies in unexpected situations. We evaluate DDT on a new navigation task suite and robotics tasks, demonstrating its superior performance over existing OSIL methods across all evaluated tasks in dynamic environments with unforeseen changes. The project page is in https://osil-ddt.github.io.

paragraphs: One-shot imitation learning aims to let an agent perform a task after seeing a single demonstration. A central difficulty arises when the environment changes after that demonstration. The demonstrated behavior may no longer fit the agent’s current situation, so successful imitation requires more than following the original sequence of actions.

Deep Demonstration Tracing addresses this problem with a demonstration transformer that encourages the agent to identify suitable states within the demonstration as execution unfolds. This gives the demonstration a more adaptive role in guiding behavior. The method also places one-shot imitation inside a meta-reinforcement-learning training framework, providing regularization for how policies behave in unexpected situations.

The authors evaluate the approach on a new navigation task suite and robotics tasks involving unforeseen environmental changes. DDT outperforms the existing one-shot imitation methods across all tasks evaluated. These results support the value of combining adaptive use of demonstration states with training aimed at generalization. The demonstrated advantage specifically concerns dynamic settings where the agent encounters situations absent from its example.
summary.tldr: Deep Demonstration Tracing helps agents adapt a single demonstration to unforeseen changes through demonstration attention and meta-reinforcement learning.

title: Deep Demonstration Tracing: Learning Generalizable Imitator Policy for Runtime Imitation from a Single Demonstration

abstract: Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) has established itself as a new scientific paradigm which enables the seamless integration of observational data with partial differential equation (PDE) based physics models. A powerful tool for the analysis, reduction and solution of PDEs is the Lie symmetry method. Nevertheless, only recently has the integration of such symmetries into PIML frameworks begun to be explored. The present work adds to this growing literature by introducing an approach for incorporating a Lie symmetry into a physics-informed Gaussian process (GP) model. The symmetry is introduced as a constraint on the GP; either in a soft manner via virtual observations of an induced PDE called the invariant surface condition, or explicitly through the design of the kernel. Experimental results demonstrate that the use of symmetry constraints improves the performance of the GP for both forward and inverse problems, and that our approach offers competitive performance with neural networks in the low-data environment.

paragraphs: Physics-informed learning combines observations with physical models expressed through partial differential equations. This paper adds another source of mathematical structure: a Lie symmetry of the governing equations. The authors investigate how that symmetry can constrain a Gaussian process model, bringing information from the equation’s structure into learning from data.

They provide two ways to incorporate the symmetry. One uses virtual observations of an additional equation, the invariant surface condition, to impose a soft constraint. The other builds the symmetry explicitly into the Gaussian process kernel. These options place symmetry information either into the model’s observational constraints or directly into the structure used to define the process.

Experiments show that symmetry constraints improve Gaussian process performance on both forward and inverse problems. The approach also performs competitively with neural networks in low-data settings. The findings support symmetry as a useful complement to physical equations and observations, particularly where the model must learn with limited measured information. Both implementations make that additional structure part of the inference process.
summary.tldr: Adding Lie symmetry constraints to physics-informed Gaussian processes improves reported forward and inverse results, with competitive low-data performance.

title: Physics and Lie symmetry informed Gaussian processes

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) exhibits dual operating modes: task learning, i.e., acquiring a new skill from in-context samples, and task retrieval, i.e., locating and activating a relevant pretrained skill. Recent theoretical work proposes various mathematical models to analyze ICL, but they cannot fully explain the duality. In this work, we analyze a generalized probabilistic model for pretraining data, obtaining a quantitative understanding of the two operating modes of ICL. Leveraging our analysis, we provide the first explanation of an unexplained phenomenon observed with real-world large language models (LLMs). Under some settings, the ICL risk initially increases and then decreases with more in-context examples. Our analysis offers a plausible explanation for this "early ascent" phenomenon: a limited number of in-context samples may lead to the retrieval of an incorrect skill, thereby increasing the risk, which will eventually diminish as task learning takes effect with more in-context samples. We also analyze ICL with biased labels, e.g., zero-shot ICL, where in-context examples are assigned random labels, and predict the bounded efficacy of such approaches. We corroborate our analysis and predictions with extensive experiments with Transformers and LLMs.

paragraphs: In-context learning can involve acquiring a skill from prompt examples or activating a relevant skill acquired during pretraining. These two mechanisms can produce similar outward behavior, yet they imply different responses to additional examples. The paper develops a generalized probabilistic model of pretraining data to analyze both mechanisms quantitatively.

The analysis offers a plausible explanation for early ascent: in some settings, prediction risk first rises and then falls as more examples are added. A small number of examples may activate the wrong pretrained skill, temporarily worsening performance. With additional examples, learning the task itself can become effective and reduce the risk. The explanation is conditional, rather than a claim that more examples routinely cause this pattern.

The authors also analyze examples with biased labels, including randomly assigned labels, and predict limits on their effectiveness. Experiments with Transformers and large language models support the analysis and predictions. The resulting framework helps explain why prompt examples can influence performance through both skill selection and new learning.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic analysis connects task retrieval and task learning, offering a plausible explanation for why additional prompt examples sometimes initially worsen performance.

title: Dual Operating Modes of In-Context Learning

abstract: Previous studies yielded discouraging results for item-level locally differentially private linear regression with $s$-sparsity assumption, where the minimax rate for $nm$ samples is $\mathcal{O}(sd / nm\varepsilon^2)$. This can be challenging for high-dimensional data, where the dimension $d$ is extremely large. In this work, we investigate user-level locally differentially private sparse linear regression. We show that with $n$ users each contributing $m$ samples, the linear dependency of dimension $d$ can be eliminated, yielding an error upper bound of $\mathcal{O}(s/ nm\varepsilon^2)$. We propose a framework that first selects candidate variables and then conducts estimation in the narrowed low-dimensional space, which is extendable to general sparse estimation problems with tight error bounds. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed methods. Both the theoretical and empirical results suggest that, with the same number of samples, locally private sparse estimation is better conducted when multiple samples per user are available.

paragraphs: This paper studies sparse linear regression when privacy must be protected locally and each user holds multiple observations. Sparsity means that only a small subset of the available variables matters. Earlier item-level privacy results included an error rate that grew linearly with the full number of variables, making high-dimensional problems particularly difficult.

The authors investigate user-level privacy with n users contributing m samples each. Their framework first identifies candidate variables, then estimates the model within that smaller space. They establish an error upper bound of O(s/(nmε²)), removing the linear dimension factor from the earlier O(sd/(nmε²)) rate. Here, s represents sparsity, d the full dimension, and ε the privacy parameter.

The framework also extends to more general sparse estimation problems with tight error bounds. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the proposed methods. Together, the results suggest that how samples are distributed across users matters: access to multiple samples per user can improve locally private estimation even when the total sample count stays the same.
summary.tldr: Using multiple samples per user enables a locally private sparse-estimation framework whose error bound removes a linear dependence on data dimension.

title: Better Locally Private Sparse Estimation Given Multiple Samples Per User

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) have emerged as a potential alternative architecture for building large language models (LLMs) compared to the previously ubiquitous transformer architecture. One theoretical weakness of transformers is that they cannot express certain kinds of sequential computation and state tracking (Merrill & Sabharwal, 2023), which SSMs are explicitly designed to address via their close architectural similarity to recurrent neural networks (RNNs). But do SSMs truly have an advantage (over transformers) in expressive power for state tracking? Surprisingly, the answer is no. Our analysis reveals that the expressive power of SSMs is limited very similarly to transformers: SSMs cannot express computation outside the complexity class $\mathsf{TC}^0$. In particular, this means they cannot solve simple state-tracking problems like permutation composition. It follows that SSMs are provably unable to accurately track chess moves with certain notation, evaluate code, or track entities in a long narrative. To supplement our formal analysis, we report experiments showing that Mamba-style SSMs indeed struggle with state tracking. Thus, despite its recurrent formulation, the "state” in an SSM is an illusion: SSMs have similar expressiveness limitations to non-recurrent models like transformers, which may fundamentally limit their ability to solve real-world state-tracking problems.

paragraphs: State-space models carry a recurrent state, suggesting that they might track sequential changes more effectively than transformers. This paper asks whether that architectural appearance translates into greater expressive power. Its theoretical analysis finds closely related limitations in the state-space models studied and in transformers.

The authors place the models' expressive power within the complexity class TC0. They connect that limit to an inability to express certain state-tracking computations, including permutation composition. The analysis also establishes consequences for accurately tracking chess moves in certain notation, evaluating code, and following entities through long narratives. These are claims about the formal computational capabilities analyzed, not simply about whether a model stores an internal vector called a state.

Experiments with Mamba-style models supplement the theory and show difficulty with state tracking. Together, the results challenge the assumption that a recurrent formulation alone supplies the sequential reasoning capabilities associated with recurrent networks. The authors conclude that the shared expressiveness limitations may fundamentally constrain performance on real-world tasks that require this kind of state tracking.
summary.tldr: The paper finds that the analyzed state-space models share transformers' formal state-tracking limitations, supported by experiments with Mamba-style models.

title: The Illusion of State in State-Space Models

abstract: Learning-based neural-network (NN) control policies have shown impressive empirical performance in a wide range of tasks in robotics and control. However, formal (Lyapunov) stability guarantees over the region-of-attraction (ROA) for NN controllers with nonlinear dynamical systems are challenging to obtain, and most existing approaches rely on expensive solvers for sums-of-squares (SOS), mixed-integer programming (MIP), or satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). In this paper, we demonstrate a new framework for learning NN controllers together with Lyapunov certificates using fast empirical falsification and strategic regularizations. We propose a novel formulation that defines a larger verifiable region-of-attraction (ROA) than shown in the literature, and refines the conventional restrictive constraints on Lyapunov derivatives to focus only on certifiable ROAs. The Lyapunov condition is rigorously verified post-hoc using branch-and-bound with scalable linear bound propagation-based NN verification techniques. The approach is efficient and flexible, and the full training and verification procedure is accelerated on GPUs without relying on expensive solvers for SOS, MIP, nor SMT. The flexibility and efficiency of our framework allow us to demonstrate Lyapunov-stable output feedback control with synthesized NN-based controllers and NN-based observers with formal stability guarantees, for the first time in literature.

paragraphs: Neural controllers can perform well empirically, but establishing formal stability for nonlinear systems remains challenging. This paper learns controllers together with Lyapunov certificates, which support stability guarantees over a region of attraction. Its training procedure combines fast empirical searches for violations with regularization designed to help obtain certifiable solutions.

The proposed formulation defines a larger verifiable region of attraction than previously shown in the literature. It also revises restrictive conditions on Lyapunov derivatives so that they focus on regions where certification is relevant. After training, branch-and-bound verification with linear bound propagation rigorously checks the Lyapunov condition, separating empirical learning from the formal verification step.

The full procedure is accelerated on GPUs and avoids the expensive SOS, MIP, and SMT solvers used by many existing approaches. The authors demonstrate formally stable output-feedback control using both learned neural controllers and learned neural observers. The guarantees concern the certified region of attraction, and the contribution expands the settings in which neural control can receive such guarantees.
summary.tldr: A joint learning and verification framework provides Lyapunov stability certificates for neural controllers, including controllers with neural observers.

title: Lyapunov-stable Neural Control for State and Output Feedback: A Novel Formulation

abstract: An old idea in optimization theory says that since the gradient is a dual vector it may not be subtracted from the weights without first being mapped to the primal space where the weights reside. We take this idea seriously in this paper and construct such a duality map for general neural networks. Our map, which we call modular dualization, forms a unifying theoretical basis for training algorithms that are a) fast and b) scalable. Modular dualization involves first assigning operator norms to layers based on the semantics of each layer, and then using these layerwise norms to recursively induce a duality map on the weight space of the full neural architecture. We derive GPU-friendly algorithms for dualizing Embed, Linear and Conv2D layers—the latter two methods are based on a Newton-Schulz iteration. We conclude with small experiments demonstrating the speed, scalability and novel numerical properties of duality-based optimizers. Our methods were used in the Muon optimizer, which recently set speed records for training NanoGPT and was scaled up to a 1.5 billion parameter transformer.

paragraphs: This paper starts from an optimization principle: a gradient belongs to a dual space, while model weights belong to a primal space. Turning the gradient into a weight update therefore calls for a mapping between the two. The authors construct such a mapping for general neural networks and call the procedure modular dualization.

The construction begins by assigning an operator norm to each layer based on that layer’s role. These layerwise choices are then combined recursively into a duality map for the full architecture. This gives a common theoretical foundation for building training algorithms from the structure of the network. The paper derives GPU-friendly implementations for embedding, linear, and two-dimensional convolution layers, using Newton-Schulz iterations for the latter two.

Small experiments demonstrate speed, scalability, and distinctive numerical properties of the resulting optimizers. The methods also contributed to Muon, which achieved NanoGPT training speed records and was scaled to a 1.5-billion-parameter transformer. Together, these results connect the mathematical treatment of gradients to implementable optimization procedures.
summary.tldr: Modular dualization builds architecture-aware gradient-to-update maps and GPU-friendly algorithms that underpin fast neural network optimizers.

title: Modular Duality in Deep Learning

abstract: We revisit the smooth convex-concave bilinearly-coupled saddle-point problem of the form $\min_x\max_y f(x) + ⟨y,\mathbf{B} x⟩- g(y)$. In the highly specific case where function $f(x)$ is strongly convex and function $g(y)$ is affine, or both functions are affine, there exist lower bounds on the number of gradient evaluations and matrix-vector multiplications required to solve the problem, as well as matching optimal algorithms. A notable aspect of these algorithms is that they are able to attain linear convergence, i.e., the number of iterations required to solve the problem is proportional to $\log(1/\epsilon)$. However, the class of bilinearly-coupled saddle-point problems for which linear convergence is possible is much wider and can involve general smooth non-strongly convex functions $f(x)$ and $g(y)$. Therefore, we develop the first lower complexity bounds and matching optimal linearly converging algorithms for this problem class. Our lower complexity bounds are much more general, but they cover and unify the existing results in the literature. On the other hand, our algorithm implements the separation of complexities, which, for the first time, enables the simultaneous achievement of both optimal gradient evaluation and matrix-vector multiplication complexities, resulting in the best theoretical performance to date.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems where one variable is minimized, another is maximized, and a bilinear term couples them. Solving these problems requires both gradient evaluations and matrix-vector multiplications. Earlier optimality results covered particular cases involving strongly convex or affine functions, leaving a broader class of linearly convergent problems unresolved.

The authors establish lower bounds on the computational work needed for this broader class and develop algorithms that match those bounds. The class can include smooth functions without strong convexity. Linear convergence means that the iteration count grows proportionally to the logarithm of inverse target error, giving a precise relationship between additional computation and tighter accuracy.

A central feature of the algorithm is separating the complexities of gradient evaluations and matrix-vector multiplications. This enables it to achieve the optimal count for both kinds of operation simultaneously. The lower bounds also subsume and unify previous results. The advance is a sharper theoretical account of the achievable efficiency for the stated problem class, with optimality measured against explicit computational lower bounds.
summary.tldr: Matching lower bounds and algorithms establish optimal linear convergence for a broader class of bilinearly coupled saddle-point problems.

title: On Linear Convergence in Smooth Convex-Concave Bilinearly-Coupled Saddle-Point Optimization: Lower Bounds and Optimal Algorithms

abstract: This paper studies the complexity and optimality of Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL) policy in the $K$-armed bandit problems. FTPL is a promising policy that achieves the Best-of-Both-Worlds (BOBW) guarantee without solving an optimization problem unlike Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL). However, FTPL needs a procedure called geometric resampling to estimate the loss, which needs $O(K^2)$ per-round average complexity, usually worse than that of FTRL. To address this issue, we propose a novel technique, which we call Conditional Geometric Resampling (CGR), for unbiased loss estimation applicable to general perturbation distributions. CGR reduces the average complexity to $O(K\log K)$ without sacrificing the regret bounds. We also propose a biased version of CGR that can control the worst-case complexity while keeping the BOBW guarantee for a certain perturbation distribution. We confirm through experiments that CGR does not only significantly improve the average and worst-case runtime but also achieve better regret thanks to the stable loss estimation.

paragraphs: In a bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among K actions while learning from limited feedback. Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader is attractive because it can provide a best-of-both-worlds regret guarantee without solving the optimization problem used by Follow-the-Regularized-Leader. However, its geometric resampling procedure for estimating losses carries an average per-round cost of O(K²).

The paper introduces Conditional Geometric Resampling, or CGR, to reduce that bottleneck. It provides unbiased loss estimates for general perturbation distributions while lowering average computational complexity to O(K log K). The regret bounds are preserved, so this improvement targets the cost of obtaining the estimates without giving up the stated learning guarantees.

That distribution-specific qualification matters for the stronger runtime control. Experiments report improvements in both average and worst-case runtime, alongside better regret attributed to more stable loss estimation. The work therefore links computational efficiency with the quality of the feedback estimates used by the policy.
summary.tldr: Conditional Geometric Resampling reduces FTPL’s average loss-estimation cost from O(K²) to O(K log K) while preserving regret bounds.

title: Geometric Resampling in Nearly Linear Time for Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader with Best-of-Both-Worlds Guarantee in Bandit Problems

abstract: Recent advances in clinical AI have enabled remarkable progress across many clinical domains. However, existing benchmarks and models are primarily limited to a small set of modalities and tasks, which hinders the development of large-scale multimodal methods that can make holistic assessments of patient health and well-being. To bridge this gap, we introduce Clinical Large-scale Integrative Multimodal Benchmark (CLIMB), a comprehensive clinical benchmark unifying diverse clinical data across imaging, language, temporal, and graph modalities. CLIMB comprises 4.51 million patient samples totaling 19.01 terabytes distributed across 2D imaging, 3D video, time series, graphs, and multimodal data. Through extensive empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that multitask pretraining significantly improves performance on understudied domains, achieving up to 29% improvement in ultrasound and 23% in ECG analysis over single-task learning. Pretraining on CLIMB also effectively improves models’ generalization capability to new tasks, and strong unimodal encoder performance translates well to multimodal performance when paired with task-appropriate fusion strategies. Our findings provide a foundation for new architecture designs and pretraining strategies to adavance clinical AI research. Code is released at https://github.com/DDVD233/climb.

paragraphs: Clinical AI benchmarks often cover only a small collection of data types and tasks. CLIMB expands that scope by bringing together imaging, language, temporal, and graph modalities in one benchmark. Its purpose is to support research on models that can combine diverse clinical information when assessing patient health.

The benchmark contains 4.51 million patient samples and 19.01 terabytes of data, spanning 2D imaging, 3D video, time series, graphs, and multimodal data. The authors use it to investigate multitask pretraining and report improvements over single-task learning of up to 29% for ultrasound and 23% for ECG analysis. These are reported gains in the evaluated settings, rather than uniform improvements across every task.

The experiments also find that CLIMB pretraining improves generalization to new tasks. Strong encoders for individual modalities translate well to multimodal performance when paired with fusion strategies suited to the task. Together, the findings connect broader training data with decisions about encoder quality and how different information sources should be combined.
summary.tldr: CLIMB unifies diverse clinical data and demonstrates benefits from multitask pretraining and task-appropriate multimodal fusion.

title: CLIMB: Data Foundations for Large Scale Multimodal Clinical Foundation Models

abstract: Achieving seamless coordination between AI agents and humans is crucial for real-world applications, yet it remains a significant open challenge. Hanabi is a cooperative card game featuring imperfect information, constrained communication, theory of mind requirements, and coordinated action – making it an ideal testbed for human-AI coordination. However, its use for human-AI interaction has been limited by the challenges of human evaluation. In this work, we introduce the Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge (AH2AC2) to overcome the constraints of costly and difficult-to-reproduce human evaluations. We develop human proxy agents on a large-scale human dataset that serve as robust, cheap, and reproducible human-like evaluation partners in AH2AC2. To encourage the development of data-efficient methods, we open-source a dataset of 3,079 games, deliberately limiting the amount of available human gameplay data. We present baseline results for both two- and three- player Hanabi scenarios. To ensure fair evaluation, we host the proxy agents through a controlled evaluation system rather than releasing them publicly. The code is available at https://github.com/FLAIROx/ah2ac2.

paragraphs: An AI teammate needs to coordinate with people whose behavior it may not already know. Hanabi makes this challenge concrete: players cooperate despite incomplete information and limited communication, and successful actions depend on interpreting teammates’ intentions. Evaluating such coordination directly with humans, however, is costly and difficult to reproduce.

The paper introduces the Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge, which uses learned human proxy agents as evaluation partners. These agents are developed from a large human gameplay dataset and are intended to provide inexpensive, reproducible, human-like interactions. This gives researchers a consistent setting for comparing how well their agents cooperate with such partners.

The challenge releases 3,079 games, deliberately restricting available human data to encourage methods that learn efficiently. It also supplies baseline results for two-player and three-player Hanabi. The proxy agents remain behind a controlled evaluation system to support fair comparisons. The central contribution is an evaluation setup that makes human-oriented coordination research more repeatable while retaining the game’s demands for communication, inference, and joint action.
summary.tldr: AH2AC2 uses learned human proxy partners to make evaluation of human-AI coordination in Hanabi cheaper and more reproducible.

title: Ad-Hoc Human-AI Coordination Challenge

abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental problem for network-structured data. However, the prevalent research paradigm tends to assume abundant observed links, overlooking more challenging scenarios with a scarcity of observed links, which results in insufficient sample sizes. In real-world networks, hierarchical modularity, characterized by structured and nested connections, remains robust even with sparsely observed links. To address the challenge of limited link samples, we propose leveraging hierarchical modularity as a prior structure. We introduce complete-tree (CT) space, a discrete metric space with latent complete-tree structures, to formalize hierarchical modularity with an emphasis on its hierarchical permutation symmetry. Utilizing the group theory to quantize and compare permutation symmetries of different spaces, we prove that the CT space provides a significantly lower bound on sample complexity than the commonly used Euclidean space. We develop leaf matching, a data-efficient network embedding that maps nodes onto the CT space and conducts discrete optimization by reducing it to decentralized search. Experiments verify the data efficiency of CT space over other spaces. Moreover, leaf matching outperforms the state-of-the-art graph transformer in data-scarce scenarios while exhibiting excellent scalability. The code is available at: https://github.com/KevinGao7/LeafMatching.

paragraphs: Link prediction asks which connections are missing from a network. Many approaches assume that enough links are already visible to learn from, but sparse observations make this difficult. This paper uses hierarchical modularity—the organization of connections into nested groups—as a prior structure that can remain useful even when relatively few links are observed.

The authors introduce complete-tree space, a discrete metric space designed to express this hierarchy and its permutation symmetries. They use group theory to compare those symmetries with ones in other spaces. Their analysis establishes a substantially lower bound on sample complexity for complete-tree space than for the commonly used Euclidean space, connecting the representation's structure to the paper's data-efficiency argument.

The accompanying algorithm, leaf matching, embeds network nodes in complete-tree space and turns discrete optimization into decentralized search. Experiments support the data efficiency of this space relative to alternatives. Leaf matching also outperforms a leading graph transformer when data are scarce and shows strong scalability, suggesting that a hierarchy-oriented representation can be valuable when observed connections are limited.
summary.tldr: Complete-tree space encodes network hierarchies to support data-efficient link prediction, with leaf matching performing well when observed links are scarce.

title: Complete-Tree Space Favors Data-Efficient Link Prediction

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) often struggle in preserving high-frequency components of nodal signals when dealing with directed graphs. Such components are crucial for modeling flow dynamics, without which a traditional GNN tends to treat a graph with forward and reverse topologies equal. To make GNNs sensitive to those high-frequency components thereby being capable to capture detailed topological differences, this paper proposes a novel framework that combines 1) explicit difference matrices that model directional gradients and 2) implicit physical constraints that enforce messages passing within GNNs to be consistent with natural laws. Evaluations on two real-world directed graph data, namely, water flux network and urban traffic flow network, demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposal.

paragraphs: Predicting flow on a directed graph requires distinguishing the direction of its connections. The paper identifies a difficulty for graph neural networks: they can fail to preserve high-frequency components of signals on nodes. These components describe detailed variation that matters for flow dynamics, and losing them can make forward and reversed graph structures appear equivalent.

The proposed framework combines two mechanisms. Explicit difference matrices model directional gradients, making changes along directed connections available to the model. Implicit physical constraints guide message passing so that information exchanged within the graph neural network remains consistent with natural laws. Together, these mechanisms aim to preserve sensitivity to detailed differences in topology.

The authors evaluate the framework on real-world water flux and urban traffic flow networks and report that it is effective. These two applications connect the architectural motivation to systems where direction is central to flow prediction. The contribution is a way to combine explicit directional information with physics-guided learning so that the network can better distinguish graph structures that imply different flow behavior.
summary.tldr: Directional difference matrices and physical constraints help graph neural networks capture topology relevant to water and traffic flow prediction.

title: Topology-aware Neural Flux Prediction Guided by Physics

abstract: We study universal properties in real-world complex and synthetically generated datasets. Our approach is to analogize data to a physical system and employ tools from statistical physics and Random Matrix Theory (RMT) to reveal their underlying structure. Examining the local and global eigenvalue statistics of feature-feature covariance matrices, we find: (i) bulk eigenvalue power-law scaling vastly differs between uncorrelated Gaussian and real-world data, (ii) this power law behavior is reproducible using Gaussian data with long-range correlations, (iii) all dataset types exhibit chaotic RMT universality, (iv) RMT statistics emerge at smaller dataset sizes than typical training sets, correlating with power-law convergence, (v) Shannon entropy correlates with RMT structure and requires fewer samples in strongly correlated datasets. These results suggest natural image Gram matrices can be approximated by Wishart random matrices with simple covariance structure, enabling rigorous analysis of neural network behavior.

paragraphs: This paper looks for statistical patterns shared by real-world and synthetic datasets by treating data like a physical system. It examines eigenvalues of feature covariance matrices, which describe how variation is distributed across combinations of features. Tools from statistical physics and random matrix theory allow the authors to compare both broad spectral patterns and local eigenvalue behavior.

The findings distinguish uncorrelated Gaussian data from real-world data in their bulk eigenvalue power laws. Introducing long-range correlations into Gaussian data reproduces that power-law behavior. At the same time, all examined dataset types exhibit chaotic random-matrix universality. These shared statistics appear at sample sizes smaller than typical training sets and correlate with power-law convergence.

The authors also find a relationship between Shannon entropy and random-matrix structure, with fewer samples needed in strongly correlated datasets. Taken together, the observations suggest that natural-image Gram matrices may be approximated using Wishart random matrices with a simple covariance structure. Such an approximation could make rigorous analysis of neural network behavior more tractable while retaining important statistical features of natural data.
summary.tldr: Covariance spectra reveal shared random-matrix structure across studied datasets and suggest simple correlated models for natural-image statistics.

title: The Underlying Universal Statistical Structure of Natural Datasets

abstract: Linear algebra is a cornerstone of neural network inference. The efficiency of popular frameworks, such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, critically depends on backend libraries providing highly optimized matrix multiplications and convolutions. A diverse range of these backends exists across platforms, including Intel MKL, Nvidia CUDA, and Apple Accelerate. Although these backends provide equivalent functionality, subtle variations in their implementations can lead to seemingly negligible differences during inference. In this paper, we investigate these minor discrepancies and demonstrate how they can be selectively amplified by adversaries. Specifically, we introduce Chimera examples, inputs to models that elicit conflicting predictions depending on the employed backend library. These inputs can even be constructed with integer values, creating a vulnerability exploitable from real-world input domains. We analyze the prevalence and extent of the underlying attack surface and propose corresponding defenses to mitigate this threat.

paragraphs: Neural network predictions depend on numerical computations performed by backend libraries. These libraries provide the matrix multiplications and convolutions used by frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. Although different backends offer equivalent operations, their implementations can produce small numerical differences. This paper investigates whether those differences can become a deliberate source of conflicting predictions.

The authors introduce Chimera examples: inputs designed to make a model predict differently depending on the backend running it. The key finding is that an adversary can selectively amplify discrepancies that would otherwise appear negligible. This connects a low-level implementation detail to a visible change in model behavior, even when the model itself is the same.

The paper also shows that these inputs can use integer values, making the vulnerability relevant to real-world input domains. It examines the prevalence and extent of the attack surface and proposes defenses. The result identifies backend choice as a potential security concern for inference, beyond its familiar role in computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: Chimera inputs amplify small numerical differences between linear algebra backends to make the same model produce conflicting predictions.

title: Adversarial Inputs for Linear Algebra Backends

abstract: Parameter-sharing (PS) techniques have been widely adopted in cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL). In PS, all the agents share a policy network with identical parameters, which enjoys good sample efficiency. However, PS could lead to homogeneous policies that limit MARL performance. We tackle this problem from the angle of gradient conflict among agents. We find that the existence of futile neurons whose update is canceled out by gradient conflicts among agents leads to poor learning efficiency and diversity. To address this deficiency, we propose GradPS, a gradient-based PS method. It dynamically creates multiple clones for each futile neuron. For each clone, a group of agents with low gradient-conflict shares the neuron’s parameters. Our method can enjoy good sample efficiency by sharing the gradients among agents of the same clone neuron. Moreover, it can encourage diverse behaviors through independently updating an exclusive clone neuron. Through extensive experiments, we show that GradPS can learn diverse policies with promising performance. The source code for GradPS is available in https://github.com/xmu-rl-3dv/GradPS.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, sharing one policy network lets agents pool learning experience efficiently. However, identical shared parameters can also encourage overly similar behavior. This paper traces part of that problem to gradient conflicts: different agents can request opposing changes to the same neuron, causing their updates to cancel.

GradPS identifies these ineffective, or futile, neurons and dynamically creates multiple copies. Agents with relatively compatible gradients share a copy, so their updates can still contribute jointly to learning. Separate copies can receive independent updates, giving agents room to develop different behaviors without abandoning parameter sharing throughout the entire network.

This makes the sharing arrangement responsive to where learning conflicts actually occur. It preserves the benefit of shared gradients within compatible groups while allowing differentiation where shared updates interfere. Extensive experiments show that GradPS learns diverse policies with promising performance. The stated findings support gradient conflict as a useful signal for deciding which neurons should remain shared and which should be separated.
summary.tldr: GradPS clones neurons whose agent gradients conflict, retaining useful parameter sharing while enabling more diverse policies.

title: GradPS: Resolving Futile Neurons in Parameter Sharing Network for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent advancements in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems have significantly enhanced the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by incorporating external knowledge retrieval. However, the sole reliance on retrieval is often inadequate for mining deep, domain-specific knowledge and for performing logical reasoning from specialized datasets. To tackle these challenges, we present an approach, which is designed to extract, comprehend, and utilize domain knowledge while constructing a coherent rationale. At the heart of our approach lie four pivotal components: a knowledge atomizer that extracts atomic questions from raw data, a query proposer that generates subsequent questions to facilitate the original inquiry, an atomic retriever that locates knowledge based on atomic knowledge alignments, and an atomic selector that determines which follow-up questions to pose guided by the retrieved information. Through this approach, we implement a knowledge-aware task decomposition strategy that adeptly extracts multifaceted knowledge from segmented data and iteratively builds the rationale in alignment with the initial query and the acquired knowledge. We conduct comprehensive experiments to demonstrate the efficacy of our approach across various benchmarks, particularly those requiring multihop reasoning steps. The results indicate a significant enhancement in performance, up to 12.6% over the second-best method, underscoring the potential of the approach in complex, knowledge-intensive applications.

summary.tldr: Knowledge-aware decomposition uses atomic questions and retrieved evidence to guide follow-up reasoning, improving performance on complex retrieval-augmented tasks.

title: From Complex to Atomic: Enhancing Augmented Generation via Knowledge-Aware Dual Rewriting and Reasoning

abstract: This paper investigates the fusion of absolute (reward) and relative (dueling) feedback in stochastic bandits, where both feedback types are gathered in each decision round. We derive a regret lower bound, demonstrating that an efficient algorithm may incur only the smaller among the reward and dueling-based regret for each individual arm. We propose two fusion approaches: (1) a simple elimination fusion algorithm that leverages both feedback types to explore all arms and unifies collected information by sharing a common candidate arm set, and (2) a decomposition fusion algorithm that selects the more effective feedback to explore the corresponding arms and randomly assigns one feedback type for exploration and the other for exploitation in each round. The elimination fusion experiences a suboptimal multiplicative term of the number of arms in regret due to the intrinsic suboptimality of dueling elimination. In contrast, the decomposition fusion achieves regret matching the lower bound up to a constant under a common assumption. Extensive experiments confirm the efficacy of our algorithms and theoretical results.
