paragraphs: This paper studies sequential decision-making with two kinds of feedback available each round: numerical rewards and relative comparisons between options. The question is how to combine them efficiently when either source may be more informative for a particular option. A regret lower bound identifies the potential benefit: an efficient algorithm may pay only the smaller feedback-specific learning cost for each arm.

The authors propose two approaches. Elimination fusion uses both feedback types to explore all arms and shares a common set of remaining candidates. Decomposition fusion instead selects the more effective feedback for exploring particular arms. Each round, it randomly assigns one feedback type to exploration and the other to exploiting what has already been learned.

The theoretical comparison reveals a meaningful difference. Elimination fusion incurs an extra multiplicative dependence on the number of arms, attributed to dueling elimination. Under a common assumption, decomposition fusion matches the lower bound up to a constant. Experiments support the algorithms and analysis, showing why allocating feedback according to its usefulness can matter.
summary.tldr: Combining numerical rewards with pairwise comparisons can achieve arm-specific learning advantages, with decomposition fusion attaining a conditionally optimal regret bound.

title: Fusing Reward and Dueling Feedback in Stochastic Bandits

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) with delays is challenging as sensory perceptions lag behind the actual events: the RL agent needs to estimate the real state of its environment based on past observations. State-of-the-art (SOTA) methods typically employ recursive, step-by-step forecasting of states. This can cause the accumulation of compounding errors. To tackle this problem, our novel belief estimation method, named Directly Forecasting Belief Transformer (DFBT), directly forecasts states from observations without incrementally estimating intermediate states step-by-step. We theoretically demonstrate that DFBT greatly reduces compounding errors of existing recursively forecasting methods, yielding stronger performance guarantees. In experiments with D4RL offline datasets, DFBT reduces compounding errors with remarkable prediction accuracy. DFBT’s capability to forecast state sequences also facilitates multi-step bootstrapping, thus greatly improving learning efficiency. On the MuJoCo benchmark, our DFBT-based method substantially outperforms SOTA baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/QingyuanWuNothing/DFBT.

paragraphs: When observations arrive late, a reinforcement learning agent must act using information about an environment that has already changed. It therefore needs an estimate of the current state. Existing forecasting approaches commonly advance through intermediate states one step at a time, creating a route for prediction errors to accumulate.

The Directly Forecasting Belief Transformer, or DFBT, predicts states directly from observations without recursively estimating each intervening state. The authors theoretically show that this reduces compounding errors relative to recursive forecasting and gives stronger performance guarantees. DFBT can also forecast sequences of states, which supports multi-step bootstrapping and improves the efficiency of learning.

Experiments using D4RL offline datasets show reduced error accumulation and strong prediction accuracy. A reinforcement learning method built around DFBT also substantially outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on MuJoCo. These results connect the forecasting change to both better state estimation and better learning outcomes. The central idea is that handling observation delay depends not only on forecasting accuracy, but also on whether the forecasting procedure repeatedly feeds its own errors forward.
summary.tldr: DFBT directly forecasts states from delayed observations, reducing compounding prediction errors and improving reinforcement learning performance.

title: Directly Forecasting Belief for Reinforcement Learning with Delays

abstract: Over 40% of the global population lives within 100 kilometers of the coast, which contributes more than $8 trillion annually to the global economy. Unfortunately, coastal ecosystems are increasingly vulnerable to more frequent and intense extreme weather events and rising sea levels. Coastal scientists use numerical models to simulate complex physical processes, but these models are often slow and expensive. In recent years, deep learning has become a promising alternative to reduce the cost of numerical models. However, progress has been hindered by the lack of a large-scale, high-resolution coastal simulation dataset to train and validate deep learning models. Existing studies often focus on relatively small datasets and simple processes. To fill this gap, we introduce a decade-long, high-resolution ($<$100m) coastal circulation modeling dataset on a real-world 3D mesh in southwest Florida with around 6 million cells. The dataset contains key oceanography variables (e.g., current velocities, free surface level, temperature, salinity) alongside external atmospheric and river forcings. We evaluated a customized Vision Transformer model that takes initial and boundary conditions and external forcings and predicts ocean variables at varying lead times. The dataset provides an opportunity to benchmark novel deep learning models for high-resolution coastal simulations (e.g., physics-informed machine learning, neural operator learning). The code and dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/spatialdatasciencegroup/CoastalBench.

The paper identifies limited training and validation data as an obstacle to developing deep learning alternatives, particularly when the goal is to represent complex processes at high spatial resolution.

The dataset covers a decade of simulated coastal conditions in southwest Florida. It uses a real-world three-dimensional mesh with around six million cells and spatial resolution finer than 100 meters. Recorded quantities include water velocities, surface level, temperature, and salinity, together with atmospheric and river inputs that influence coastal behavior.

The authors evaluate a customized Vision Transformer that predicts ocean variables at different lead times from initial conditions, boundary conditions, and external forcings. The central contribution is a shared resource for testing models on detailed coastal simulations. Its combination of geometry, evolving ocean variables, and external drivers creates opportunities to benchmark approaches such as physics-informed learning and neural operators.
summary.tldr: CoastalBench supplies a decade of detailed coastal simulations to support training and evaluation of machine learning emulators.

title: CoastalBench: A Decade-Long High-Resolution Dataset to Emulate Complex Coastal Processes

abstract: Recent studies show that Hypergraph Neural Networks (HGNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, while adversarial learning in the context of hypergraphs remains substantially under-investigated. In particular, all existing attacks on HGNNs are white-box and customized for either structural or feature perturbation. But in reality, the attacker might not have access to the target model parameters. Motivated by this knowledge gap, we propose a generic meta-objective-based learning framework, MeLA, that leverages the hypergraph Laplacian to conduct gray-box, structural, and feature perturbations under explicit perturbation budgets. In contrast to the attack literature, there is no adversarial training mechanism for HGNNs to defend against such attacks. Hence, we propose a novel adversarial training mechanism for HGNNs to obtain a robust classifier. We further prove the convergence of our robust training. Extensive experiments across various HGNN models and datasets show that (a) our proposed attack is effective in poisoning and evasion settings, and (b) our adversarial training enhances defense against adversarial attacks.

paragraphs: Hypergraph neural networks learn from relationships involving groups of entities, but those relationships and their associated features can be manipulated. This paper addresses a gap in adversarial evaluation: existing attacks described in the abstract require access to model parameters and specialize in either structural changes or feature changes. An attacker may have less access in practice.

The proposed framework, MeLA, uses a meta-objective and the hypergraph Laplacian to support attacks with partial model knowledge. It accommodates both structural and feature perturbations, with explicit budgets restricting how much the attacker can change. This brings several attack settings into one framework instead of requiring a separate specialized approach for each kind of modification.

The authors also introduce adversarial training for hypergraph neural networks and prove convergence of their training procedure. Across the tested models and datasets, MeLA is effective both when corrupting training data and when attacking at evaluation time. The defense improves resistance to adversarial attacks in those experiments, pairing a broader attack methodology with a corresponding approach to robust training.
summary.tldr: MeLA attacks hypergraph neural networks under partial model access, while a companion adversarial-training method improves their defenses.

title: Adversarial Attacks and Robust Training for Hypergraph Neural Networks

abstract: We study the problem of private hypothesis selection: given samples from an unknown distribution drawn from a finite hypothesis class, the goal is to identify the best hypothesis under the constraint of differential privacy. Existing algorithms for this problem are either computationally expensive or achieve sub-optimal statistical rates. We propose new algorithms that achieve near-optimal rates while running in nearly linear time in the number of hypotheses. Rather than applying the exponential mechanism directly with a score function that requires pairwise comparisons between hypotheses, our approach introduces a carefully designed loss function based on a small set of strong hypotheses. This structure allows the score to be evaluated efficiently for most hypotheses, yielding significant computational savings. We further extend our algorithms to the agnostic setting, where the true distribution may not belong to the hypothesis class. As an application, we obtain faster differentially private algorithms for universal statistical estimation in low dimensional settings.

paragraphs: Private hypothesis selection asks which candidate distribution best explains observed samples while satisfying differential privacy. The challenge is to obtain strong statistical accuracy without making selection computationally expensive. This paper introduces algorithms that achieve near-optimal statistical rates with running time nearly linear in the number of candidate hypotheses.

A major computational obstacle is scoring candidates through comparisons with other candidates. Applying the exponential mechanism directly to such scores can require substantial comparison work. The authors instead construct a loss using a small collection of strong hypotheses. That structure makes the score efficient to evaluate for most candidates, reducing the computational burden of private selection.

The algorithms also extend to the agnostic setting, where none of the candidate distributions need equal the true distribution. This broadens the selection problem beyond finding a correctly specified candidate. As an application, the authors obtain faster differentially private algorithms for universal statistical estimation in low dimensions. The contribution is a way to combine efficient computation with near-optimal statistical performance under a privacy requirement.
summary.tldr: A loss built from a small set of strong hypotheses enables nearly linear-time private selection with near-optimal statistical rates.

title: Fast and Near-Optimal Algorithms for Private Hypothesis Selection

abstract: Human evaluation remains the primary standard for assessing modern AI systems, yet annotator disagreement, bias, and variability make system rankings fragile under standard majority vote aggregation. Majority vote discards annotator reliability and item-level ambiguity, often yielding unstable comparisons across annotator subsets. We introduce STABLEVAL, a disagreement-aware evaluation framework that models latent item correctness and annotator-specific confusion patterns to produce posterior expected item credit and calibrated agent-level scores. Unlike label-denoising approaches such as Dawid–Skene, STABLEVAL is explicitly designed for stable and uncertainty-aware system evaluation rather than hard label recovery. We formalize ranking stability as a first-class evaluation objective and analyze how aggregation methods preserve or distort underlying annotator behavior. Across controlled synthetic experiments and multiple real-world human-annotated benchmarks, majority vote exhibits increasing score error and ranking instability under annotator heterogeneity and adversarial noise, while STABLEVAL yields more stable and statistically grounded system rankings. These results demonstrate that modeling disagreement is essential for robust and reproducible AI evaluation.

paragraphs: Human judgments are a central standard for evaluating AI, but different annotators can produce different system rankings. Majority voting discards information about annotator reliability and how ambiguous an individual item is. STABLEVAL treats this disagreement as something to model explicitly when estimating system quality and assessing the stability of comparisons.

The framework models latent item correctness together with annotator-specific confusion patterns. It uses those estimates to assign posterior expected credit to items and calibrated scores to systems. Its objective is stable evaluation with uncertainty represented in the scores, rather than recovering a single hard label for each example. Ranking stability is formalized as an evaluation objective in its own right.

Controlled synthetic experiments and multiple human-annotated benchmarks show that majority voting becomes less accurate and less stable under annotator heterogeneity and adversarial noise. STABLEVAL produces more stable, statistically grounded rankings in these evaluations. The findings show why the way judgments are aggregated can materially affect conclusions about AI systems, even when the underlying collection of human evaluations is the starting point.
summary.tldr: STABLEVAL models annotator disagreement and item uncertainty to produce more stable AI system scores and rankings.

title: STABLEVAL: Disagreement-Aware and Stable Evaluation of AI Systems

abstract: Long-video temporal reasoning remains a bottleneck for Large Video Language Models (LVLMs). Existing reinforcement-learning approaches reward only final-answer correctness, so they cannot distinguish answers reached through grounded reasoning from those reached through fabricated chronology; the intermediate temporal claims that constitute the reasoning are never verified. We trace this gap to a structural correspondence between two kinds of traces: a video has its own temporal trace, an ordered sequence of how events unfold, while a model’s answer is built up through a reasoning trace, an ordered sequence of intermediate temporal claims. Correct reasoning requires the latter to mirror the former, claim by claim. We act on this correspondence with two contributions. We introduce Temporal Reasoning Traces (TRT), a structured index of a video’s ordered event chains that exposes a small set of deterministic verification primitives, materializing the temporal trace as a programmatically queryable object. We then propose temporal-enhanced GRPO, a reinforcement-learning procedure whose reward decomposes into per-block components, each computed by a TRT primitive on a typed think block of the reasoning trace. Because the reward is fully symbolic, fabricated temporal claims are caught at the per-claim level rather than masked by a correct final answer. Across long-video reasoning benchmarks, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance, with the largest gains on out-of-domain reasoning tasks such as Video-Holmes, CG-Bench-Reasoning, and VRBench.

paragraphs: A model can answer a question about a long video correctly while inventing the order of events in its explanation. Rewarding only final-answer correctness cannot distinguish that behavior from grounded reasoning. VideoTrace-R1 addresses the intermediate temporal claims themselves, seeking correspondence between the video’s event sequence and the model’s reasoning sequence.

Temporal Reasoning Traces provide a structured index of ordered event chains with deterministic operations for checking temporal claims. The authors combine this representation with temporal-enhanced GRPO, a reinforcement-learning procedure that assigns reward separately to typed blocks of reasoning. Each block is evaluated through a corresponding symbolic operation on the trace, allowing fabricated chronology to be detected at the claim level.

The model achieves state-of-the-art performance across long-video reasoning benchmarks, with its largest gains on out-of-domain tasks including Video-Holmes, CG-Bench-Reasoning, and VRBench. These findings support using programmatically checkable intermediate evidence as a learning signal. The approach makes chronological grounding part of what training rewards, so a correct final response does not by itself conceal unsupported temporal steps.
summary.tldr: VideoTrace-R1 improves long-video reasoning by symbolically checking and rewarding intermediate temporal claims against structured event traces.

title: VideoTrace-R1: Long Video-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In this paper, we study a class of non-convex optimization problems known as multi-affine quadratic equality constrained problems, which appear in various applications–from generating feasible force trajectories in robotic locomotion and manipulation to training neural networks. Although these problems are generally non-convex, they exhibit convexity or related properties when all variables except one are fixed. Under mild assumptions, we prove that the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) converges when applied to this class of problems. Furthermore, when the "degree" of non-convexity in the constraints remains within certain bounds, we show that ADMM achieves a linear convergence rate. We validate our theoretical results through practical examples in robotic locomotion.

paragraphs: This paper studies multi-affine quadratic equality constrained optimization problems, a non-convex class appearing in neural-network training and robotic force-trajectory generation. Their useful structure emerges when variables are considered separately: fixing all but one variable leaves a problem with convexity or related properties. That structure motivates analyzing an alternating optimization method.

The authors prove, under assumptions they describe as mild, that the alternating direction method of multipliers converges on this problem class. The result concerns convergence of the method’s iterates, giving theoretical support for applying ADMM to these structured non-convex problems. The guarantee remains tied to the stated assumptions and problem structure.

A stronger result applies when the degree of non-convexity in the constraints stays within certain bounds: ADMM then has a linear convergence rate, meaning its error decreases geometrically. Practical robotic-locomotion examples validate the theoretical findings. The contribution connects structure that remains manageable one variable at a time to convergence guarantees for a problem that is non-convex when considered as a whole.
summary.tldr: The paper proves conditional convergence guarantees for ADMM on structured non-convex equality-constrained problems, including linear rates under bounded constraint non-convexity.

title: Last-iterate Convergence of ADMM on Multi-affine Quadratic Equality Constrained Problem

abstract: Despite rapid progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for robotic control, instruction drift remains a persistent failure mode in long-horizon tasks. This paper reconceptualizes this phenomenon, positing that instruction drift is fundamentally a systematic sampling error: local greedy sampling is prone to collapsing into “Negative Pivotal Windows”—irreversible local optima with high local probability that sever global success pathways. To address this, we propose Context-Aware Power Sampling (CAPS), a training-free inference-time computation framework. CAPS leverages power distributions to sharpen global trajectory probabilities, enabling lookahead search over the model’s conditional generative trajectory distribution. Furthermore, we introduce a metacognitive control mechanism based on Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR). This mechanism triggers adaptive MCMC search solely when drift risk is detected, enabling a dynamic transition from “intuitive fast thinking” to “rational slow search.” Experiments on RoboTwin, Simpler-WindowX, and Libero-long benchmarks show that CAPS achieves substantial improvements over strong baselines, including OpenVLA and TACO, without parameter updates. These results support the effectiveness of adaptive inference-time computation for improving long-horizon robustness in embodied control.

paragraphs: A robot following a long instruction can make locally plausible choices that undermine eventual completion. This paper proposes viewing such instruction drift as systematic sampling error. Its account centers on highly probable local choices that enter irreversible traps and cut off successful longer-term trajectories.

Context-Aware Power Sampling, or CAPS, addresses this at inference time without updating model parameters. It uses power distributions to sharpen probabilities over whole trajectories and supports lookahead search through the model’s conditional trajectory distribution. An additional controller uses a signal-to-noise measure to detect drift risk and trigger adaptive Markov chain Monte Carlo search only when that risk is detected.

The intended benefit is selective use of extra computation: routine decisions can remain fast, while risky situations receive more search. Experiments on RoboTwin, Simpler-WindowX, and Libero-long report substantial improvements over strong baselines, including OpenVLA and TACO. These results support adaptive inference-time computation for longer-horizon robotic control in the evaluated settings. The sampling-error explanation is the paper’s proposed account of drift, while the benchmark improvements establish the reported effectiveness of its intervention.
summary.tldr: CAPS detects instruction-drift risk and selectively searches future trajectories, improving long-horizon robot performance without parameter updates.

title: Rethinking Instruction Drift as a Sampling Error: SNR-Aware Power Distributions for Long-Horizon Robotic Planning

abstract: While many-shot ICL achieves remarkable performance, prior studies of its scaling behavior have mainly focused on non-reasoning tasks. In this work, we study many-shot ICL on reasoning tasks, with a particular focus on many-shot chain-of-thought in-context learning (CoT-ICL). Analyzing across non-reasoning and reasoning tasks and across non-reasoning and reasoning-oriented LLMs, we identify several distinctive properties of many-shot CoT-ICL. We further interpret these findings by viewing many-shot CoT-ICL as in-context test-time learning rather than scaled pattern matching, and suggest two principles: (i) demonstrations should be easy for the target model to understand, and (ii) they should be ordered to support a smooth conceptual progression. Guided by the principle, we propose Curvilinear Demonstration Selection (CDS), a simple ordering method that yields up to a 5.42 percentage-point gain on a math task with 64 demonstrations. Overall, our results reframe the long context window from a retrieval buffer into a structured curriculum for in-context test-time learning.

title: Many-Shot CoT-ICL: Making In-Context Learning Truly Learn

abstract: There have been numerous attempts to distill quadratic attention-based large language models (LLMs) into sub-quadratic linearized architectures. However, despite extensive research, such distilled models often fail to match the performance of their teacher LLMs on various downstream tasks. We set out the goal of lossless distillation, which we define in terms of tolerance-corrected Win-and-Tie rates between student and teacher on sets of tasks. To this end, we introduce an effective distillation pipeline for xLSTM-based students. We propose an additional merging stage, where individually linearized experts are combined into a single model. We show the effectiveness of this pipeline by distilling base and instruction-tuned models from the Llama, Qwen, and Olmo families. In many settings, our xLSTM-based students recover most of the teacher’s performance, and even exceed it on some downstream tasks. Our contributions are an important step towards more energy-efficient and cost-effective replacements for transformer-based LLMs.

paragraphs: Distilling a large language model into an architecture with lower computational scaling is attractive, but the smaller-cost student often loses downstream capability. This paper studies xLSTM-based students as replacements for models built around quadratic attention. The results point toward more cost-effective and energy-efficient alternatives while retaining substantial language-model capability.
summary.tldr: A distillation pipeline that merges linearized experts produces xLSTM-based students that recover most teacher performance in many tested settings.

title: Effective Distillation to Hybrid xLSTM Architectures

abstract: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) can be effectively realized through an iterative refinement via the Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) cycle, which is a common workflow used by human experts. However, most conventional deep learning-based models as one-shot generators that lack feedback mechanisms, leaving the DMTA loop disconnected. In this work, we propose K-BTS, a Knowledge-Driven Bi-level Thompson Sampling framework that formalizes iterative SBDD as a Dynamic Hierarchical Multi-Armed Bandit problem. K-BTS closes the DMTA loop by decoupling decisions into two levels: an upper-level policy that prioritizes high-potential molecular lineages and a lower-level mechanism that retrieves explicit chemical rules to guide LLM generation. By integrating a dual-level Bayesian update, the framework transforms sparse docking scores into reusable experience. On the CrossDocked2020 benchmark, K-BTS achieves a state-of-the-art Top-1 average docking score. The results from diverse dimensions show that K-BTS ensures search determinism through a smooth, monotonic convergence that synchronizes structural drift with affinity improvement.

paragraphs: K-BTS brings feedback-driven iteration to structure-based molecular design. The paper contrasts the repeated Design-Make-Test-Analyze workflow used by experts with one-shot generative models that leave feedback disconnected from future design. It formulates iterative search as a dynamic hierarchical multi-armed bandit problem, allowing successive design decisions to use accumulated experience.

An upper policy prioritizes promising molecular lineages, while a lower mechanism retrieves explicit chemical rules to steer language-model generation. The findings support an iterative search process in which chemical knowledge and docking feedback jointly guide molecular refinement through successive rounds of generation.
summary.tldr: K-BTS uses hierarchical Bayesian search and chemical rules to steer iterative language-model molecular design using docking feedback.

title: Steering Large Language Models through the DMTA Cycle: Structure-Based Drug Design via Knowledge-Driven Bi-Level Thompson Sampling

abstract: Watermarking offers a promising solution for detecting LLM-generated content, yet its robustness under realistic query-free (black-box) evasion remains an open challenge. Existing query-free attacks often achieve limited success or severely distort semantic meaning. We bridge this gap by theoretically analyzing rewriting-based evasion, demonstrating that reducing the average conditional probability of sampling green tokens by a small margin causes the detection probability to decay exponentially. Guided by this insight, we propose the Bias-Inversion Rewriting Attack (BIRA), a practical query-free method that applies a negative logit bias to a proxy suppression set identified via token surprisal. Empirically, BIRA achieves state-of-the-art evasion rates ($>99%$) across diverse watermarking schemes while preserving semantic fidelity substantially better than prior baselines. Our findings reveal a fundamental vulnerability in current watermarking methods and highlight the need for rigorous stress tests. Our code is available at https://github.com/ml-postech/LLM-Watermark-Evasion-via-Bias-Inversion.

paragraphs: Language-model watermarks aim to make generated text detectable through statistical patterns in token choices. This paper studies rewriting-based evasion in a query-free black-box setting, where existing attacks often either have limited success or substantially change the text's meaning. The central question is how fragile detection is to small changes in token-selection bias.

The theoretical analysis shows that a small reduction in the average conditional probability of choosing watermark-favored green tokens causes detection probability to decay exponentially. Guided by this result, the authors propose Bias-Inversion Rewriting Attack. It uses token surprisal to identify a proxy suppression set and applies a negative logit bias during rewriting.

Across the tested watermarking schemes, the method achieves evasion rates above 99% while preserving meaning substantially better than prior baselines. The findings connect a theoretical sensitivity in watermark statistics with an empirical rewriting method. They support the authors' call for rigorous stress testing of watermarking robustness, particularly against attacks that do not rely on detector queries.
summary.tldr: Bias-inversion rewriting exploits sensitivity in watermark token statistics, exceeding 99% evasion across tested schemes while better preserving meaning than prior baselines.

title: LLM Watermark Evasion via Bias Inversion

abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification at unobserved spatial locations is a key challenge in spatial statistics, particularly for complex and heterogeneous datasets. While traditional methods such as Kriging rely on strong distributional assumptions, conformal prediction (CP) offers a distribution-free alternative. However, although non-i.i.d. CP theory is well established for time-series data, a significant gap remains for spatial data, where the lack of a natural ordering and discrete index complicates theoretical guarantees. Existing CP theory for spatial data often relies on exchangeability. We propose Localized Spatial Conformal Prediction (LSCP), a model-agnostic framework that bridges this gap by coupling local quantile regression with conformal calibration. LSCP conditions on spatial neighborhoods to capture local heterogeneity. We show that LSCP retains finite-sample marginal coverage under spatial exchangeability and attains asymptotic conditional coverage under stationarity and spatial mixing. Across synthetic and real datasets, LSCP consistently achieves near-nominal coverage with tighter and more stable prediction intervals than existing methods that fail to capture these spatial dependencies.

paragraphs: Localized Spatial Conformal Prediction estimates uncertainty at spatial locations where observations are unavailable. Spatial data create a challenge because locations can have different local behavior and dependent observations, without the natural sequence found in time series. The paper develops conformal prediction specifically around these spatial features.

LSCP combines local quantile regression with conformal calibration and can work with different underlying prediction models. Conditioning on spatial neighborhoods allows its intervals to reflect local heterogeneity. Its guarantees depend on distinct assumptions: spatial exchangeability gives finite-sample marginal coverage, while stationarity and spatial mixing give asymptotic conditional coverage. The latter concerns increasingly large samples under the stated spatial dependence conditions.

On synthetic and real datasets, LSCP achieves coverage close to the intended level while producing tighter and more stable intervals than methods that fail to capture those dependencies. This matters because useful uncertainty estimates must balance coverage with precision. The contribution combines practical local adaptation with theoretical guarantees that explicitly distinguish overall finite-sample coverage from conditional coverage obtained asymptotically.
summary.tldr: LSCP combines neighborhood-aware quantile regression and conformal calibration to produce tighter spatial prediction intervals with assumption-dependent coverage guarantees.

title: Spatial Conformal Inference through Localized Quantile Regression

abstract: For approximating a target distribution given only its unnormalized log-density, stochastic gradient-based variational inference (VI) algorithms are a popular approach. For example, Wasserstein VI (WVI) and black-box VI (BBVI) perform gradient descent in measure space (Bures-Wasserstein space) and parameter space, respectively. Previously, for the Gaussian variational family, convergence guarantees for WVI have shown superiority over existing results for black-box VI with the reparametrization gradient, suggesting the measure space approach might provide some unique benefits. In this work, however, we close this gap by obtaining identical state-of-the-art iteration complexity guarantees for both. In particular, we identify that WVI’s superiority stems from the specific gradient estimator it uses, which BBVI can also leverage with minor modifications. The estimator in question is usually associated with Price’s theorem and utilizes second-order information (Hessians) of the target log-density. We will refer to this as Price’s gradient. On the flip side, WVI can be made more widely applicable by using the reparametrization gradient, which requires only gradients of the log-density. We empirically demonstrate that the use of Price’s gradient is the major source of performance improvement.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a target distribution by optimizing a simpler distribution. For Gaussian approximations, earlier convergence results favored Wasserstein variational inference, which optimizes in distribution space, over black-box variational inference using reparameterization gradients in parameter space. This paper examines what actually accounts for that apparent advantage.

The authors obtain matching state-of-the-art iteration-complexity guarantees for both approaches. They identify the gradient estimator as the decisive ingredient: Wasserstein inference's estimator, associated with Price's theorem, can also be used in black-box inference with minor modifications. Price's gradient uses Hessians, which encode second-order information about the target log-density.

The exchange also works in the other direction. Wasserstein inference can use reparameterization gradients requiring only first-order derivatives, making it more widely applicable. Experiments indicate that Price's gradient is the main source of the observed performance improvement. The result separates the choice of optimization space from the information used to estimate updates, showing that the earlier theoretical gap need not be an inherent advantage of distribution-space optimization.
summary.tldr: Price's gradient lets parameter-space variational inference match Wasserstein inference's iteration guarantees, identifying the estimator as the key advantage.

title: Stochastic Gradient Variational Inference with Price’s Gradient Estimator from Bures-Wasserstein to Parameter Space

abstract: Constraint-based causal discovery is widely used for learning causal structures, but heavy reliance on conditional independence (CI) testing makes it computationally expensive in high-dimensional settings. To mitigate this limitation, many divide-and-conquer frameworks have been proposed, but most assume causal sufficiency, i.e., no latent variables. In this paper, we show that divide-and-conquer strategies can be theoretically generalized beyond causal sufficiency to settings with latent variables. Specifically, we propose a recursive decomposition framework, termed DiCoLa, that enables divide-and-conquer causal discovery in the presence of latent variables. It recursively decomposes the global learning task into smaller subproblems and integrates their solutions through a principled reconstruction step to recover the global structure. We theoretically establish the soundness and completeness of the proposed framework. Extensive experiments on synthetic data demonstrate that our approach significantly improves computational efficiency across a range of causal discovery algorithms, while experiments on a real-world dataset further illustrate its practical effectiveness.

paragraphs: Learning a causal structure often involves repeatedly testing whether two variables become independent after accounting for others. These conditional independence tests become expensive when many variables are involved. Splitting the problem into smaller pieces can help, but existing divide-and-conquer frameworks commonly assume that there are no unobserved variables affecting the causal system.

DiCoLa extends this decomposition approach to settings with latent, or unobserved, variables. It recursively breaks the overall discovery task into smaller subproblems, solves those pieces, and then combines their results through a principled reconstruction procedure. Reconstruction is central: the smaller answers must fit together into a coherent global structure despite the presence of hidden variables.

The paper establishes soundness and completeness for its framework, providing theoretical support for the decomposition and reconstruction process. Synthetic-data experiments show substantial computational efficiency improvements across several causal discovery algorithms, while a real-world dataset illustrates practical effectiveness. The contribution is a framework for making causal discovery more manageable when the usual no-hidden-variables assumption does not apply.
summary.tldr: DiCoLa makes causal discovery more computationally efficient by recursively solving and recombining smaller problems while allowing hidden variables.

title: A Recursive Decomposition Framework for Causal Structure Learning in the Presence of Latent Variables

abstract: Users increasingly face the challenge of selecting an appropriate LLM for a given task from a rapidly growing pool of LLMs, each with distinct but often opaque latent properties. Compounding this challenge, users may lack the vocabulary or awareness to explicitly articulate the characteristics they value in an LLM’s responses or deployment. We propose an interaction-efficient active learning framework in which a dueling bandit algorithm iteratively selects pairs of LLMs, collects user feedback about their responses, and updates its belief about the user’s latent preferences. We introduce a novel belief-aware upper confidence bound strategy that balances exploration of the model pool with exploitation of inferred preferences, enabling efficient alignment between user needs and LLM capabilities under user-specified cost and time budgets. Through diverse experiments on LLMs and human studies, we experimentally verify that our model can efficiently match users to LLMs at a lower cost.

paragraphs: Choosing a language model is difficult when models have opaque strengths and users cannot fully describe what they want. CUPID treats selection as an interactive learning problem. It infers preferences from comparisons between model responses, allowing users to reveal what matters through feedback instead of requiring a complete specification upfront.

A dueling bandit algorithm repeatedly selects pairs of models, collects user feedback, and updates its belief about the user’s preferences. The authors introduce a belief-aware upper confidence bound strategy to guide those comparisons. It balances investigating less-understood models with focusing on models that already appear suitable, while operating under user-specified cost and time budgets.

Experiments involving language models and human studies show that the framework can match users to models efficiently at lower cost. The findings support spending interactions selectively: each comparison contributes information about both the available models and the user’s priorities. The resulting recommendation is shaped by inferred personal preferences within the available resource budget.
summary.tldr: CUPID uses strategically chosen model comparisons to infer user preferences and select suitable LLMs under cost and time budgets.

title: CUPID in the Model Zoo: Online Matchmaking for Selecting Your Dream LLM

abstract: State space models (SSMs) have emerged as efficient linear-time alternatives to attention for long-sequence modeling. However, existing SSMs often suffer from instability and memory degradation over extended horizons due to poorly conditioned first-order updates and unbalanced update geometry. We introduce MuonSSM, a general framework that stabilizes SSM training by explicitly conditioning the geometry of memory updates rather than the recurrent transition matrix. MuonSSM augments SSMs with a momentum-based pathway and a lightweight Newton-Schulz transformation on low-rank input injections, yielding bounded and spectrally conditioned updates while preserving parallel scan complexity. Theory shows that MuonSSM improves gradient propagation, mitigates spectral amplification, and enriches memory representations over long horizons. Extensive experiments across language, vision, and time-series benchmarks show consistent gains in accuracy, robustness, and long-context performance when integrated into diverse SSM backbones. These results establish geometric conditioning of updates as a principled pathway to stable, scalable sequence modeling.

paragraphs: State space models process long sequences efficiently, but their memory can degrade or become unstable over extended horizons. MuonSSM targets the geometry of the updates entering memory. The paper attributes difficulties in existing models to poorly conditioned first-order updates and an imbalance in how those updates act across directions.

The framework adds a momentum-based pathway and applies a lightweight Newton-Schulz transformation to low-rank input injections. These operations produce bounded updates with better spectral conditioning while preserving parallel scan complexity. The intervention focuses on how new information changes memory, rather than conditioning the recurrent transition matrix itself.

The theoretical analysis shows improved gradient propagation, reduced spectral amplification, and richer long-horizon memory representations. Experiments across language, vision, and time-series tasks report consistent improvements in accuracy, robustness, and long-context performance when the framework is integrated into diverse SSM backbones. Together, these findings support conditioning memory updates as a general design approach for more stable sequence modeling.
summary.tldr: MuonSSM conditions incoming memory updates to improve state space model stability and long-context performance while preserving parallel scan complexity.

title: MuonSSM: Orthogonalizing State Space Models for Sequence Modeling

abstract: Neural compression is currently dominated by Nonlinear Transform Coding (NTC), which maps data to real-valued latents via continuous transforms. Despite its success, NTC suffers from train-test mismatch due to non-differentiable quantization, a "smoothness bias" inherent in continuous transforms that precludes optimality for certain sources, and a loss of "shaping gain" due to its use of scalar quantization. We propose SoftBinary Coding (SBC), an end-to-end learning paradigm that bypasses these limitations by using a stochastic binary latent space. In the spirit of vector quantization, SBC employs discrete representations and compresses them through a novel fast binary channel simulation scheme, for which we provide a proof of rate optimality. Experimental gains on information-theoretic sources address NTC’s limitations both theoretically and practically, establishing discrete binary structures as a viable path toward reaching optimal rate–distortion bounds. Surprisingly, SBC also achieves state-of-the-art performance on vector quantization of i.i.d. sources, exceeding Trellis Coded Quantization of the Gaussian source.

paragraphs: Neural compression commonly transforms data into continuous latent values and then quantizes them for storage. This paper identifies three problems with that approach: quantization creates a mismatch between training and use, continuous transforms impose a smoothness bias that prevents optimality for certain sources, and scalar quantization loses potential shaping gains.

SoftBinary Coding replaces those continuous latents with stochastic binary representations. It learns end to end and compresses the representations through a new fast binary channel-simulation scheme. The authors prove rate optimality for that scheme. The design follows the spirit of vector quantization, using discrete representations to address limitations of the conventional transform-and-quantize pipeline.

Experiments on information-theoretic sources show gains that address the stated limitations both analytically and practically. The method also reports state-of-the-art vector quantization performance on independent, identically distributed sources, exceeding Trellis Coded Quantization for a Gaussian source. These findings support binary latent structures as a route toward optimal rate–distortion performance. The rate-optimality proof concerns the channel-simulation scheme, while the broader compression benefits are also supported by the reported source-specific experiments.
summary.tldr: SoftBinary Coding uses stochastic binary latents and rate-optimal channel simulation to address limitations of continuous-transform neural compression.

title: SoftBinary Coding: A New Information-Theoretic Paradigm for Neural Compression via Fast Channel Simulation

abstract: LLM-based agents already operate in production across many industries, yet we lack an understanding of what technical methods make deployments successful. We present the first systematic study of Measuring Agents in Production, MAP, using first-hand data from agent developers. We conducted 20 case studies via in-depth interviews and surveyed 86 deployed systems practitioners across 26 domains. We investigate why organizations build agents, how they build them, how they evaluate them, and their top development challenges. Our study finds that production agents are built using simple, controllable approaches: 68% execute at most 10 steps before human intervention, 70% rely on prompting off-the-shelf models instead of weight tuning, and 74% depend primarily on human evaluation. Reliability (consistent correct behavior over time) remains the top development challenge, which practitioners currently address through systems-level design. MAP documents the current state of production agents, providing the research community with visibility into deployment realities and underexplored research avenues.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how language-model agents are actually built and evaluated in production. Rather than proposing a new agent architecture, Measuring Agents in Production gathers first-hand evidence from developers. The study includes 20 detailed interview-based case studies and a survey of 86 practitioners working on deployed systems across 26 domains.

The findings emphasize relatively simple approaches that preserve control. In the study, 68% execute no more than ten steps before human intervention, while 70% use prompting with off-the-shelf models instead of tuning model weights. Human evaluation is also central: 74% depend primarily on it. These observations describe the surveyed deployments rather than establishing a universal recipe for successful agents.

Reliability, defined as consistently correct behavior over time, emerges as the leading development challenge. Practitioners currently respond through systems-level design. By examining motivations, implementation choices, evaluation practices, and development obstacles together, MAP provides a grounded picture of deployment work. Its value for researchers is to make practical priorities visible, particularly the importance of controllability and dependable behavior in the systems represented.
summary.tldr: A study of deployed agents finds that simple, controllable designs and human evaluation are common, while reliability remains the leading challenge.

title: Measuring Agents in Production

abstract: Reward models are fundamental to Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), yet real-world datasets are inevitably corrupted by noisy feedback. Conventional training objectives tend to overfit these errors, while existing denoising approaches often rely on homogeneous noise assumptions that fail to capture the complexity of linguistic preferences. To handle these challenges, we propose SelectiveRM, a framework grounded in optimal transport. We first devise a Joint Consistency Discrepancy to align the distribution of model predictions with preference data. Furthermore, to address the limitation of strict mass conservation which compels the model to fit outliers, we incorporate a Mass Relaxation mechanism via partial transport. This enables the autonomous exclusion of samples with noisy feedback that contradict semantic consistency. Theoretically, we demonstrate that SelectiveRM optimizes a tighter upper bound on the unobserved clean risk. Extensive experiments validate that our approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reward models learn which language-model responses people prefer, but incorrect preference labels can distort that learning. Standard objectives may fit those errors, while denoising approaches that assume uniform noise can miss the complexity of language preferences. SelectiveRM uses optimal transport to align model predictions with preference data while allowing inconsistent feedback to be excluded.

The framework first introduces a Joint Consistency Discrepancy for comparing prediction and preference distributions. It then relaxes the strict mass-conservation requirement of transport. Under partial transport, every sample need not participate in the alignment, so noisy feedback that conflicts with semantic consistency can be left out rather than forcing the model to fit it.

The authors show theoretically that SelectiveRM optimizes a tighter upper bound on the risk associated with the unobserved clean data. Experiments also report significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks. Together, these findings support selective distribution alignment as a way to train reward models from imperfect feedback while reducing pressure to explain inconsistent examples.
summary.tldr: SelectiveRM uses partial optimal transport to exclude semantically inconsistent feedback while training language-model reward models.

title: Optimal Transport for LLM Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback

abstract: We propose a simple, scalable algorithm based on stochastic interpolants for sampling from unnormalized densities and for fine-tuning generative models. The approach, Tilt Matching, arises from a dynamical equation relating the flow matching velocity to one targeting the same distribution tilted by a reward, implicitly solving a stochastic optimal control problem. The resulting velocity inherits the regularity of stochastic interpolant transports while minimizing an objective with strictly lower variance than flow matching itself. The update to the velocity field can be interpreted as the sum of all joint cumulants between the interpolant velocity and the reward, and to first order is their covariance. The method requires neither reward gradients nor backpropagation through trajectories of the flow or diffusion. We empirically demonstrate that the approach is efficient and highly scalable, providing state-of-the-art results on sampling under Lennard-Jones systems and competitive performance for fine-tuning Stable Diffusion, without requiring reward multipliers. The framework also applies directly to tilting few-step flow map models.

paragraphs: Tilt Matching provides a method for sampling from unnormalized densities and adapting generative models toward rewards. It starts from stochastic interpolants and relates the velocity used in flow matching to a velocity targeting a reward-tilted distribution. This relationship implicitly solves a stochastic optimal control problem, connecting reward-directed generation with transport dynamics.

The update can be expressed through joint cumulants of velocity and reward; at first order, it is their covariance. Experiments report state-of-the-art sampling results for Lennard-Jones systems and competitive Stable Diffusion fine-tuning, without requiring reward multipliers. The framework also applies directly to few-step flow-map models. These findings support a scalable way to modify generative dynamics using reward information, with both the mathematical formulation and the experiments emphasizing efficient updates.
summary.tldr: Tilt Matching adapts generative dynamics toward rewards without reward gradients or trajectory backpropagation, supporting scalable sampling and fine-tuning.

title: Tilt Matching for Scalable Sampling and Fine-Tuning

abstract: High-performance GPU kernels are critical for efficient LLM serving, yet their optimization remains a bottleneck requiring deep system expertise. While code LLMs show promise in generating functionally correct code, kernel optimization is intrinsically a search problem over a vast optimization space. This fundamental mismatch prevents existing LLM agents from efficiently exploring the optimization space for diverse hardware and compute patterns. To bridge the gap, we present KernelBand, a framework that formulates kernel optimization as a Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem, explicitly balancing exploration and exploitation to unlock the potential of code LLMs. To navigate the infinite arm space of optimization strategies applied to candidate kernels, we design two key mechanisms: a hardware-aware pruning strategy via profiling bounds and a runtime-behavior clustering algorithm that leverages Lipschitz continuity. Extensive experiments on TritonBench-G with three GPU architectures and four code LLMs show that KernelBand consistently outperforms the strongest available agent baseline, achieving up to 1.91$\times$ geometric mean speedup over correctly optimized kernels with 39–140% relative improvement in Fast@1 success rate. Our code is available at https://github.com/TongmingLAIC/KernelBand.

paragraphs: Writing a GPU kernel that produces the right answer is different from finding one that runs efficiently on a particular device. KernelBand treats this second task as a search problem over possible optimization strategies. Its purpose is to guide code-generating language models through that space while accounting for hardware and computation patterns.

The framework formulates optimization as a multi-armed bandit problem, balancing attempts at new strategies with further use of promising ones. Because the possible strategies form an unbounded search space, it adds two mechanisms: pruning based on hardware profiling bounds and clustering based on runtime behavior. The clustering uses Lipschitz continuity to organize the search.

Experiments cover TritonBench-G, three GPU architectures, and four code language models. KernelBand consistently outperforms the strongest available agent baseline, reporting up to a 1.91-fold geometric mean speedup over correctly optimized kernels and 39–140% relative improvements in Fast@1 success rate. These results support structured, hardware-aware search as a way to turn code-generation ability into more effective kernel optimization.
summary.tldr: KernelBand guides LLM kernel optimization with hardware-aware bandit search, improving speed and optimization success across the tested GPUs and code models.

title: KernelBand: Steering LLM-based Kernel Optimization via Hardware-Aware Multi-Armed Bandits

abstract: In this paper, we provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and its momentum variants (Polyak Heavy-Ball and Nesterov) for tracking time-varying optima under strong convexity and smoothness. Our finite-time bounds reveal a sharp decomposition of tracking error into transient, noise-induced, and drift-induced components. This decomposition exposes a fundamental trade-off: while momentum is often used as a gradient-smoothing heuristic, under distribution shift it incurs an explicit drift-amplification penalty that diverges as the momentum parameter $\beta$ approaches 1, yielding systematic tracking lag. We complement these upper bounds with minimax lower bounds under gradient-variation constraints, proving this momentum-induced tracking penalty is not an analytical artifact but an information-theoretic barrier: in drift-dominated regimes, momentum is unavoidably worse because stale-gradient averaging forces systematic lag. Our results provide theoretical grounding for the empirical instability of momentum in dynamic settings and precisely delineate regime boundaries where vanilla SGD provably outperforms its accelerated counterparts.

paragraphs: Momentum combines gradient information over time, but old information can become misleading when the optimum moves. This paper analyzes stochastic gradient descent and its Polyak Heavy-Ball and Nesterov momentum variants in that tracking setting. The analysis assumes strongly convex, smooth objectives, making the question precise within a defined class of changing optimization problems.

Finite-time bounds divide tracking error into three parts: the transient effect of initialization, the contribution of stochastic noise, and the contribution of optimum drift. This exposes a specific cost of momentum under distribution shift. Its drift-amplification penalty diverges as the momentum parameter approaches one, producing systematic lag because the update continues to average stale gradients.

Lower bounds under gradient-variation constraints show that this penalty reflects a genuine information-theoretic barrier rather than looseness in the upper-bound analysis. In drift-dominated regimes, momentum is provably worse. The paper identifies regime boundaries where ordinary SGD outperforms its accelerated counterparts, providing a theoretical explanation for instability observed with momentum in dynamic settings without claiming that momentum is inferior in every regime.
summary.tldr: Under strong convexity and smoothness, momentum provably amplifies tracking lag enough for ordinary SGD to outperform it in drift-dominated regimes.

title: On the Provable Suboptimality of Momentum SGD in Nonstationary Stochastic Optimization

abstract: Modern neural classifiers can achieve remarkable predictive performance, yet often suffer from miscalibration. In this paper, we introduce a unified calibration framework applicable to arbitrary distribution-based classifiers. The proposed calibration objective guarantees a monotone Probably Approximately Individually Calibrated (mPAIC) predictor, which theoretically implies the properties of a Probably Approximately Calibrated Classifier (PACC) with explicit error bounds. To enable stable and effective optimization, we further devise a Decoupled Dual-Stream Optimization (DDSO) strategy with gradient detachment to reconcile discriminative representation learning and continuous calibration. Notably, our framework bridges calibration paradigms, supporting flexible deployment either as an end-to-end pre-calibration objective or as a lightweight post-calibration adapter. Extensive experiments across nine real-world datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms strong baselines, achieving superior performance on both accuracy and multi-level calibration.

paragraphs: A classifier can predict labels accurately while assigning confidence values that do not reliably reflect its correctness. This paper proposes a unified calibration framework for arbitrary distribution-based classifiers. Its aim is to connect a mathematically specified form of individual calibration with reliable classifier behavior, while keeping the method usable within practical neural-network training.

The calibration objective guarantees a monotone Probably Approximately Individually Calibrated predictor, abbreviated mPAIC. The authors show that this property implies Probably Approximately Calibrated Classifier guarantees with explicit error bounds. The probabilistic and approximate qualifications are part of the result: the framework supplies bounded calibration claims rather than asserting perfect confidence estimates for every prediction.

For optimization, Decoupled Dual-Stream Optimization uses gradient detachment to reconcile learning discriminative representations with continuous calibration. The framework can serve either as an end-to-end training objective or as a lightweight adapter applied after training. Across nine real-world datasets, the authors report improvements over strong baselines in both accuracy and calibration at multiple levels, supporting the framework's practical use alongside its theoretical guarantees.
summary.tldr: A calibration framework links individual-level guarantees to classifier reliability and improves accuracy and calibration across nine datasets.

title: From Individual Calibration to Reliable Classifiers: ALD Parameterization with mPAIC Guarantees

abstract: The alignment of large language models with human preferences is commonly achieved through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or Direct Preference Optimization. However, these methods are vulnerable to the significant noise prevalent in real-world preference datasets. To address this critical issue, we present a theoretical framework for unbiased alignment, introducing the Unbiased Reward Model (URM) loss and the Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization (UDPO) loss. By mathematically correcting the distortion induced by preference noise, our novel objectives enable unbiased model training directly from noisy datasets, without requiring clean ground-truth supervision. We provide rigorous theoretical analyses demonstrating that our methods are noise-tolerant, parameter downward compatible, and classification-calibrated. Comprehensive experiments across diverse datasets demonstrate that our approaches outperform state-of-the-art baselines. Code available at: https://github.com/cswjl/unbiased-alignment.

paragraphs: Language-model alignment often learns from comparisons expressing which response people prefer. Real preference datasets contain substantial noise, which can distort training through reward models or Direct Preference Optimization. This paper develops a theoretical framework for correcting that distortion within the training objective, allowing learning directly from noisy preferences.

The authors introduce two losses: Unbiased Reward Model loss for reward-model training and Unbiased Direct Preference Optimization loss for direct alignment. Both mathematically adjust for preference-noise distortion without requiring clean ground-truth supervision. Their analyses establish noise tolerance, parameter downward compatibility, and classification calibration. The correction is therefore presented with formal properties as well as a practical training objective.

Experiments across diverse datasets show the proposed approaches outperforming state-of-the-art baselines. The work’s significance is that unreliable preference labels can be addressed through the loss used to learn from them. Its stated theoretical contribution provides a basis for unbiased alignment within the proposed framework, while the experiments demonstrate practical benefits in the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: URM and UDPO correct preference-noise distortion in alignment losses, enabling theoretically unbiased training without clean ground-truth supervision.

title: Unbiased Alignment for Large Language Models with Noisy Preferences

abstract: State-of-the-art single-image 3D reconstruction methods often rely on complex hybrid architectures and loss functions, or compress geometry into latent spaces in order to leverage pre-trained latent diffusion models. In this work, we show that such architectural overhead and intricate loss formulations are unnecessary. We introduce a minimalist pixel-space Diffusion Transformer, built on a plain ViT, that operates directly on raw 3D point map patches and is conditioned on image tokens from a pre-trained DINOv3. Unlike existing latent diffusion approaches, we train our diffusion backbone entirely from scratch, eliminating the need for point map tokenizers. Despite its simplicity, our approach surpasses complex latent-based diffusion models while remaining significantly simpler than hybrid alternatives. Notably, it produces sharper geometric structure and is more robust in highly ambiguous regions, such as transparent objects.

paragraphs: Recovering three-dimensional geometry from one image often involves elaborate architectures or compressed geometry representations. PointDiT investigates whether a much simpler diffusion model can perform this task directly. Its target representation is a raw 3D point map, organized into patches instead of being passed through a separate learned point-map tokenizer.

The model uses a plain Vision Transformer as its diffusion backbone and conditions geometry generation on image tokens from a pretrained DINOv3. The diffusion backbone itself is trained from scratch. This distinction matters: the approach uses pretrained visual information while avoiding dependence on a pretrained latent diffusion backbone or a tokenizer for compressing geometry.

The authors report that this design outperforms complex latent-based diffusion approaches while remaining considerably simpler than hybrid alternatives. They also report sharper geometric structure and stronger performance in ambiguous regions, including transparent objects. The findings show that direct point-map modeling can be competitive in this setting, challenging the need for the architectural and loss-function complexity used by the compared approaches.
summary.tldr: PointDiT estimates 3D geometry directly with a simple point-map diffusion transformer, reporting sharper results than complex latent-based approaches.

title: PointDiT: Pixel-Space Diffusion for Monocular Geometry Estimation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained at significant computational and data cost, making them valuable intellectual property (IP). Existing IP verification methods primarily rely either on invasive watermarking that degrades model utility, or on superficial behavioral signatures disrupted by fine-tuning and model merging. This apparent trade-off between model utility and IP protection has constrained practical deployment. We challenge this trade-off and propose CircuitPrint, a non-invasive IP fingerprinting framework that enables robust verification through standard model queries by leveraging stable internal computational circuits of LLMs. We show that these circuits function as a persistent computational backbone across model derivatives, allowing them to serve as stable fingerprints for distinguishing LLMs. Building on this stability, CircuitPrint constructs IP signatures by identifying mechanistically essential supernodes that causally produce specific predictions within these circuits. Specifically, trigger queries are synthesized to replicate the internal suppression of these supernodes, thereby inducing distinctive and observable output shifts. Experimental results demonstrate that CircuitPrint substantially outperforms existing baselines while remaining robust under aggressive fine-tuning and model merging, effectively resolving this trade-off without altering model parameters.

paragraphs: CircuitPrint addresses verification of language-model intellectual property without modifying model parameters. The paper argues that existing approaches face a difficult choice: invasive watermarks can reduce utility, while surface-level behavioral signatures can change during fine-tuning or model merging. It instead seeks identifying evidence in internal computations that persist across model derivatives.

The framework identifies mechanistically essential groups of components, called supernodes, that causally contribute to particular predictions. It then synthesizes trigger queries intended to reproduce the effect of suppressing those supernodes internally. The resulting output shifts form a signature that can be checked through ordinary model queries, connecting an internal causal mechanism to an externally observable response.

The authors report that the relevant circuits remain stable enough across derivatives to distinguish models. Experiments show substantial improvements over existing baselines and robustness under aggressive fine-tuning and merging. These results support computational circuits as a useful basis for persistent fingerprints. Because the framework leaves parameters unchanged, its reported protection does not require embedding a watermark through changes to the model itself.
summary.tldr: CircuitPrint uses query-visible signatures of stable internal computations to verify model identity without modifying parameters.

title: CircuitPrint: Mechanistic Circuit Fingerprints for Large Language Models

abstract: In distributed machine learning, efficiently training across multiple agents with heterogeneous data distributions remains a central challenge. We address the problem of stochastic, strongly convex distributed optimization by applying accelerated gradient ascent to the dual variables and multi-step stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to the primal variables in the Lagrangian formulation. This approach naturally enables local computation, as the inner SGD loops require no inter-agent communication. We prove that the method converges for any number of local updates, attaining the optimal communication complexity when local computation is sufficient. Our analysis builds on an inexact accelerated gradient framework, where the partial gradient of the Lagrangian with respect to the dual variables is treated as an inexact gradient of the dual function. A notable byproduct of this framework is an algorithm that achieves optimal reproducibility guarantees under biased gradient estimates.

paragraphs: Distributed training must balance work performed locally against communication between agents, especially when their data distributions differ. This paper studies that tradeoff for stochastic, strongly convex optimization. It develops a method that combines accelerated updates to dual variables with several stochastic gradient descent steps on the primal variables in a Lagrangian formulation.

The local gradient steps require no communication between agents. To analyze their effect, the authors view the resulting partial gradient with respect to the dual variables as an approximate gradient of the dual objective. This connects incomplete local optimization to an inexact accelerated gradient framework, allowing the analysis to account for the errors introduced by local updates.

The method is proved to converge for any number of local updates. It reaches optimal communication complexity when enough local computation is available, so that stronger conclusion is explicitly conditional. The same analytical framework also yields an algorithm with optimal reproducibility guarantees under biased gradient estimates, extending its relevance beyond the communication tradeoff.
summary.tldr: An inexact-gradient analysis supports accelerated distributed optimization with local updates and conditionally optimal communication complexity.

title: Accelerated Dual Method for Distributed Optimization: An Inexact-Gradient View of Local Updates

abstract: The “thinking with images” paradigm has led multimodal large language models to generate intermediate visual steps—such as cropping, annotation, spatial localization, and sketches—to enhance high-resolution perception and complex reasoning. However, existing multimodal Process Reward Models (PRMs) evaluate only textual reasoning and cannot judge the correctness of these visual steps, creating a key gap when visual reasoning is essential for solving tasks. We propose Discriminative Visual Process Reward Model (DiscPRM), a multimodal PRM that jointly evaluates textual and visual intermediate steps by modeling visual reasoning trajectories, image operations, and text-image consistency. To support this, we build VTReward-100K, a dataset of step-by-step visual reasoning sequences with supervision. Experiments show that using DiscPRM for Best-of-N process supervision substantially improves multimodal reasoning performance on tasks requiring visual intermediate steps, achieving over 5% gains across benchmarks. We further introduce VABench, the first benchmark for evaluating PRMs on visual reasoning error detection. We hope this work can provide foundational support for advancing the emerging direction of visual–textual process reward.

paragraphs: Some multimodal models reason through intermediate images as well as text, using crops, annotations, spatial localization, or sketches. Evaluating only their written reasoning leaves a gap: a textual explanation can depend on an incorrect visual operation. This paper develops a process reward model that can assess both kinds of intermediate steps.

DiscPRM evaluates visual reasoning trajectories, the image operations within them, and consistency between text and images. To train this capability, the authors construct VTReward-100K, a dataset containing supervised sequences of visual reasoning steps. The focus is on judging the process as it unfolds, including whether the visual evidence and accompanying explanation fit together.

When used to supervise Best-of-N selection among candidate reasoning processes, DiscPRM produces reported gains of over 5% across benchmarks requiring visual intermediate steps. The paper also introduces VABench to evaluate process reward models on detecting visual reasoning errors. Together, the model, training data, and benchmark extend process supervision to reasoning whose correctness depends on what happens inside intermediate images.
summary.tldr: DiscPRM evaluates intermediate visual and textual reasoning steps, improving candidate selection on tasks that require thinking with images.

title: Discriminative Visual Process Rewards for Scaling Thinking at Test-Time with Images

abstract: Token-level reweighting is a simple yet effective mechanism for controlling supervised fine-tuning, but common indicators are largely one-dimensional: the ground-truth probability reflects downstream alignment, while token entropy reflects intrinsic uncertainty induced by the pre-training prior. Ignoring entropy can misidentify noisy or easily replaceable tokens as learning-critical, while ignoring probability fails to reflect target-specific alignment. RankTuner introduces a probability–entropy calibration signal, the Relative Rank Indicator, by comparing the rank of the ground-truth token with its expected rank under the predictiondiction distribution. The inverse indicator is used as a token-wise Relative Scale to reweight the fine-tuning objective, focusing updates on truly under-learned tokens without over-penalizing intrinsically uncertain positions. Experiments on multiple backbones show consistent improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, transfer gains on out-of-distribution reasoning, and pre code generation performance over probability- or entropy-only reweighting baselines.
