Ignoring entropy can misidentify noisy or easily replaceable tokens as learning-critical, while ignoring probability fails to reflect target-specific alignment. RankTuner introduces a probability–entropy calibration signal, the Relative Rank Indicator, by comparing the rank of the ground-truth token with its expected rank under the predictiondiction distribution. The inverse indicator is used as a token-wise Relative Scale to reweight the fine-tuning objective, focusing updates on truly under-learned tokens without over-penalizing intrinsically uncertain positions. Experiments on multiple backbones show consistent improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, transfer gains on out-of-distribution reasoning, and pre code generation performance over probability- or entropy-only reweighting baselines.

paragraphs: During supervised fine-tuning, weighting individual tokens determines where a model spends its learning effort. The probability assigned to the correct token indicates alignment with the target, while prediction entropy describes uncertainty. The paper argues that either signal alone can misallocate effort by overlooking the other aspect of a prediction.

RankTuner combines these perspectives through a Relative Rank Indicator. It compares the correct token’s rank with the expected rank under the model’s predicted distribution. The inverse of this indicator becomes a token-specific scale on the training objective. This calibration is intended to emphasize tokens that are under-learned while avoiding excessive penalties at positions where uncertainty is intrinsic.

Experiments across multiple model backbones report consistent improvements on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and transfer gains on reasoning outside the training distribution. The abstract also reports better code-generation performance than probability-only or entropy-only weighting baselines. These findings support evaluating a target token relative to the surrounding predictive distribution when deciding how strongly it should influence a fine-tuning update.
summary.tldr: RankTuner calibrates token-level fine-tuning weights using the correct token’s rank relative to the model’s predictive distribution.

title: Probability-Entropy Calibration: An Elastic Indicator for Adaptive Fine-tuning

abstract: The maximal coding rate reduction ($\text{MCR}^2$) objective is proposed for learning low-dimensional subspace representations and for principled deep model design, where layer structures are derived by unrolling its optimization steps. However, existing methods motivated by this objective do not fully adhere to design principles implied by the $\text{MCR}^2$ gradient, which weakens the principled and interpretable foundations of the resulting models. In this work, we introduce PACEAttention, a novel principled attention mechanism inspired by the geometric insight of $\text{MCR}^2$, whose gradient-based updates move features along directions shaped by the underlying low-dimensional feature structure. Our method captures this structure by leveraging randomization to guide feature updates. This principled construction enables the resulting PACENet to exhibit enhanced interpretability, with different heads attending to distinct image regions and capturing fine-grained structures under simple supervised training. Experiments demonstrate that PACEAttention achieves superior performance and more stable scalability than previous principled modules while remaining low complexity.

paragraphs: The maximal coding rate reduction objective, MCR², supports learning representations organized into low-dimensional subspaces. It can also guide neural-network design by turning optimization steps into layers. The paper argues that existing designs inspired by this objective do not fully follow the implications of its gradient, weakening the connection between the mathematical principle and the resulting architecture.

PACEAttention uses the geometry of that gradient to guide feature updates. The relevant directions depend on the low-dimensional structure within the features, and the mechanism uses randomization to capture that structure. Its attention design is therefore tied to how the objective suggests features should move, providing a more explicit basis for interpreting the computation.

The resulting PACENet develops attention heads that focus on distinct image regions and capture fine-grained structures under simple supervised training. Experiments show better performance and more stable scaling than previous principled modules while retaining low complexity. These findings connect the proposed geometric construction with both useful visual organization and empirical performance, within the comparisons reported by the authors.
summary.tldr: PACEAttention uses MCR² geometry and randomized structure estimation to build efficient attention with interpretable visual features.

title: PACEAttention: Principled and Adaptive Feature Compression-Expansion Grounded in the Geometry of $\textMCR^2$

abstract: Many robot control problems of practical importance, including operational space control, can be reformulated as immediate reward reinforcement learning problems. However, few of the known optimization or reinforcement learning algorithms can be used in online learning control for robots, as they are either prohibitively slow, do not scale to interesting domains of complex robots, or require trying out policies generated by random search, which are infeasible for a physical system. Using a generalization of the EM-base reinforcement learning framework suggested by Dayan & Hinton, we reduce the problem of learning with immediate rewards to a reward-weighted regression problem with an adaptive, integrated reward transformation for faster convergence. The resulting algorithm is efficient, learns smoothly without dangerous jumps in solution space, and works well in applications of complex high degreeof-freedom robots.

paragraphs: The paper addresses robot control problems that can be reformulated as immediate-reward reinforcement learning, including operational space control. Online robot learning places practical demands on optimization: updates must be efficient, scale to complex robots, and avoid requiring trials of policies generated through infeasible random searches on a physical system.

The authors generalize an expectation-maximization-based reinforcement learning framework to reduce immediate-reward learning to reward-weighted regression. This reformulation makes regression the central learning operation. It also incorporates an adaptive reward transformation intended to accelerate convergence, treating the handling of rewards as an integrated part of the algorithm.

The resulting method is reported to be efficient, to learn smoothly without dangerous jumps in solution space, and to work well on complex robots with many degrees of freedom. These claims address the computational and behavioral requirements motivating the work. The contribution applies to the stated immediate-reward formulation, showing how that structure can support a practical learning procedure for demanding robot-control applications.
summary.tldr: Reward-weighted regression with an adaptive reward transformation provides efficient, smooth learning for robot-control problems formulated with immediate rewards.

title: Reinforcement learning by reward-weighted regression for operational space control

abstract: Graph data such as chemical compounds and XML documents are getting more common in many application domains. A main difficulty of graph data processing lies in the intrinsic high dimensionality of graphs, namely, when a graph is represented as a binary feature vector of indicators of all possible subgraph patterns, the dimensionality gets too large for usual statistical methods. We propose an efficient method to select a small number of salient patterns by regularization path tracking. The generation of useless patterns is minimized by progressive extension of the search space. In experiments, it is shown that our technique is considerably more efficient than a simpler approach based on frequent substructure mining.

paragraphs: Graphs can represent objects such as chemical compounds and XML documents, but turning them into features creates a major size problem. One possible representation records whether each possible subgraph pattern is present. Because the collection of possible patterns is enormous, the resulting binary feature space can become too large for ordinary statistical methods.

This paper proposes selecting a small set of salient patterns by tracking a regularization path. The approach connects pattern selection with changes in regularization, which controls how complex the selected representation can become. Crucially, it expands the pattern search space progressively, minimizing the generation of patterns that will prove useless.

The computational strategy therefore addresses both which patterns to retain and how much of the possible pattern space to generate. Experiments show considerably greater efficiency than a simpler approach based on frequent substructure mining. The stated finding supports the value of coordinating pattern generation with regularization-based selection, rather than treating the huge collection of candidate graph features as something that must all be available in advance.
summary.tldr: Regularization-path tracking selects salient graph patterns while progressively expanding the search space to reduce unnecessary pattern generation.

title: Entire regularization paths for graph data

abstract: Algorithms for learning to rank Web documents usually assume a document's relevance is independent of other documents. This leads to learned ranking functions that produce rankings with redundant results. In contrast, user studies have shown that diversity at high ranks is often preferred. We present two new learning algorithms that directly learn a diverse ranking of documents based on users' clicking behavior. We show that these algorithms minimize abandonment, or alternatively, maximize the probability that a relevant document is found in the top k positions of a ranking. We show that one of our algorithms asymptotically achieves the best possible payoff obtainable in polynomial time even as user's interests change. The other performs better empirically when user interests are static, and is still theoretically near-optimal in that case.

This leads to learned ranking functions that produce rankings with redundant results. In contrast, user studies have shown that diversity at high ranks is often preferred. We present two new learning algorithms that directly learn a diverse ranking of documents based on users' clicking behavior. We show that these algorithms minimize abandonment, or alternatively, maximize the probability that a relevant document is found in the top k positions of a ranking. We show that one of our algorithms asymptotically achieves the best possible payoff obtainable in polynomial time even as user's interests change. The other performs better empirically when user interests are static, and is still theoretically near-optimal in that case.

paragraphs: A document can be relevant on its own while adding little to a ranking already filled with similar results. The paper argues that treating relevance as independent across documents can therefore produce redundancy. It develops two algorithms that learn diverse rankings directly from users’ clicking behavior, motivated by users’ preference for variety near the top.

The algorithms target reduced abandonment or, alternatively, a higher probability of finding a relevant document among the first k positions. This frames ranking quality around what the collection of highly placed documents provides to a user. Click behavior supplies the feedback used to learn that collection.

The two algorithms have different strengths. One asymptotically reaches the best payoff achievable in polynomial time even when user interests change. The other performs better empirically when interests remain static and has a near-optimality guarantee in that setting. The results distinguish adaptation to changing interests from stronger observed performance under stable interests, while preserving diversity as the common objective.
summary.tldr: Two click-driven ranking algorithms learn diversity, with different theoretical and empirical strengths for changing versus static user interests.
